0.title: The LORD Fights for His People: The Book of Joshua
0.overview:
The book of Joshua opens with a death and a charge. Moses, the servant of the LORD, is dead — and the man who could split the sea, who spoke with God face to face, who carried a stiff-necked people through forty years of wilderness, lies buried in an unmarked grave on the far side of the Jordan. And God says to Joshua, 'Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise' (1:2). The law could lead Israel to the edge of the land, but the law could not bring them in. Moses must die; another must take them across. And the name of that other is Yeshua — Joshua — the very name that, centuries later, the angel would give to a child born in Bethlehem: 'You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people' (Matt. 1:21). The whole book is a shadow cast forward by the cross. What Moses (the law) could not accomplish, Jesus (grace) does. He brings us into the rest.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Old Testament and the first of the so-called Former Prophets in the Hebrew canon. It records the conquest of Canaan, the division of the land among the twelve tribes, and the covenant renewals that bracket the nation's entry into its inheritance. The driving theological claim of the book is announced in its title and proven on every page: the LORD fights for his people. Israel does not earn the land; God gives it. The walls of Jericho do not fall by siege engines but by trumpets and a shout, so that no flesh may boast. As Calvin observed, the conquest is a prolonged sermon on the faithfulness of God to his promise to Abraham — the down payment on a redemption that reaches its consummation in Christ.

Modern readers stumble over the violence of the conquest — the herem, the devotion of cities to destruction. We must not soften it dishonestly, nor must we read it as a charter for human aggression. It is, rather, a localized, time-bound, divinely commanded judgment upon a civilization whose iniquity had, in God's patient reckoning, finally become full (Gen. 15:16). The Canaanite cult burned infants to Molech. The conquest is an eruption of final judgment into history — a sober preview of the day when the King of kings returns with a sword from his mouth (Rev. 19). And astonishingly, in the middle of this judgment stands Rahab the Canaanite prostitute, saved by a scarlet cord, grafted into the line of the Messiah. Judgment and mercy meet, as they always meet, at the place of the blood.

Read Joshua, then, not as ancient military history but as gospel. Hear in 'Be strong and courageous' the voice that says 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' (Heb. 13:5). See in the Jordan your baptism, in the ark your Christ going before, in the cities of refuge your only hiding place, and in the rest that Israel entered the deeper rest that 'remains for the people of God' (Heb. 4:9). The God who was faithful to Israel — of whom it could be said, 'Not one word of all the good promises had failed' (21:45) — is the God who keeps every promise to you in his Son.

1.title: The Commissioning of Joshua
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,<sup>2</sup>"Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel.<sup>3</sup>Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.<sup>4</sup>From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory.<sup>5</sup>No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.<sup>6</sup>Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.<sup>7</sup>Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.<sup>8</sup>This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.<sup>9</sup>Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua commanded the officers of the people,<sup>11</sup>"Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"<sup>12</sup>And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said,<sup>13</sup>"Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.'<sup>14</sup>Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them,<sup>15</sup>until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."<sup>16</sup>And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.<sup>17</sup>Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses!<sup>18</sup>Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
1.overview:
The book begins where the gospel begins: with a death. 'Moses my servant is dead.' The mediator of the old covenant, the man who spoke with God as a friend, is gone, and the work is unfinished. That is the law's limitation set out as a story. Moses can bring a people to the threshold; he cannot bring them in. The charge passes to a man whose name is Yeshua, the LORD saves — and the letter to the Hebrews, having watched him lead the nation over the river, says that if Joshua had given them rest, God would not later have spoken of another day (Heb. 4:8). He gets them into the land. He does not get them into the rest.

One imperative dominates the chapter. Three times God says be strong and courageous (vv. 6, 7, 9), and at the end the people say it back to Joshua (v. 18). Each time the ground of the courage is outside the man. Never 'be strong because you are capable' — always 'be strong, for you shall cause this people to inherit,' and 'be strong, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.' Courage here is commanded rather than felt, and it rests on an outcome that has already been decided.

The middle command is the one nobody expects. The most courageous thing required of a general on the eve of a war is to keep a book: to have it in his mouth, meditate on it day and night, and turn from it neither to the right hand nor to the left (vv. 7-8). Before a plan is drawn or a sword is issued, the campaign is located in the soul of one man who reads.

The chapter ends in logistics and in loyalty. Provisions are packed, a deadline is set, and the tribes who already hold land east of the Jordan are told to leave it and fight for their brothers until everyone is home. Nobody in this book enters his rest alone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens on a grave. Moses is dead, and God's first word to his successor is not consolation but a marching order: arise, go over this Jordan (vv. 1-2). The land is spoken of as already handed over — I have given, past tense, before a foot has touched it (v. 3) — and its borders are sketched on a scale Israel will never occupy in Joshua's lifetime (v. 4). Then the promise everything else rests on: I will not leave you or forsake you (v. 5). Three times the command comes, and each has a different anchor: be strong, for you shall cause this people to inherit (v. 6); be strong and very courageous, and keep the Book (vv. 7-8); and at the last, have I not commanded you, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Grace arrives before duty and grounds it. The land is given in verse 3 and fought for from chapter 6 onwards, which is the pattern of the whole Bible: God announces the accomplished gift and then calls his people to walk into it. Israel does not fight to earn Canaan; they fight because it is already theirs.
verseByVerse.examples: The middle command is the surprising one. The most courageous thing required of a general on the eve of a war is not to storm a wall but to keep a book — to meditate on it day and night and not turn from it to the right hand or to the left (vv. 7-8). Before a single battle plan is drawn, the campaign is located in the soul of the man who reads.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant.'

The book is hinged on a grave. The greatest figure in Israel's history is gone — the man who stood in the sea-bed, who spoke with God as a man speaks to his friend, who carried a whole nation on his back for forty years — and the work is not finished.

See how little time is allowed to pass. There is no interregnum, no committee, no anxious pause while the nation wonders what happens now. Moses dies and God speaks. There is no power vacuum in the kingdom of God, because the King does not die.

Read the two titles side by side, because the writer has put them there on purpose. Moses is the servant of the LORD, the highest description any man is given in the Old Testament. Joshua is Moses' assistant — the Hebrew word is used of the man who waits at table and carries his master's things.

That had been Joshua's job for decades. He held up Moses' arms on the hill while the battle went on below (Ex. 17:12). He stayed behind in the tent of meeting after Moses had gone back to the camp (Ex. 33:11). He stood with Caleb against ten frightened men and a nation ready to stone him (Num. 14:6-10). None of it made him famous. All of it made him ready.

His name matters more than the chapter says out loud. Joshua is Yeshua, the LORD saves — the name that would be given to a carpenter's son in Nazareth. The letter to the Hebrews makes the connection and then makes the limitation: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Heb. 4:8). This man will get them into the land. He will not get them into the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.'

God says it himself: Moses my servant is dead. The grief is not denied and not hurried. But the next word is arise, and it is the right word to a man who has been sitting down for thirty days of mourning.

There is a kind of loss that persuades a person the story has stopped. It has not. God's answer to a funeral, here, is a river and a date.

Then the tense in verse 3, which is the engine of the entire book. Not I will give you but I have given to you — before a single Israelite has crossed the water, the land is deeded over. Every battle in the next eleven chapters is fought on ground that already belongs to them.

That is the shape of the Christian life and not merely an Old Testament curiosity. Nobody fights sin in order to become a child of God; the fighting is what a child of God does about territory the Father has already put in his name.

Yet the gift has to be walked on. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread — the promise is title deed, and the foot is possession. Faith is the foot set down on the promise. A man may own a field for years and never once walk it, and there is a way of holding the promises of God that amounts to exactly that.

verseByVerse.quote: From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory. No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory. No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.'

The borders are drawn wide — south to the desert, north to Lebanon, east to the Euphrates, west to the Mediterranean. These are the boundaries God swore to Abraham (Gen. 15:18), and they are enormous.

They were never occupied. Chapter 13 opens with God telling an old man that very much land remains, and the fullest extent was reached only briefly, centuries later. The book is honest about the gap between what was promised and what was held, and the gap is not a failure in the promise; it is a signpost. Paul says the promise to Abraham was never really about a strip of coastline but that he should be heir of the world (Rom. 4:13), and the last chapters of the Bible show what that finally means.

Then verse 5, which is the bedrock the whole chapter is quarried out of: I will not leave you or forsake you.

It is worded with care. Not no one will attack you, but no man shall be able to stand before you. Not I will make it easy, but I will be with you. The promise is presence, not exemption.

The letter to the Hebrews lifts this sentence out of a general's commissioning and hands it to ordinary Christians worried about money, and the Greek piles up negatives in a way English cannot quite carry: he will never, never leave you; he will never, no never forsake you. The conclusion drawn is a matter of nerve — so we can confidently say, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear (Heb. 13:5-6).

verseByVerse.quote: Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.'

The first of three, and the first thing to see is that it is an imperative. Courage here is not a temperament some men are born with and others are not. It is commanded, which means it must be available to whoever is commanded to have it.

What makes it available is the clause attached to it. Joshua is not told to attempt the conquest and hope. He is told he shall cause this people to inherit, because God swore it to their fathers. The outcome is settled before the courage is required, and the courage is simply the appropriate response to a settled outcome.

Turn that over slowly, because most fear works the other way round. We wait to see how a thing will turn out and take our courage from the evidence. God reverses it: here is how it turns out, now be strong.

The oath reaches back through Moses to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — four hundred years and more. God's covenant memory does not shorten with time, and his word does not expire with the generation that first heard it. Joshua leads as the trustee of a promise much older than himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.'

The second command raises the temperature — very courageous — and then attaches it to something nobody expects. Not the walls of Jericho. The law.

The hardest thing asked of this man is to keep a book, and the reason is in the middle clause: do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left. Both directions are named because there are two ways off a road, and a leader in a long campaign will be pressed to take either — the shortcut on one side, the compromise on the other. Straight on is the harder walk.

'This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.'

Three organs are named, and the order is instructive: the mouth, then the mind, then the hands. The book is to be spoken, chewed over, and done.

The word for meditate is hagah, and it does not mean an empty mind. It is a low muttering, the noise of a man reading half-aloud to himself, the same word used of a lion over its prey and of the blessed man in Psalm 1. Meditation in the Bible is not emptying but gnawing.

A word about the prosperity, since the sentence is often quoted badly. The success promised is the success of this specific commission — getting a people into a land God had sworn to give them. It is not a formula for turning devotions into money. What the verse does teach, and teaches at the worst possible moment for it, is that the campaign will be won or lost long before the army forms up, in the quiet of one man's reading.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.'

The third time, and it opens with a question that lands like a hand on the shoulder: have I not commanded you? Joshua is not being encouraged. He is being reminded that he has orders.

This puts fear in an uncomfortable light. If courage is commanded, then settled fear is not merely a weakness of the nerves; it is a way of not taking God at his word. That should be said carefully — Scripture is full of frightened people who are handled gently, and God does not shout at the trembling. But it does mean that fear is answerable to something, and that a believer is allowed to argue with his own dread rather than obey it.

Then the ground, for the third time in nine verses: the LORD your God is with you. And the last two words are the best in the chapter. Not wherever I send you, which would cover obedient errands only, but wherever you go — including the places Joshua would choose badly, the valley at Ai after a bad decision, the day he believed the Gibeonites without asking.

The repetition is not God running out of things to say. It is a promise being hammered until it lodges. He knows what is in this man; he says it three times because it will need to be remembered three hundred.

The whole chapter narrows to those five words, and the New Testament does not improve on them so much as give them a face. A child is born and called Immanuel, God with us; and the last thing the risen Christ says on a hillside, to men about to be scattered across the world, is that he is with them always, to the end of the age (Matt. 1:23; 28:20). The promise made to one soldier at a river has turned out to be the standing arrangement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — The Charge to the People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God said in private, Joshua says in public within a day. The officers go through the camp with an order about food and a deadline: provisions ready, the Jordan crossed in three days (vv. 10-11). Then he turns to the two and a half tribes who already have their land east of the river and holds them to a promise: wives, children and cattle stay, and every fighting man crosses over armed ahead of his brothers (vv. 12-14) — and stays there until the LORD gives rest to the brothers as he has to them (v. 15). The chapter closes with the people's pledge, their prayer that God would be with Joshua as he was with Moses, and the words of God given back to him by the men he commands (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: No tribe rests while its brothers are still fighting. The men of Reuben and Gad have their inheritance in hand and are sent to war for somebody else's, which is plainly what Paul means by bearing one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2).
verseByVerse.examples: The last sentence of the chapter is the people saying to Joshua exactly what God said to Joshua: only be strong and courageous (v. 18). Courage in this chapter is not generated. It is handed down from God to a leader and passed along from a people back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua commanded the officers of the people, "Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Joshua commanded the officers of the people, "Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"'

The word spoken in private becomes an order in public, and the gap between them is nothing at all. God speaks; Joshua turns and mobilises the camp. Obedience that waits for better feelings has already begun to be disobedience.

The order itself is wonderfully unspiritual: prepare your provisions. Pack food. Faith in this book does not sit still waiting for God to do everything; it gets the bread ready for the journey it believes God will provide.

Both halves of the sentence are true at once and neither cancels the other. God has given the land, and the people are to pack lunches. Divine sovereignty and human effort are not rivals sharing out the work between them; the certainty of the outcome is what makes the preparation confident rather than anxious.

There is also a quiet change of era in that instruction. These are people who have eaten manna every morning for forty years and have never had to think about supplies. The manna will stop within a month of this order (5:12). God's provision does not become less; it stops being miraculous and starts being a harvest, which is how he feeds nearly everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said, "Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.' Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said, "Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you... Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you."'

Two and a half tribes had asked for the land east of the river and been granted it, on one condition (Num. 32). Joshua now collects on the condition, and the phrase he uses is remember the word.

Look at what is actually being asked. These men already have their inheritance. Their farms are allocated, their families are safe, their cattle are grazing. They are told to leave all of it and cross a river to fight a seven-year war for land that not one of them will ever own.

Verse 15 sets the term of service, and it is not a number of years: until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you. They go home when everyone else is home.

Here is the principle, and it is one the church needs about as badly as Israel did: my inheritance does not excuse me from my brother's battle. It is entirely possible to be settled, provided for, and spiritually comfortable while people you are bound to are still fighting for their lives, and this chapter treats that arrangement as a debt rather than a blessing. Paul says it in four words — bear one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2) — and this is what it looks like with boots on.

Something greater than Reuben is faintly visible here. One who was at rest, at home, and in possession of everything crossed over armed into a war he had no need to fight, for the sake of an inheritance that would belong to his brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses! Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses!"'

The pledge is total, and the sentence that matters most is the last one. Their loyalty to Joshua is real, but it is conditioned on something they cannot give him: only may the LORD your God be with you.

They have understood the arrangement exactly. Joshua's authority is borrowed. They will follow him not because he is impressive but because they believe God's hand is on him, and their one anxiety about the new leadership is not competence but presence.

'Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous.'

The clause about death is severe and it is not decoration. In a covenant nation crossing into a war, rebellion against God's appointed leader was rebellion against God, and the penalty says how seriously the arrangement was meant. It is one of the places where the Old Testament feels a long way from a Sunday morning, and the distance is real; the mediator now is not a man with an army but a Son with a cross, and the stakes have gone up rather than down.

Then the last four words of the chapter, and they are the same four God used. Only be strong and courageous. God said it to Joshua three times; now the people say it back to him.

That is how courage travels. It begins in the mouth of God, is spoken over one frightened man at a riverbank, and comes back to him out of the mouths of the people he is supposed to be leading. The LORD who will not leave or forsake gives his own words away, and they go round the camp all day and come home to him at evening, undiminished.

1.theology:
Grace before duty. The land is given in verse 3, past tense, before a foot has touched it; the fighting begins five chapters later. Israel does not battle in order to earn Canaan but because Canaan is already theirs. That order is never reversed anywhere in Scripture, and it is the whole difference between obedience and bargaining.

The sufficiency of God's presence. 'I will not leave you or forsake you' (v. 5) and 'the LORD your God is with you wherever you go' (v. 9) are the foundation of the book. What is promised is presence, not exemption — not that no one will attack, but that no one will stand. Hebrews lifts the sentence straight out of a soldier's commissioning and gives it to Christians anxious about money (Heb. 13:5-6), and it finds its face in Immanuel and in the last words of the risen Christ (Matt. 1:23; 28:20).

The Word as the source of strength. Meditation is commanded before strategy (v. 8), and the Hebrew hagah is not an emptied mind but a low muttering, the noise of a man reading half-aloud — the word used of the blessed man in Psalm 1. The promised 'good success' is the success of this commission, getting a people into a land God swore to give them, and not a formula for turning devotions into money.

No one rests alone. The eastern tribes hold their inheritance already and are sent to war for somebody else's, until the LORD gives rest to their brothers as he has to them (v. 15). Being settled is not a discharge from a brother's battle. It is the Old Testament in its plainest form of what Paul means by bearing one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2).
1.examples:
Then: A nation stood at a river with its leader newly buried, forty years of wilderness behind it and walled cities ahead. They had no army to match Canaan's, no experience of siege warfare, and no successor of Moses' stature — only a sentence spoken over them: I have given you the land. Everything that followed depended on whether that sentence was treated as a fact.

Now: The cure prescribed for fear here is not a change of circumstances, and God never offers Joshua one. It is a presence and a book. When the props go — a person dies, a job ends, a diagnosis lands — the promise held out is not that the river will be easier to cross but that the same God will be on both banks. Ask what you have actually been waiting for before you will be at peace. If the answer is a change in the facts, this chapter is offering something else, and calling it better.

2.title: Rahab and the Spies
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.<sup>2</sup>And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land."<sup>3</sup>Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."<sup>4</sup>But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from.<sup>5</sup>And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them."<sup>6</sup>But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof.<sup>7</sup>So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out.<sup>8</sup>Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof<sup>9</sup>and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.<sup>10</sup>For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction.<sup>11</sup>And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.<sup>12</sup>Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign<sup>13</sup>that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death."<sup>14</sup>And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! If you do not tell this business of ours, then when the LORD gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you."<sup>15</sup>Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, so that she lived in the wall.<sup>16</sup>And she said to them, "Go into the hills, or the pursuers will encounter you, and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way."<sup>17</sup>The men said to her, "We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear.<sup>18</sup>Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and you shall gather into your house your father and mother, your brothers, and all your father's household.<sup>19</sup>Then if anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head, and we shall be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head.<sup>20</sup>But if you tell this business of ours, then we shall be guiltless with respect to your oath that you have made us swear."<sup>21</sup>And she said, "According to your words, so be it." Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.<sup>22</sup>They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned, and the pursuers searched all along the way and found nothing.<sup>23</sup>Then the two men returned. They came down from the hills and passed over and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.<sup>24</sup>And they said to Joshua, "Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us."
2.overview:
Of all the surprises in Scripture, few rival this: the conquest of Canaan begins not with a battle but with a conversion — and the convert is a Canaanite prostitute. The two spies cross into Jericho and find shelter in the most unlikely place, the house of Rahab, a woman whose trade and nationality marked her doubly for destruction under the coming judgment. Yet here, in the very city devoted to the ban, grace breaks in. The harlot of Jericho will end up in the genealogy of Jesus Christ (Matt. 1:5), named alongside Abraham and David in the hall of faith (Heb. 11:31), and held up by James as a model of living faith (James 2:25).

Rahab's confession in verse 11 is the theological summit of the chapter — and one of the great confessions of the Old Testament: 'the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.' This pagan woman, with no Scripture, no temple, no covenant heritage, has heard the reports of the Red Sea and the defeat of the Amorite kings, and she has reasoned her way to monotheism and surrender. Her fellow Canaanites heard the same reports and their hearts 'melted' in terror; Rahab heard them and her heart melted in faith. Calvin marveled that God's election finds its objects in the most degraded soil, that the gospel might be wholly of grace.

The scarlet cord she hangs in her window (v. 18) is one of Scripture's most luminous types. As the blood of the lamb on the doorposts spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt, so this scarlet thread will mark the one house in Jericho that judgment passes over. It is the blood of Christ in shadow — the sign that saves, the mark of the covenant, the line drawn between death and life. Where the scarlet cord hangs, the destroyer cannot enter.

The chapter pulses with the theme of the whole book: 'the LORD has given you the land' (v. 24). The spies return not with military intelligence about Jericho's defenses but with a report of melted hearts and a saved soul. The walls have already fallen in the hearts of the Canaanites; the conquest is the LORD's, and he is already gathering his elect from among the nations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Spies Sheltered and Hidden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua sends two spies into Jericho. They lodge with Rahab, and when the king's men come searching, she hides them and sends the pursuers on a false trail, risking her life to protect the men of Israel's God.
verseByVerse.theology: Rahab's protection of the spies is the first fruit of saving faith — faith that acts. Her courage in defying her own king flows from a heart already turned to the LORD. Salvation reaches into the most unlikely lives and produces immediate, costly obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin notes that God providentially guided the spies to the one house in Jericho where faith was stirring. Ferguson observes that grace often works secretly behind enemy lines long before the visible victory; God had a people in Jericho before the trumpets ever sounded.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, Go, view the land, especially Jericho. And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua sends only two men, and sends them secretly — a quiet contrast to the twelve spies of the previous generation whose public report spread fear (Num. 13). Where Jericho is concerned, the strategy is reconnaissance, but God's strategy is salvation. The men come 'into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab.' The narrator states her trade plainly, without euphemism and without scorn. This is the soil in which grace will plant a flower for the Messiah's lineage. Why a harlot's house? Practically, it was a place where strangers could come and go without arousing suspicion, often built into the city wall. Providentially, it was the one house in Jericho where a heart had been prepared to believe. MacArthur notes that the Hebrew and the New Testament references (Heb. 11:31; James 2:25) consistently call her a prostitute — Scripture does not sanitize her past, that grace might shine brighter against it. Calvin observes that God 'so directs the steps of his servants' that they are led, unknowing, precisely to the one in whom faith is stirring. The spies sought intelligence; God was gathering an elect soul. The whole conquest opens not with a sword but with a sinner saved.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told to the king of Jericho, Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land. Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, Bring out the men who have come to you...
verseByVerse.commentary: The spies' presence is detected; word reaches the king, and the machinery of the state turns against them. The king's demand is direct: 'Bring out the men.' This is the moment of crisis for Rahab. To obey her king is to betray the spies and side with the doomed city; to protect them is treason, punishable by death. Everything hangs on where her heart truly lies. Wenham notes the dramatic tension the narrator builds — the reader does not yet know which way Rahab will turn. The king's swift action also reveals the terror gripping Jericho; they are watching their borders, dreading the people whose God dried up the sea. The city's fear is not unfounded, but it is misdirected — they fear Israel rather than fearing and submitting to Israel's God. Rahab, by contrast, has drawn the right conclusion from the same reports. Sproul observed that the same revelation of God's power produces hardening in some and softening in others; the difference is not the evidence but the heart God is at work upon. The king represents Jericho's settled rebellion; Rahab, standing between the king's men at her door and the spies on her roof, represents the dividing line where judgment and mercy will part.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from... she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax... So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan...
verseByVerse.commentary: Rahab acts, and her action is faith with its sleeves rolled up. She has already hidden the spies under stalks of flax on her roof before the king's men arrive, and she sends the pursuers off on a false trail toward the Jordan fords. Much ink has been spilled over Rahab's lie. Scripture commends her faith and her works (Heb. 11; James 2) without explicitly endorsing the deception itself. Calvin took the view that while the dissimulation was not in itself pleasing to God, her faith and mercy were genuinely commended, and God in his grace accepted the imperfect service of a newborn believer. We need not make Rahab a flawless ethicist to see her as a true convert; she is a Canaanite only days into faith, casting her lot decisively and at great peril with the people of God. What is unmistakable is the direction of her loyalty: she has chosen Israel's God over her own king, eternal life over earthly safety. Ferguson notes that genuine conversion always involves a decisive transfer of allegiance — Rahab burns her bridges with Jericho. Her concealment of the spies under the flax (which she had laid out to dry on the roof) shows forethought; she had counted the cost and committed herself before the crisis came.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the spies sleep, Rahab climbs to the roof and pours out the most remarkable confession of faith in the book. She recounts the reports of the Red Sea and the Amorite kings, declares the LORD God of heaven and earth, and begs for covenant mercy for her family.
verseByVerse.theology: Rahab's confession is a model of saving faith: she hears the report of God's mighty acts, she believes the testimony, and she throws herself wholly on God's mercy. Her words 'he is God in heaven above and on earth beneath' are pure monotheistic confession from a pagan heart — evidence of sovereign, electing grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Stott noted that Rahab heard the same news as all Jericho but responded with faith rather than terror. Keller stressed that her confession shows faith comes by hearing — she had no Scripture, only the report of God's deeds, yet she believed and was saved, a foretaste of the gospel going to the Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof and said to the men, I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I know that the LORD has given you the land.' Astonishing words from a Canaanite. She uses the covenant name — the LORD, Yahweh — and she speaks of the land as already given, echoing the very promise God made to Joshua in chapter 1 ('I have given you the land,' 1:3). This pagan woman has grasped by faith what some in Israel still doubted. She perceives the spiritual reality behind the political situation: 'the fear of you has fallen upon us... all the inhabitants melt away before you.' The Canaanites are not melting because of Israel's army — they have no army to speak of — but because they sense that the God of Israel is real and irresistible. This fulfills the song of Moses at the sea: 'terror and dread fall upon them' (Exod. 15:16). Wenham observes that Rahab functions as a true prophet here, declaring God's purposes more clearly than the spies themselves. Calvin marveled that the Lord drew so clear a confession from one buried in the darkness of paganism, proving that faith is the gift of God and not the fruit of privilege. While the city melts in despair, Rahab melts in surrender — and that difference is everything.

verseByVerse.quote: For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you... And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the summit. Rahab recounts the two great signs — the drying of the Red Sea (forty years past) and the recent destruction of Sihon and Og — and she draws the only right conclusion: 'the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.' This is full-throated monotheism, a confession that the God of Israel is not a tribal deity among many but the sole sovereign of all creation, of sky and soil alike. No Canaanite altar could have taught her this; it is the work of God's Spirit illuminating a darkened mind. 'Faith comes by hearing' (Rom. 10:17), and Rahab had heard — the news of God's deeds had traveled the caravan routes, and where Jericho heard only a threat, Rahab heard a revelation. Ferguson notes that this confession exceeds in clarity what many Israelites managed in the wilderness; the harlot believes while the privileged grumble. Sproul observed that the same providence that hardened Pharaoh's heart at the sea now softens Rahab's at Jericho — the difference lies wholly in the secret operation of grace. This verse is a Gentile Pentecost in seed form: a foreigner confessing the true God, a preview of the day when the gospel would gather a people from every nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house... and deliver our lives from death. And the men said to her, Our life for yours even to death!...
verseByVerse.commentary: Faith always issues in petition. Having confessed the LORD, Rahab now casts herself and her family on his mercy: 'swear to me by the LORD... deliver our lives from death.' She asks for hesed — covenant kindness, steadfast love — the very word that describes God's loyal mercy to his own people. She does not presume; she pleads. And notice the breadth of her concern: not only her own life but her father, mother, brothers, sisters — her whole household. True faith reaches outward to gather others under the shelter of grace. The spies respond with a solemn oath: 'Our life for yours even to death!' They pledge their own lives as surety for hers — a faint echo of the great Substitution, the One who would give his life for those who had no claim on mercy. Calvin notes that the spies bind themselves with an oath in the name of the LORD, making the promise sacred and unbreakable. The condition follows in the next verses, but the heart of it is set: a Canaanite has sought refuge in Israel's God and will not be turned away. As Jesus would later say, 'whoever comes to me I will never cast out' (John 6:37) — and Rahab is the first Gentile to prove it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rahab lets the spies down the wall by a rope. They instruct her to bind a scarlet cord in her window, gather her family into the house, and stay inside — only then will they be spared when Jericho falls.
verseByVerse.theology: The scarlet cord is a vivid type of the blood of Christ. As the blood on the doorposts spared Israel at Passover, this scarlet thread marks the one house judgment will pass over. Salvation is found only inside the house, under the sign of the cord — there is no safety apart from the appointed means of grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Early church fathers and the Reformers alike saw in the scarlet cord a figure of the blood of Christ. Begg notes that Rahab's entire family had to be gathered inside under the sign — salvation is by the blood, received by faith, and it is offered to households. To leave the house was to forfeit the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall... And she said to them, Go into the hills... and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way.
verseByVerse.commentary: Rahab lowers the spies by a rope through her window — her house, we learn, was built into the city wall itself, which makes her later survival all the more miraculous, for when those walls collapse her portion will stand. She gives them shrewd, practical counsel: flee to the hills, not toward the Jordan where the pursuers went, and wait three days until the search is abandoned. Her faith is not naïve; it is intelligent and resourceful, working wisely within God's providence. Wenham notes the irony that the very wall that symbolizes Jericho's security and defiance becomes the avenue of the spies' escape and the site of Rahab's salvation — the city's strength serves God's purposes. There is also a quiet foreshadowing: the house in the wall that will not fall when all else falls. Calvin observes that Rahab's wisdom in directing the spies shows that genuine faith engages the mind and acts prudently; trusting God does not mean acting foolishly. The 'three days' echoes the timing of the whole campaign (1:11) and, for the eye of faith, whispers of resurrection — deliverance on the third day. Rahab, the newest believer in the story, becomes the protector and counselor of God's own messengers.

verseByVerse.quote: The men said to her, We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear. Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window... and you shall gather into your house your father and mother...
verseByVerse.commentary: The spies set the terms of the covenant of rescue, and at its center is the scarlet cord. The very rope by which she let them down — scarlet, blood-red — is to hang in her window as the sign that marks her house for mercy. The conditions are precise: the cord must be displayed, and every soul she would save must be gathered inside the house; whoever goes out into the street forfeits the promise and bears his own blood. Here the Passover pattern is unmistakable. As Israel's firstborn were safe only behind doorposts marked with the lamb's blood, so Rahab's household is safe only within the house marked by the scarlet cord. The fathers of the church saw Christ here, and rightly: the scarlet thread is the blood of the Lamb, the line drawn between judgment and grace. Begg presses the application — salvation is located. There is one house, one sign, one place of safety, and outside of it there is only the falling wall. So Christ is the one door (John 10:9); there is no salvation in any other name (Acts 4:12). The spies declare themselves 'guiltless' if the terms are broken, underscoring that the blood-sign must be honored. Grace is free, but it is not vague; it is found under the cord, inside the house.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said, According to your words, so be it. Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'According to your words, so be it' — Rahab's amen to the covenant of rescue. She submits entirely to the terms, asking for no modification, and then immediately acts: 'she tied the scarlet cord in the window.' She does not wait for the army to appear at the gates; she hangs the sign of salvation at once, the moment the spies depart. This is the obedience of faith — instant, unhesitating, public. The cord hangs in the window for days, perhaps weeks, before Jericho falls, a standing confession that she has staked everything on the word of Israel's God. Calvin notes that her prompt obedience is the proof of genuine faith; she does not delay or hedge but binds the cord as a perpetual testimony of her trust. There is something deeply moving in this picture: a Canaanite woman, formerly a prostitute, now sits in a doomed city beneath a scarlet thread, waiting in hope for a salvation she cannot see, resting wholly on a promise sworn in the name of a God she met only days ago. Ferguson observes that this is the very posture of the Christian — living under the sign of the blood, in a world under judgment, trusting the word of the One who has sworn to save. The cord is hung; her fate is sealed in mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–24 — The Spies Return with Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The spies hide in the hills for three days, then return to Joshua and report not on Jericho's defenses but on the LORD's victory: 'the LORD has given all the land into our hands; and also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away before us.'
verseByVerse.theology: The spies' report is a confession of faith, echoing Rahab's own words. Where the previous generation's spies brought back fear (Num. 13), this report rings with confidence in God's promise. The battle is already won in the courts of heaven; the conquest is the working out of an accomplished gift.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes the deliberate contrast with the unbelieving report of the twelve spies a generation earlier. The same land, the same giants — but now the report is full of faith. The difference is a generation that has learned to take God at his word.

verseByVerse.quote: They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned... Then the two men returned... and they came to Joshua the son of Nun, and told him all that had happened to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The spies follow Rahab's counsel exactly, hiding three days in the hills until the pursuit dies down, then crossing back to report to Joshua. The narrative is spare and swift, but the obedience is total — they trusted the word of a Canaanite convert and were preserved by it. The mission, on its surface a military reconnaissance, has become a salvation story; what they have chiefly to report is not the height of Jericho's walls but the melting of Jericho's heart and the rescue of a believing household. Wenham notes the careful framing: the spies come 'to Joshua the son of Nun,' the same full naming as the chapter's opening, closing the narrative arc. They tell him 'all that had happened' — including, surely, the encounter with Rahab, which is why her family is later spared by name (6:17, 22–25). Calvin observes that God's providence governed the whole expedition, preserving the spies and gathering an elect soul, so that the campaign opens with a demonstration that the LORD, not Israel, is the author of the conquest. The three days in the hills, like the three days before the crossing, mark a pattern of waiting that ends in deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to Joshua, Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away before us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The spies' report is itself a sermon. 'Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands' — they echo word for word the promise God made to Joshua (1:3) and the confession Rahab made on her roof (2:9). Faith has spread; the same conviction now sounds from God, from a Canaanite convert, and from Israel's scouts. The contrast with the previous generation could not be sharper. A generation earlier, ten spies surveyed the same land and reported, 'We are not able... the people are too strong; there are giants; we seemed like grasshoppers' (Num. 13:31–33). Now two spies report, 'the LORD has given... all the inhabitants melt away before us.' Same land, same fortified cities, same Anakim — but a transformed report, because a transformed faith. Sproul observed that circumstances had not changed nearly so much as hearts; the wilderness generation died in unbelief, and the new generation has learned to see the world through the lens of God's promise. MacArthur notes that the spies' confidence rests not on their own assessment of military odds — they found a city melting in fear and a household won to faith — but on the bare word of God. This is the spirit in which the whole conquest will proceed: not 'can we take it?' but 'the LORD has given it.' The chapter ends as it began, with the certainty of grace.

2.theology:
Sovereign, Electing Grace. Rahab is the unanswerable proof that salvation is by grace alone. A Canaanite, a prostitute, with no covenant heritage and no Scripture, is sovereignly drawn to faith while her whole city melts in unbelieving terror at the same reports. God gathers his elect from the most unlikely soil, that no flesh may boast — and grafts a harlot into the lineage of the Messiah (Matt. 1:5).

Justification by a Faith That Works. Rahab is the rare figure cited by both Paul's school (Heb. 11:31, 'by faith') and James (2:25, 'justified by works'). Her faith was real because it acted — hiding the spies, hanging the cord, casting her lot with God's people at the risk of her life. Reformed theology holds these together: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

The Scarlet Cord and the Blood of Christ. The crimson thread in the window, recalling the Passover blood, is a luminous type of the blood of the Lamb. Salvation is located under the sign, inside the house. There is one door, one place of safety, one name under heaven by which we must be saved.
2.examples:
Then: A doomed city heard the report of God's mighty deeds and trembled, but one woman heard and believed. Rahab staked her life and her family's lives on the bare word of Israel's God, hung the scarlet cord in her window, and waited in a city under sentence of death for a salvation she could not yet see.

Now: Every sinner stands where Rahab stood — in a world under judgment, hearing the report of God's mighty acts in Christ. The same God who saved a Canaanite harlot saves the worst of us by grace through a faith that flees to the blood. The gospel is not for the deserving but for the desperate who, hearing, believe, and shelter under the scarlet sign. If Rahab's house was safe, yours is too — for the blood of Christ never fails to save the one who hides beneath it.

3.title: Crossing the Jordan
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over.<sup>2</sup>At the end of three days the officers went through the camp<sup>3</sup>and commanded the people, "As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it.<sup>4</sup>Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."<sup>5</sup>Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you."<sup>6</sup>And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.<sup>7</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.<sup>8</sup>And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'"<sup>9</sup>And Joshua said to the people of Israel, "Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua said, "Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites.<sup>11</sup>Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan.<sup>12</sup>Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man.<sup>13</sup>And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing, and the waters coming down from above shall stand in one heap."<sup>14</sup>So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people,<sup>15</sup>and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest),<sup>16</sup>the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho.<sup>17</sup>Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
3.overview:
Forty years earlier, an older generation had passed through the Red Sea on dry ground as they left Egypt. Now a new generation passes through the Jordan on dry ground as they enter Canaan. The two water-crossings frame the wilderness, and together they preach a single gospel: the God who delivers out of bondage is the God who brings into the inheritance. What the exodus began, the conquest completes — and at the center of both stands the saving power of the LORD.

But there is a crucial difference between the two crossings, and it is full of meaning. At the Red Sea, Moses lifted his staff and the waters parted before the people set out. At the Jordan, the waters do not part until the priests carrying the ark step into the river — and the Jordan was at flood stage (v. 15). Faith must get its feet wet before the path appears. The people must follow the ark into the very edge of the flood, trusting that the God who promised will make a way. Begg loved to note that the miracle waited on the obedience; the path opened only as the priests committed themselves to the water.

At the center of the crossing is the ark of the covenant, going before the people at a distance of two thousand cubits (v. 4). The ark — the throne of God, the place of his presence — leads the way into the land. 'You shall follow it, for you have not passed this way before' (v. 4). The people did not know the way, but they knew the One who did. Here is a portrait of Christ, who goes before his people into death and out the other side, who has gone 'this way before' and bids us follow. As the ark stood firm in the midst of the Jordan while all Israel passed over (v. 17), so Christ stands firm in the midst of death's flood, holding back the waters until every last one of his people has crossed safely into the promised rest.

The chapter is also about the exaltation of Joshua: 'This day I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you' (v. 7). The crossing authenticates the new mediator, as the Red Sea had authenticated Moses. And the deepest fulfillment is in the greater Joshua, exalted before all by passing through the waters of death and rising — proof that God is with him, and through him, with us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel breaks camp and comes to the Jordan. The officers instruct the people to follow the ark at a distance, for they have not passed this way before. Joshua calls them to consecrate themselves, promising that the LORD will do wonders among them.
verseByVerse.theology: The ark — the visible throne of God's presence — leads the people into the land. Consecration must precede the experience of God's wonders; holiness is the prerequisite for witnessing God's power. The God who goes before is the ground of all confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin notes that following the ark at a set distance taught reverence — God's presence is gracious but holy. Ferguson observes that 'you have not passed this way before' is the recurring experience of faith: we follow not because we know the road but because we know the One who leads.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over. At the end of three days the officers went through the camp...
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Joshua rose early in the morning' — the mark of a man eager to obey, the same phrase used of Abraham going to offer Isaac. There is no dragging of feet at the edge of the promise. Israel moves from Shittim, the camp on the plains of Moab, down to the very brink of the Jordan, and there they lodge, gazing across at the land of promise now within sight. The three days of preparation (cf. 1:11) reach their climax. There is a holy pause here, a night spent on the threshold. Calvin notes that the encampment at the river's edge tested their faith — the Jordan at flood stage lay before them, impassable to human strength, and they must wait for God to act. Wenham observes the deliberate echoes of the exodus narrative; the writer wants us to see the Jordan crossing as the bookend to the Red Sea, the entry that answers the exit. The people who were born in the wilderness, who never saw Egypt or the parted sea, now stand where their faith will be tested as their parents' was. Will they follow the ark into the flood? The whole inheritance hangs on whether this generation will trust the God of their fathers at the water's edge.

verseByVerse.quote: ...When you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it. Yet there shall be a distance between you and it... that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before.
verseByVerse.commentary: The people are to follow the ark — the gold-covered chest that was the throne of God's presence, where he met his people between the cherubim. The ark goes first; the people follow. This is the gospel order: God leads, we follow. And they are to keep a distance of two thousand cubits, about half a mile — a reverent gap that kept the holy presence visible to all and unmixed with the press of the crowd. Why follow the ark? Because 'you have not passed this way before.' Here is one of the tenderest lines in the chapter. The people did not know the road; they had no map for the Jordan, no experience of conquest. But they did not need to know the way — they needed only to follow the One who knew. Begg observed that this is the perpetual condition of the believer: we walk into an unknown future, but we follow a known God. Calvin notes that the distance taught reverence, that familiarity might not breed contempt for the holy. The ark, here, is a shadow of Christ, who has gone 'this way before' — through death and out the other side — and who bids his people follow where he leads, even when the road is wholly unknown to us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said to the people, Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders.' Before the miracle comes the call to holiness. Consecration meant ritual cleansing, the washing of garments, the setting apart of oneself for the holy. The principle is profound: the people who would witness God's wonders must first be made fit to behold them. God does not display his power among the careless and the unclean; he reveals himself to a consecrated people. Sproul stressed that holiness is not the reward of seeing God's works but the precondition — 'without holiness no one will see the Lord' (Heb. 12:14). There is also a beautiful expectancy in Joshua's word: 'tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.' He speaks with the certainty of faith; the miracle is not hoped for but announced. Ferguson notes that genuine spiritual leadership cultivates expectancy — Joshua prepares the people not merely to act but to witness, to see God do what only God can do. The word 'wonders' (the Hebrew niphla'ot) is the language of the exodus plagues and the parting of the sea; Joshua is telling them that the God of their fathers is about to act again. The proper response to the promise of God's power is not presumption but consecration — the cleansing of the heart to receive the wonder.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua said to the priests, Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people. So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.
verseByVerse.commentary: The priests are commanded to take up the ark and go before the people — and they obey at once. There is no hesitation recorded, though they are being asked to carry the throne of God straight into a flooded river. The ark, normally kept in the holy of holies, screened from every eye, now goes out at the head of the procession, the most visible object in Israel. The presence of God leads his people into the land. Calvin notes the priests' faith and obedience: they shouldered the ark and stepped out, trusting that the God whose presence they bore would make a way through impassable water. There is a deep Christological resonance here. The priests bearing the ark of the covenant prefigure Christ, our great High Priest, who is himself the true meeting-place between God and man, the true throne of grace. He goes before his people, carrying the very presence of God into the floodwaters of death, leading the way into the inheritance. Wenham observes that the repeated, almost liturgical phrasing — 'the ark of the covenant' named again and again throughout the chapter — keeps the focus relentlessly on God's presence as the agent of the miracle. The priests carry it; but it is the LORD enthroned upon it who parts the flood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The LORD's Promise and Joshua's Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD promises to exalt Joshua before all Israel as he did Moses. Joshua tells the people that the living God will drive out the nations, and that as soon as the priests' feet touch the Jordan, the waters will be cut off.
verseByVerse.theology: The crossing authenticates Joshua as God's appointed mediator, just as the Red Sea authenticated Moses. The 'living God' (v. 10) is contrasted with the dead idols of Canaan — a polemic against false gods and an assurance that the conquest is the work of the one true God.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul noted that God's exaltation of his servant is always for the people's sake — that they might trust and follow. Keller observed that the title 'living God' grounds Israel's confidence: their God acts, speaks, and saves, while the gods of the nations are lifeless.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: God announces that the crossing will serve to exalt Joshua publicly: 'Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel.' The purpose is not Joshua's glory but the people's confidence — 'that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.' The authentication of the mediator is for the sake of those he leads. Israel had followed Moses through the sea; now they must learn to follow Joshua through the Jordan, and God graciously provides the sign that proves the same divine presence rests upon the new leader. Calvin notes that God 'begins' to exalt him — the process is gradual, building credibility over the campaign, beginning here at the river. There is a magnificent Christological trajectory in this verse. Joshua, whose name is Jesus, is exalted before all the people by passing through the waters — a faint shadow of the greater Joshua, who would be exalted before all by passing through the waters of death and rising on the third day, declared to be the Son of God with power by the resurrection (Rom. 1:4). Ferguson observes that God authenticates his appointed savior so that the people will entrust themselves to him. The exaltation of Joshua at the Jordan whispers of the exaltation of Christ, that we might know God is with him, and through him, with us.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan. And Joshua said to the people of Israel, Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary: God instructs Joshua to command the priests: when they reach the brink of the waters, they are to 'stand still in the Jordan.' The priests will step into the flood and then stand firm in its midst, holding their ground while all Israel passes. There is great faith required in standing still in a riverbed at flood stage, trusting that the waters heaped upstream will not come crashing down. Joshua gathers the people — 'Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God' — for the miracle must be framed by the Word. Israel is not to gawk at a wonder of nature but to hear and heed the speech of their God. Wenham notes the emphasis on hearing before seeing; the crossing is a word-event before it is a sight-event, an enacted sermon on God's covenant faithfulness. Calvin observes that Joshua, like a faithful pastor, prepares the people's hearts by directing them to God's word before God's work, so that they will rightly interpret what they are about to behold. The standing-still of the priests in the midst of the flood is itself a picture: the place of the ark, the place of God's presence, is the place where the waters of death are held back. Where God stands, the flood cannot prevail.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua said, Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites... Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The living God is among you' — this is the heart of Israel's hope. In contrast to the dead idols of Canaan, gods of wood and stone who cannot speak or save, the God of Israel is the living God, who acts in history, parts rivers, and drives out nations. Joshua promises that this living God will 'without fail' drive out the seven nations of Canaan. The certainty is absolute — not 'may' but 'will without fail.' And the proof, the guarantee, is the ark: 'the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you.' Note the magnificent title — 'the Lord of all the earth.' Israel's God is not a regional deity confined to one territory; he owns the whole earth, including Canaan, and so he has every right to give it to whom he pleases. Keller stressed that the description 'living God' grounds all of Israel's confidence: a dead god cannot help, but the living God acts and saves. Sproul observed that the conquest is, at its root, a question of ownership — the Lord of all the earth disposes of his own land as he wills. Calvin notes that the title rebukes the folly of idolatry: while the nations trust gods who cannot move, Israel follows the ark of the Lord who moves the very waters of the Jordan. The living God is among them; the outcome is not in doubt.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man. And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off...
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua commands that twelve men be chosen, one from each tribe — preparing for the memorial of chapter 4, and underscoring that the whole covenant nation, all twelve tribes, shares in this crossing. Then comes the precise promise: when the priests' feet 'rest in the waters,' the Jordan 'shall be cut off' and 'stand in a heap.' Here is the great difference from the Red Sea, where the waters parted before the people moved. At the Jordan, the waters will not divide until the feet of faith are planted in the flood. The promise is given in advance, but its fulfillment waits on obedience. Begg pressed this beautifully: the path through the Jordan opened only as the priests committed themselves to the water; faith must often act before it sees. The phrase 'stand in a heap' deliberately echoes the song of Moses at the Red Sea: 'the floods stood up in a heap' (Exod. 15:8). The writer wants us to see one continuous work of God, from the sea of the exodus to the river of the conquest. Wenham notes the repeated title 'the Lord of all the earth' — the same Lord who made the waters now commands them. The God who owns the earth can move its rivers at the touch of a priest's foot. The stage is set; all now waits on the step of faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The Waters Stand in a Heap
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the priests' feet touch the brink of the flooding Jordan, the waters upstream stand in a heap far away at Adam, and the waters downstream flow off to the Dead Sea. The priests stand firm on dry ground in the midst of the riverbed until all Israel has passed over.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle waits on faith: the waters do not part until the priests step in. The ark standing firm in the midst of the flood while all Israel passes is a picture of Christ standing firm in death's flood until every one of his people crosses safely into the inheritance.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg notes that faith must get its feet wet before the path appears — God honored the step into the flood. Ferguson sees in the ark holding back the waters a portrait of Christ, who 'stands in the midst' of judgment so that his people pass over on dry ground.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people, and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest)...
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator heightens the drama with a parenthesis: 'now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest.' This was not a low-water ford that any traveler might wade. It was springtime, the season of the barley harvest, when the snowmelt from Hermon swelled the river into a churning flood that burst its banks. Humanly speaking, the crossing was impossible — and that is precisely the point. God times his deliverances for the moment of greatest impossibility, that the glory may be unmistakably his.
