And the priests 'dipped' their feet 'in the brink of the water.' They stepped into the flood before it parted. Here is the great act of faith in the chapter. Begg observed that the miracle followed the obedience; had the priests waited on the bank for the waters to part first, they would have waited forever. Faith puts its foot in the river on the strength of the bare promise. Calvin notes that God deliberately chose the flood season to magnify the wonder and to test whether Israel would believe his word against all appearance. Wenham observes the deliberate parallel and contrast with the Red Sea — there the waters parted at a distance before Moses' staff; here they part only at the touch of obedient feet. The God who promised honored the step into the water.

verseByVerse.quote: ...the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary: The moment the feet touch the water, the miracle erupts. The waters from upstream 'stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam' — some sixteen miles north — while the waters downstream drained off completely toward the Dead Sea. The riverbed lay bare. The detail of the place-name Adam is striking; some have seen in it a quiet echo of the first Adam, the floodwaters of death held back so that a people might pass into life. The phrase 'rose up in a heap' is the very language of Exodus 15:8, sealing the connection between the two crossings. And 'the people passed over opposite Jericho' — the destination is named, the doomed city already in view across the dry riverbed. Calvin marvels that God did not merely lower the river but heaped the waters into a standing wall, a visible monument to his power that all Israel might behold. Sproul observed that such a miracle is not a manipulation of natural law but the direct intervention of the Lord of all the earth, who commands the waters he created. Wenham notes the precision of the geography, anchoring the miracle in real history, real places, real time. The flood that should have been impassable now stands frozen in a heap, and a whole nation walks across the bed of a river in flood — into the land of promise, opposite the city that will be the first to fall.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with one of its most resonant images: the priests bearing the ark 'stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan... until all the nation finished passing over.' The ark — the throne of God's presence — stands fixed in the very heart of the riverbed, holding the position while every last Israelite crosses safely to the other side. Not until 'all the nation' had passed did the priests move. Here is a picture too rich to pass over. The ark stands in the midst of death's flood, and as long as it stands, the waters cannot return; the people pass over on dry ground. Ferguson and many before him saw here a shadow of Christ, our great High Priest, who stands firm in the midst of the flood of judgment and death, holding back the waters by his presence until every last one of his people has crossed safely into the inheritance. He will not move from the riverbed until 'all the nation' — all whom the Father has given him — has finished passing over. 'Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one' (John 18:9). Calvin notes the priests' steadfastness as a model of perseverance; they did not flinch in the midst of the heaped waters. The detail 'on dry ground' is repeated twice — God's deliverance is complete, not partial; not one foot was muddied. The whole nation stands now on the soil of the promise, and the conquest has begun with a wonder that proclaims: the LORD fights for his people.

3.theology:
The Presence of God Goes Before His People. The ark leads Israel into the land, and the priests bearing it stand firm in the midst of the flood until all have crossed. God does not send his people into the unknown alone; he goes before them. This is fulfilled in Christ, who has gone 'this way before' through death and resurrection, leading his people into the inheritance.

Faith Acts Before It Sees. The waters do not part until the priests step into the flood. The promise is given in advance, but its fulfillment waits on the obedience of faith. The believer is repeatedly called to put a foot into the river on the strength of God's bare word, and to discover that God makes a way only as we follow.

The Authentication of the Mediator. As the Red Sea authenticated Moses, the Jordan authenticates Joshua: 'as I was with Moses, so I will be with you' (v. 7). This points to the exaltation of the greater Joshua, declared Son of God with power by passing through death and rising, that his people might trust and follow him into the rest.
3.examples:
Then: A new generation stood at a flooded river with no bridge and no boats, commanded to follow a golden box into the torrent. They could not see the path; they could only trust the God who carried the throne. When the priests' feet touched the water, the impossible flood stood up in a heap, and a nation walked into its inheritance on dry ground.

Now: The Christian life is a long crossing of waters we have not passed before. We do not know the road, but we follow the One who does — Christ, who has gone before through death itself. Like Israel, we must often get our feet wet before the path appears, trusting the bare promise of God against the evidence of the flood. And our confidence is the ark in the riverbed: Christ stands firm in the midst of judgment until every last one of his people has crossed safely home.

4.title: The Twelve Memorial Stones
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>2</sup>"Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man,<sup>3</sup>and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"<sup>4</sup>Then Joshua called the twelve men from the people of Israel, whom he had appointed, a man from each tribe.<sup>5</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Pass on before the ark of the LORD your God into the midst of the Jordan, and take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel,<sup>6</sup>that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?'<sup>7</sup>then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it passed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever."<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded and took up twelve stones out of the midst of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, just as the LORD told Joshua. And they carried them over with them to the place where they lodged and laid them down there.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.<sup>10</sup>For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people passed over in haste.<sup>11</sup>And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them.<sup>13</sup>About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho.<sup>14</sup>On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>16</sup>"Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan."<sup>17</sup>So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan."<sup>18</sup>And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.<sup>19</sup>The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho.<sup>20</sup>And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.<sup>21</sup>And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?'<sup>22</sup>then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground.'<sup>23</sup>For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over,<sup>24</sup>so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."
4.overview:
The crossing is complete, but God is not finished. Before the army marches on Jericho, he commands the building of a memorial — twelve stones taken from the midst of the Jordan, set up at Gilgal, so that the wonder of this day will never be forgotten. The conquest pauses for the sake of memory. God knows the human heart; he knows how quickly we forget the very mercies that should anchor our faith forever. And so he plants a heap of stones in the land as a perpetual sermon.

The theology of memory dominates this chapter. Three times the question of the children is anticipated: 'When your children ask in time to come, What do these stones mean?' (vv. 6, 21). The stones exist for the next generation — for catechesis, for the passing on of faith from parents to children. Calvin observed that God provides for the instruction of posterity, that the testimony of his deeds might not die with the eyewitnesses. The Reformed conviction that faith is handed down through families, through the deliberate teaching of God's mighty acts, is written into these stones. We are to tell our children what God has done.

There are, in fact, two sets of twelve stones in this chapter — one set up at Gilgal where the people lodged (v. 8, 20), and another set up by Joshua in the midst of the Jordan where the priests had stood (v. 9). The visible stones at Gilgal would teach the generations; the hidden stones in the riverbed, soon to be covered again by the returning flood, were a memorial known to God and to those who placed them — a witness that the dry path had truly been there, that the deliverance was real even when the waters closed over it again.

The chapter ends with the great purpose of the whole crossing: 'that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever' (v. 24). The memorial serves a horizontal purpose (witness to the nations) and a vertical purpose (the fear of the LORD in Israel). The God who acts in history means his acts to be remembered, retold, and to issue in worship — generation after generation, until the whole earth knows that his hand is mighty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Stones Taken Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD commands that twelve men, one from each tribe, take up twelve stones from the midst of the Jordan where the priests stood, to carry to the lodging place as a memorial. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the riverbed itself.
verseByVerse.theology: The memorial stones embody the theology of remembrance. God commands tangible signs so that his mighty acts will be retold to children who did not witness them. Faith is preserved and transmitted across generations through the deliberate teaching of what God has done.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin stresses that God provides for posterity's instruction. Ferguson notes that the Christian life depends on remembering — the Lord's Supper itself is a 'do this in remembrance of me,' a memorial of a greater crossing through the waters of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua, Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man, and command them, Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.
verseByVerse.commentary: The moment the nation finishes crossing, God speaks again — the work of deliverance is to be immediately sealed in memory. Twelve men, one from each tribe, are to take twelve stones 'from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly.' The stones are not random rocks but quarried from the holy ground of the miracle, the spot where the ark held back the flood. Each tribe is represented, so the memorial belongs to the whole covenant nation; no tribe is omitted from the testimony. The stones are to be laid down 'in the place where you lodge tonight' — Gilgal — to become a standing witness in the land. Calvin notes the wisdom of God in commanding the memorial at once, before the freshness of the wonder could fade; gratitude is to be fixed in stone while the heart is still warm. Wenham observes that the involvement of all twelve tribes underscores the corporate nature of the deliverance — this was God's act for the whole people, and the whole people must remember it together. There is a beautiful instinct here that the Christian church has always shared: to mark the mighty acts of God with tangible signs — water, bread, wine — that the memory of redemption might be carried forward and never lost in the rush of years.

verseByVerse.quote: ...Joshua said to them, ...take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder... that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, What do those stones mean to you? then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD...
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the heart of the chapter — and one of the great texts on the catechizing of children. The stones are 'a sign,' and their purpose is anticipated in the question of a future generation: 'When your children ask in time to come, What do these stones mean?' The memorial exists for those not yet born, for the children who will play among the stones at Gilgal and one day ask their fathers what they mean. And the answer is fixed: 'then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD.' Calvin draws out the principle that God provides for the instruction of posterity, lest the testimony of his deeds perish with the eyewitnesses. The Reformed conviction — that faith is transmitted through families, through deliberate, intentional teaching — finds one of its clearest Old Testament charters here. Ferguson notes that the parents are given both the question and the answer; God anticipates the curiosity of children and equips parents to seize the teachable moment. There is a holy strategy in this: God means his redemptive acts to be retold around the fire, from parent to child, until the whole earth knows. The Lord's Supper carries the same instinct — 'do this in remembrance of me.' Faith remembers, and faith tells.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded... And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The people obey exactly, and then we learn of a second set of stones — twelve set up by Joshua himself 'in the midst of the Jordan,' in the very place where the priests had stood with the ark. There are thus two memorials: the visible stones carried to Gilgal for the instruction of generations, and these hidden stones planted in the riverbed itself. Soon the returning flood would cover them, yet 'they are there to this day' — a witness known to God and to those who placed them, attesting that the dry path had truly been there, that the deliverance was real even when the waters closed over it again. Wenham notes the interpretive debate over whether there were one or two sets of stones; the text most naturally reads as two, each with its own testimony. There is a quiet beauty in the hidden memorial. Some of God's works are public and visible, set up at Gilgal for all to see; others are hidden beneath the waters, known only to God and to faith. Sproul observed that not every monument to God's faithfulness is public; the believer carries hidden memorials in the heart, secret testimonies of grace that the world never sees but God never forgets. The stones in the riverbed, soon submerged, declare that the path of deliverance was real — even when the evidence is hidden beneath the flood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — The Priests Come Up; The Waters Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests stand in the midst of the Jordan until everything is finished. The armed men of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh cross over before their brothers. On this day the LORD exalts Joshua in the eyes of all Israel. When the priests come up, the Jordan returns to flood stage.
verseByVerse.theology: The exaltation of Joshua is realized: 'they stood in awe of him, just as they had stood in awe of Moses' (v. 14). The waters return only after the last of the people and the ark have crossed, sealing the completeness of the deliverance. God's salvation leaves no one behind.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the Transjordan tribes faithfully kept their pledge (ch. 1), crossing armed ahead of their brothers. Sproul observed that the returning flood, sealing the dry path behind them, marks a decisive, irreversible passage — like baptism, there is no going back to the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people... The people passed over in haste. And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people. The sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them. About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle...
verseByVerse.commentary: The priests hold their post 'until everything was finished' — steadfast in the riverbed while the whole nation passes, a model of patient perseverance in the place of duty. 'The people passed over in haste,' the narrator notes; there was holy urgency, perhaps awe at the heaped waters towering nearby. And then the Transjordan tribes — Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh — cross over armed at the head of the army, exactly as they had pledged in chapter 1 and as Moses had commanded. About 40,000 warriors march 'before the LORD for battle.' Their faithfulness is quietly commended; they kept their word, leaving their families settled east of the Jordan and crossing to fight for their brothers' inheritance. Wenham notes that this fulfillment of the pledge confirms the covenant unity of the tribes — no one rests while brothers fight. The phrase 'before the LORD for battle' is striking: they march not merely before Joshua but before the LORD himself, as if going to war in the very presence of God. Calvin observes that the ordering of the crossing — people first, then priests with the ark — shows the ark's role as rear guard as well as vanguard, God's presence surrounding his people on every side. The army of God advances, the tribes united, the warriors armed, the presence of God in their midst and at their back.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise of 3:7 is now fulfilled: 'On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel.' The crossing has done its authenticating work; the people now revere Joshua 'just as they had stood in awe of Moses.' The succession is complete, the new mediator confirmed, and Israel's confidence in his leadership secured for the rest of his life. Note that the LORD exalts Joshua — the honor is God-given, not self-grasped. Joshua did not promote himself; he simply obeyed, and God lifted him before the people. This is the biblical pattern: 'Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you at the proper time' (1 Pet. 5:6). Sproul observed that true spiritual authority is always conferred from above, never seized from below; the leader whom God exalts is the leader the people may safely follow. And once more the Christological shadow falls across the text. Joshua — Jesus — is exalted before all the people by passing through the waters. The greater Joshua would be exalted before all by passing through the waters of death and rising, 'highly exalted' by God and given 'the name that is above every name' (Phil. 2:9). The awe Israel felt before Joshua is a faint shadow of the worship every knee will one day bring to Christ. God exalts his savior that his people might trust and follow.

verseByVerse.quote: ...Joshua commanded the priests, Come up out of the Jordan. And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.
verseByVerse.commentary: At Joshua's command — itself given at the LORD's word — the priests come up out of the riverbed, and the moment their feet touch dry land, 'the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.' The ark goes last; only when God's presence has crossed do the waters rush back. The deliverance is complete; not one Israelite was left behind, and the flood returns to seal the passage. There is profound assurance in the timing. The waters did not return while a single soul was still crossing; they waited until the very last of the people and the ark itself had come up. God's salvation leaves no one stranded in the riverbed. And then the flood closes over the path. Sproul observed that the returning waters mark a decisive, irreversible passage — like baptism, there is no going back to the far bank, no return to the wilderness. The way behind is closed; the way forward is into the land. Calvin notes that the immediate return of the flood the instant the priests stepped onto dry ground proved beyond doubt that the parting was no natural ebb but the direct act of God, beginning and ending at his command. The hidden stones now lie beneath the torrent, but the people stand on the soil of promise. The crossing is finished; the conquest begins.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — The Stones at Gilgal and the Purpose of the Memorial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel comes up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camps at Gilgal, where Joshua sets up the twelve stones. He explains again that the stones will prompt children's questions, so that the deliverance may be retold — that all the earth may know the LORD's mighty hand and Israel may fear him forever.
verseByVerse.theology: The dual purpose of the memorial is declared: that the nations may know the LORD's hand is mighty (witness), and that Israel may fear the LORD forever (worship). God's redemptive acts are meant to be remembered, retold, and to issue in reverent worship across generations.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller noted that the gospel, like these stones, is meant to be retold to each generation; faith is always one generation from extinction if not deliberately transmitted. Begg observed that the proper fruit of remembering God's deeds is not nostalgia but the fear of the LORD — reverent, joyful worship.

verseByVerse.quote: The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho. And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary: The date is significant: 'the tenth day of the first month.' This was the very day on which, forty years earlier, Israel had selected the Passover lamb in Egypt (Exod. 12:3) — the threshold of the exodus. Now, on that same date, Israel enters the land. The deliverance that began at Passover finds its destination at Gilgal; the God who brought them out brings them in, and he marks the entry on the anniversary of the exit. The people encamp at Gilgal, on the border of Jericho, and there Joshua sets up the twelve stones — the visible, permanent memorial of the crossing. Wenham notes the careful chronological detail, anchoring the event in the sacred calendar and binding the conquest to the exodus as one unbroken work of redemption. Gilgal will become Israel's first base of operations in the land, the place where the camp returns again and again. Calvin observes that the setting up of the stones at the very place of encampment ensured the memorial would be daily before their eyes, a constant prompt to gratitude and a perpetual lesson for the children growing up in the camp. The God who saves also dates his salvation, weaving each new deliverance into the long story of his faithfulness, that his people might see the whole as one.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the people of Israel, When your children ask their fathers in times to come, What do these stones mean? then you shall let your children know, Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground. For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea...
verseByVerse.commentary: Once more the question of the children is set before the parents — 'What do these stones mean?' — and once more the answer is supplied: tell them how Israel passed over on dry ground. But now Joshua draws the crucial parallel explicitly: 'as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over.' The two crossings are bound together as one continuous testimony to God's saving power — the sea that brought them out of bondage and the river that brought them into the inheritance. The catechism of the children must include both: the God who redeems from slavery is the God who brings into rest. Keller stressed that the gospel, like these stones, must be retold to each rising generation; faith is always one generation from extinction if it is not deliberately and lovingly transmitted. Calvin notes that Joshua links the present wonder to the past one so that the children might see not isolated miracles but the consistent character of a covenant-keeping God. There is great pastoral wisdom here for every Christian home: we are to tell our children not only the doctrines but the deeds — what God has done, in history and in our own lives — so that their faith rests not on abstraction but on the mighty acts of a God who saves. The stones preach; the parents proclaim; the children believe.

verseByVerse.quote: ...so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends by lifting the whole event to its highest purpose, and that purpose is two-fold. First, horizontal and missionary: 'that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty.' The drying of the Jordan was not for Israel alone; it was a sign to the nations, a public display of the power of the true God, that the whole earth might know him. Already in chapter 2 the report of God's deeds had reached and converted Rahab; the conquest is, among other things, a proclamation to the Gentiles. Second, vertical and doxological: 'that you may fear the LORD your God forever.' The proper fruit of remembering God's mighty acts is not mere nostalgia but the fear of the LORD — reverent, awe-filled, joyful worship, sustained 'forever.' Begg observed that the goal of all God's wonders is worship; he acts in history that his people might bow in adoration. Sproul noted that the fear of the LORD is the only adequate response to the revelation of his might — not cringing terror, but the reverent awe that is the beginning of wisdom. The memorial stones, then, point beyond Israel to the whole earth, and beyond history to eternity: that all peoples might know him, and that his people might fear and worship him forever. This is the final purpose of every mighty act of God — including the greatest, the cross and resurrection — that the earth might know and his people might worship.

4.theology:
The Theology of Memory. God commands a tangible memorial because he knows how quickly the human heart forgets. The stones exist for the children — 'when your children ask, What do these stones mean?' — establishing the duty of every generation to retell God's mighty acts. Faith is preserved and transmitted through deliberate remembrance, the same instinct embodied in the Lord's Supper: 'do this in remembrance of me.'

One Unbroken Work of Redemption. The Jordan crossing is explicitly bound to the Red Sea (v. 23): the God who brought Israel out of bondage is the God who brings them into the inheritance. Salvation is one seamless work, from exodus to conquest, from justification to glorification — and the date (the tenth of the first month) ties the entry to the Passover that began it.

Salvation for the Sake of God's Glory Among the Nations. The final purpose (v. 24) is that 'all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty' and that Israel may 'fear the LORD forever.' God's redemptive acts are missionary and doxological — meant to make him known to the world and worshiped by his people forever.
4.examples:
Then: A nation fresh from a miracle was commanded to gather stones from the riverbed and build a heap that would outlast them all. God knew their children would forget unless the memory was set in stone and the story told around the fire. The monument at Gilgal became Israel's catechism in rock — a standing answer to the children's question, 'What do these stones mean?'

Now: We too are prone to forget the mercies that should anchor our faith forever. The Christian builds memorials of grace — in the sacraments, in testimony, in the deliberate telling of God's deeds to our children. Faith is always one generation from extinction if it is not retold. So we tell the next generation what God has done, supremely at the cross, that all the earth may know his mighty hand and that our children may fear and worship the LORD forever.

5.title: Circumcision, Passover, and the Commander of the LORD's Army
5.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth.<sup>4</sup>And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they had come out of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Though all the people who came out had been circumcised, yet all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness after they had come out of Egypt had not been circumcised.<sup>6</sup>For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD; the LORD swore to them that he would not let them see the land that the LORD had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>7</sup>So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. For they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.<sup>8</sup>When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.<sup>10</sup>While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho.<sup>11</sup>And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.<sup>12</sup>And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.<sup>13</sup>When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?"<sup>14</sup>And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come." And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?"<sup>15</sup>And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
5.overview:
Israel has crossed the Jordan and stands in the land — and the first thing God commands is not a battle plan but a knife. Before Jericho can fall, the people must be marked again as the covenant people of God. The whole generation born in the wilderness had not been circumcised; the sign of the covenant had lapsed during the forty years of judgment. Now, in the land of promise, God renews the sign. There is a striking vulnerability in this: an uncircumcised, recovering army camped within sight of a hostile city. But the God who fights for his people does not need a fit army; he needs a consecrated one. Holiness precedes conquest.

'Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you' (v. 9), God declares, and names the place Gilgal — 'rolling.' The reproach of Egypt, the shame of slavery and of the wilderness wandering, is rolled away as the foreskins fall. The people who were a generation of death in the desert are reconstituted as the people of promise in the land. Sproul observed that God deals first with the spiritual identity of his people before he deals with their enemies; the inward renewal of the covenant must come before the outward victory.

Then Israel keeps the Passover in the land for the first time (v. 10) — the feast of redemption celebrated now in the place of inheritance. And the next day the manna ceases (v. 12). For forty years bread had fallen from heaven; now the people eat the produce of Canaan. The age of wilderness provision gives way to the age of inheritance. The miraculous sustenance ends not because God's care ends but because his promise has arrived; the people now eat at the table he prepared for them in the land.

The chapter climaxes with one of the most awesome theophanies in Scripture. Joshua, surveying Jericho, meets a man with a drawn sword and demands, 'Are you for us, or for our adversaries?' The answer reframes everything: 'No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD.' This is no mere angel — Joshua falls on his face and worships, and is commanded to remove his sandals, for the ground is holy. The same words that came to Moses at the burning bush now come to Joshua. This is the pre-incarnate Christ, the Captain of the LORD's hosts, who has come not to take sides but to take over. The real commander of the conquest is the Son of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of Canaan lose heart when they hear the Jordan has been dried up. God commands Joshua to circumcise the new generation, which had not been circumcised in the wilderness. The reproach of Egypt is rolled away, and the place is named Gilgal.
verseByVerse.theology: The renewal of circumcision restores the covenant sign before any battle. Holiness and covenant identity precede conquest. Circumcision points forward to the circumcision of the heart (Deut. 30:6; Rom. 2:29) and ultimately to baptism, the sign of the new covenant (Col. 2:11–12).
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul noted that God consecrates his people before he uses them. Ferguson observed the vulnerability of an army recovering from circumcision within sight of the enemy — proof that the conquest depends not on Israel's strength but on God's protection. The melting hearts of the kings (v. 1) show God fighting before a sword is drawn.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them...
verseByVerse.commentary: The news of the Jordan crossing spreads, and the effect on the kings of Canaan is exactly what Rahab had reported (2:11): 'their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them.' Before Israel lifts a sword, the LORD has already defeated the enemy's morale. The God who fights for his people had won the psychological battle through the report of his deeds. Notice the divine timing: the kings are paralyzed with terror at precisely the moment Israel becomes most vulnerable, for the very next command will leave the army incapacitated by circumcision. While Israel lies recovering, the Canaanites are too demoralized to attack. This is the providence of God arranging the enemy's fear to cover his people's weakness. Wenham notes that the melting hearts fulfill the song of Moses (Exod. 15:15–16) and Rahab's confession, confirming that the conquest proceeds under God's sovereign orchestration. Sproul observed that God often wins his battles before they are fought, defeating the enemy in the unseen realm of the heart. The kings 'by the sea' and 'beyond the Jordan to the west' — the whole land trembles. The God of Israel needs no advantage of arms; he melts the hearts of kings with a rumor of his power, and clears the field before his recovering people can be threatened.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the LORD said to Joshua, Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time... For all the people who came out had been circumcised, but all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness... had not been circumcised...
verseByVerse.commentary: God's first command in the land is startling: 'Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel.' The entire generation born during the forty years of wandering had not received the covenant sign; during the years of judgment in the wilderness, circumcision had lapsed. Now, in the land of promise, the sign of the Abrahamic covenant must be restored before anything else proceeds. The renewal of the covenant sign precedes the conquest of the land. There is rich theology here. Circumcision was the seal of belonging to God's covenant people, the mark in the flesh of the promise to Abraham. A generation that had been under the shadow of judgment is now reconstituted as the people of promise. Ferguson notes the vulnerability — an army laid up and incapacitated within sight of a hostile city — which proves dramatically that Israel's security rests not in military readiness but in God's protection. Calvin observes that God deliberately ordered this exposure to teach Israel that the land would be won by his power, not their strength. And the deeper trajectory points to the heart: the prophets and apostles would speak of the circumcision of the heart (Deut. 30:6; Rom. 2:29), and Paul would link circumcision to baptism, the sign of the new covenant (Col. 2:11–12). The flint knives at Gilgal anticipate the inward cutting away of the flesh that only the Spirit can perform.

verseByVerse.quote: When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed. And the LORD said to Joshua, Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you. And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The whole nation is circumcised and then waits, healing, in the camp. And God speaks one of the great gospel words of the book: 'Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you.' The 'reproach of Egypt' was the shame of slavery, the taunt of the nations that Israel's God had brought them out only to let them die in the wilderness (cf. Exod. 32:12; Num. 14:13–16) — the reproach of a generation that had perished under judgment. Now, with the covenant sign renewed and the people standing in the land, that shame is 'rolled away.' The place is named Gilgal, from a Hebrew root meaning 'to roll.' The image is of a heavy stone of reproach rolled off the people. There is gospel here that takes the breath away. The God who rolls away reproach is the God who would one day roll away a far greater stone — the stone from the tomb — and roll away forever the reproach of sin from his people. Sproul observed that God deals with the identity and standing of his people before he deals with their enemies; the inward renewal must precede the outward victory. Calvin notes that the rolling away of reproach signifies the full restoration of Israel to covenant favor. What slavery and judgment had shamed, grace now rolls away. The people stand healed, renewed, marked again as God's own — and ready, at last, for the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — The Passover and the Cessation of Manna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel keeps the Passover at Gilgal on the fourteenth day of the month. The day after, they eat the produce of the land — unleavened cakes and parched grain. The manna ceases, for they now eat the fruit of Canaan.
verseByVerse.theology: The Passover, the feast of redemption, is kept for the first time in the land — celebrating in the inheritance what was inaugurated in Egypt. The cessation of manna marks the transition from wilderness provision to the inheritance: God's miraculous sustenance gives way to the promised land's fruit, not because his care ends but because his promise has arrived.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg notes that the Passover in the land ties the whole journey together — redemption from Egypt finds its rest in Canaan. Keller observed that the end of manna is not abandonment but maturation; God provides differently in different seasons, but always faithfully.

verseByVerse.quote: While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho. And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.
verseByVerse.commentary: With the covenant sign renewed, Israel keeps the Passover — and this is the first Passover celebrated in the promised land. The feast of redemption, instituted on the night of the exodus when the blood of the lamb spared the firstborn, is now kept in the land of inheritance. The whole journey is bound together: the redemption that began with blood on the doorposts in Egypt finds its destination in the land flowing with milk and honey. Begg notes the beautiful symmetry — the Passover that started the exodus now crowns the entry, redemption finding its rest. And 'the day after the Passover... they ate of the produce of the land.' For the first time, Israel eats Canaan's own grain, unleavened cakes and parched grain from fields they did not plant. They are tasting the inheritance. The Passover is, of course, the great type of Christ: 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed' (1 Cor. 5:7). Israel cannot enter the land's blessings except through the blood of the lamb; neither can we enter our inheritance except through the blood of the true Lamb. Calvin observes that the prompt keeping of the feast, the moment the people were able, shows their renewed devotion. The redeemed people, marked by the covenant sign and sheltered by the paschal blood, now sit down to eat the fruit of the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The manna ceased.' For forty years, bread had fallen from heaven every morning — a daily, visible miracle, a standing testimony that God could feed his people in a barren waste. Now, the day after they eat Canaan's grain, the manna stops. An era ends. But notice: the manna does not cease because God's provision fails, but because God's promise has arrived. The people no longer need bread from the sky because they now eat the fruit of the land God swore to give them. The miraculous gives way to the inherited; wilderness provision yields to the abundance of the promise. Keller observed that the end of manna is not abandonment but maturation — God provides differently in different seasons, but always faithfully; the same God who rained bread from heaven now gives the harvest of the land. There is a lesson here about the changing modes of God's faithfulness: we must not cling to one form of God's provision so tightly that we miss the new and better form he is giving. Wenham notes that the cessation of manna marks decisively the close of the wilderness period and the dawn of the settled life in the land. The forty years are over. The people who ate the bread of pilgrimage now eat the bread of inheritance — a foretaste of the day when God's people, their pilgrimage complete, will eat at the marriage supper of the Lamb in the land that has no end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–15 — The Commander of the LORD's Army
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Joshua surveys Jericho, he sees a man with a drawn sword and asks whose side he is on. The man answers that he is the commander of the army of the LORD. Joshua falls in worship and is told to remove his sandals, for the place is holy.
verseByVerse.theology: This is widely held to be a Christophany — an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ. He accepts worship (which a created angel would refuse, Rev. 22:9) and declares the ground holy, echoing the burning bush. He comes not to take sides but to take command: the true Captain of the conquest is the Son of God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin and many Reformers identified the commander as the eternal Word, the Angel of the LORD. Sproul stressed that the question 'are you for us?' is the wrong question — the issue is never whether God is on our side but whether we are on his. Begg noted that Joshua, the great general, falls on his face: the real commander has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, Are you for us, or for our adversaries?
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua, surveying the city he is about to attack, suddenly sees 'a man standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand.' The drawn sword signals a warrior ready for battle. Joshua, ever the soldier, approaches and demands the password of every sentry: 'Are you for us, or for our adversaries?' It is a natural question for a general on the eve of war — but it is, as the answer will reveal, the wrong question. Joshua assumes the categories of human warfare: friend or foe, our side or theirs. But the One before him does not fit those categories, because he is the LORD's own commander, and the LORD does not take sides — he takes over. Sproul stressed this with characteristic force: the issue is never whether God is on our side, but whether we are on his. We are forever asking God to bless our plans, to join our cause, to fight our battles; the right question is whether we have submitted to his cause, enlisted in his army, surrendered to his command. Begg noted the irony that Joshua, the great general of Israel, is about to discover that the real commander has just arrived on the field, and it is not him. The drawn sword is a sword of judgment poised over Jericho; the LORD himself has come to lead the conquest. Joshua's question betrays the smallness of his vision; the answer will enlarge it beyond all measure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come. And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, What does my lord say to his servant?
verseByVerse.commentary: 'No' — neither of Joshua's categories applies. 'I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come.' This is no ordinary soldier and no mere mortal. He commands the hosts of heaven, the angelic armies of God. And Joshua's response is decisive for identifying him: he 'fell on his face to the earth and worshiped.' Now, throughout Scripture, holy angels consistently refuse worship — 'You must not do that... worship God!' (Rev. 22:9). But this commander accepts Joshua's worship without rebuke. This is the great clue. Calvin and the Reformers identified him as the Angel of the LORD, the eternal Word, the pre-incarnate Christ — for he receives the worship due to God alone. Here is the Son of God, the Captain of the LORD's hosts, come down to lead the conquest of the land. The true commander of the conquest is not Joshua but Christ. And Joshua's reply is the reply of true faith: 'What does my lord say to his servant?' The general becomes a servant; the commander of Israel kneels before the Commander of heaven, ready to obey. Sproul observed that the moment we glimpse who Christ truly is, the only fitting posture is on our faces in worship and surrender. The conquest of Jericho will not be Joshua's strategy but Christ's command. The Son of God has taken the field, and the outcome is already certain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy. And Joshua did so.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy.' These are nearly the exact words spoken to Moses at the burning bush (Exod. 3:5). The parallel is unmistakable and intentional: the same divine Presence that commissioned Moses now commissions Joshua. The ground is holy not because of anything in the soil but because the holy God stands upon it. Wherever Christ is, there is holy ground. This seals the identification of the commander: he is the same One who spoke from the bush, the eternal God, the pre-incarnate Christ. Joshua, like Moses, must remove his sandals — the posture of a creature before the Creator, of a sinner before the Holy One. And note: there is no further command recorded in this verse; the instructions for taking Jericho come in chapter 6. The point of this encounter is not primarily strategy but worship. Before the battle, Joshua must learn who truly commands. Begg observed that the great lesson of Gilgal's holy ground is that the conquest belongs to the LORD; the general must first be a worshiper. Calvin notes that the removal of the sandals signifies reverence and the laying aside of all self-confidence in the presence of God. The chapter that began with a knife and a Passover ends on holy ground, with Israel's commander on his face before the true Commander. The conquest of Jericho begins, as all true victory begins, in worship.

5.theology:
Consecration Before Conquest. Before a single battle, God renews the covenant sign (circumcision), the people keep the Passover, and Joshua worships on holy ground. Holiness precedes victory; God consecrates his people before he uses them. The conquest depends not on a fit army but on a sanctified one, for the LORD himself does the fighting.

The Pre-incarnate Christ as Commander. The commander of the LORD's army, who accepts worship and declares the ground holy, is the pre-incarnate Son of God. He comes not to take sides but to take command — the true Captain of the conquest. This reframes the entire book: the wars of Joshua are the wars of Christ, and the question is never whether God is on our side but whether we are on his.

From Wilderness Provision to Inheritance. The manna ceases and Israel eats the fruit of Canaan; the reproach of Egypt is rolled away at Gilgal. God's modes of provision change with the seasons of his promise, but his faithfulness never fails. Redemption that began at Passover finds its rest in the land — a foretaste of the people of God entering their final inheritance through the blood of the true Lamb.
5.examples:
Then: An army stood in enemy territory and, instead of sharpening swords, submitted to the knife of circumcision, kept the Passover, watched the manna stop, and fell on its face before a stranger with a drawn sword. Israel learned at Gilgal that the conquest would be won not by readiness for war but by consecration to a holy God whose Son was its true Commander.

Now: We are forever asking God to bless our plans and join our side; the risen Christ confronts us, as he confronted Joshua, with the truth that he comes to take command, not sides. The Christian life begins where the conquest began — on our faces in worship, the reproach of our slavery rolled away, sheltered by the blood of the true Passover Lamb, eating the fruit of an inheritance we did not earn, following the Captain of the LORD's hosts into every battle he has already won.

6.title: The Fall of Jericho
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.<sup>3</sup>You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days.<sup>4</sup>Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets.<sup>5</sup>And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."<sup>6</sup>So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."<sup>8</sup>And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them.<sup>9</sup>The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>10</sup>But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout."<sup>11</sup>So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.<sup>12</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually. And the armed men were walking before them, and the rear guard was walking after the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>14</sup>And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.<sup>15</sup>On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times.<sup>16</sup>And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.<sup>17</sup>And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent.<sup>18</sup>But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it.<sup>19</sup>But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD."<sup>20</sup>So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city.<sup>21</sup>Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.<sup>22</sup>But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her."<sup>23</sup>So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.<sup>26</sup>Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. "At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates."<sup>27</sup>So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
6.overview:
Jericho was a fortress — high double walls, a gated city sealed up tight against the people of Israel. By every measure of military science, it should have required a long siege, battering rams, and great loss of life. Instead, God commands the most absurd battle plan in the history of warfare: march around the city once a day for six days, and on the seventh day march around seven times, blow trumpets, and shout. No siege engines, no scaling ladders, no swords drawn until the walls have already fallen. Why? So that no flesh may boast. The fall of Jericho is salvation by grace through faith, dramatized in stone and trumpet. 'God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise... that no human being might boast in the presence of God' (1 Cor. 1:27–29).

The strategy is an offense to human pride, and that is precisely the point. Calvin observed that God deliberately chose a method that gave Israel no occasion to credit their own strength or skill; the walls fell by the power of God alone, in answer to the obedience of faith. Hebrews 11:30 makes the lesson explicit: 'By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been encircled for seven days.' Faith marched in silence around an impregnable wall for a week on the bare word of God, and at the appointed moment the wall came down.

At the heart of the conquest stands grace. The city is 'devoted to destruction' (herem) — given wholly to the LORD as the firstfruits of the land, an eruption of God's judgment upon a civilization whose iniquity had become full. Yet in the midst of judgment, mercy: Rahab and her household are spared, gathered out by the scarlet cord, the only survivors of the doomed city. Judgment and mercy meet, as they always meet, at the place of the blood. The harlot of Jericho walks out of the falling city into the people of God and into the line of the Messiah.

And the seven-day pattern, the seven trumpets, the seventh-day climax — all of it breathes the theology of God's appointed time. The walls fall not when Israel decides but when God decrees, on the seventh day, at the seventh circuit, at the sound of the trumpet and the shout. So too the walls of this world's defiance will fall at the last trumpet, when the King returns. Jericho is a preview of the final judgment and the final salvation — the city of man falling before the city of God, the foolishness of God confounding the wisdom of the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Battle Plan of Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jericho is shut up tight. The LORD declares, 'I have given Jericho into your hand,' and gives the strange instructions: march around the city once daily for six days with seven priests blowing trumpets before the ark, and on the seventh day march around seven times.
verseByVerse.theology: The victory is announced as already given (v. 2) before a single step is taken — grace precedes the act. The bizarre, unmilitary strategy ensures that the glory goes wholly to God. Faith obeys the foolish-seeming command of God, and the power is all his.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin notes that God chose a method giving Israel no room to boast. MacArthur observed that the seven priests with the ark show the conquest is a worship procession, not merely a military operation — God's presence, not human force, brings down the wall.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in. And the LORD said to Joshua, See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Jericho was shut up inside and outside' — the city is sealed, locked down in terror, its gates barred against Israel. From a human standpoint, it is an impregnable fortress; no one goes out, no one comes in. And against this picture of total human defense, God speaks the decisive word: 'See, I have given Jericho into your hand.' Note the tense again — 'I have given.' Before a single Israelite has marched, before a trumpet has sounded, the victory is already accomplished in the courts of heaven. The city that is humanly shut up is divinely handed over. This is the gospel grammar of the whole book: God gives, and faith takes. The contrast is deliberate and beautiful. Jericho's strength — its shut-up walls — is precisely what makes the coming miracle so glorious; the more impregnable the fortress, the clearer it will be that God alone brought it down. Calvin notes that God speaks of the conquest as accomplished to bolster Joshua's faith for the strange task ahead. MacArthur observes that 'its king and mighty men of valor' are explicitly included — even the strongest defenders are already given over to defeat. The walls that shut Israel out cannot shut God out; the city that bars its gates has already been handed to the One who needs no gate. Faith now has only to march on the strength of the accomplished promise.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days. Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets... and all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat...
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the battle plan, and it is gloriously absurd by every standard of military science. March around the city once a day for six days. Seven priests blowing seven rams'-horn trumpets are to go before the ark of the covenant. On the seventh day, march around seven times, blow the trumpets, and let the people shout — and the wall will 'fall down flat.' No siege engines, no battering rams, no scaling ladders. The conquest of the mightiest fortress in the land will come by trumpets and a shout. Why such a plan? So that no flesh may boast. As Paul would later write, 'God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise... that no human being might boast in the presence of God' (1 Cor. 1:27–29). The number seven, the number of completion and covenant, saturates the instructions — seven priests, seven trumpets, seven days, seven circuits on the seventh day — marking the whole event as God's appointed, perfect work. MacArthur observed that the seven priests bearing the ark reveal that this is fundamentally a worship procession, not a military operation; God's presence at the center brings down the wall. Calvin notes that the very strangeness of the command was a test of faith — would Israel obey a plan that made no sense to human reason? The trumpets of rams' horns were the trumpets of jubilee and of festival, not of war; Jericho falls to a sound of celebration, the announcement that the LORD reigns.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD. And he said to the people, Go forward. March around the city. Let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua obeys without hesitation or modification. The man who fell on his face before the commander of the LORD's army now relays the strange command exactly as given. There is no recorded argument, no attempt to supplement the plan with conventional tactics — only obedience. 'Take up the ark of the covenant' — once again, the presence of God is placed at the center of the procession. The ark goes with the trumpets and the people, signifying that it is the LORD enthroned upon the ark who will bring down the wall. The order of march is significant: armed men in front, then the seven priests with trumpets, then the ark, then a rear guard. The whole nation is arranged around the central reality of God's presence. Calvin notes that Joshua's prompt and exact obedience is the proof of his faith; he does not lean on his own understanding as a general but submits wholly to the word of the divine Commander. There is great instruction here for the church: the leader's task is not to improve on God's commands but to carry them out faithfully, however foolish they may appear to worldly wisdom. Wenham observes the liturgical, processional character of the whole scene — this is less a battle than a sacred parade, a week-long act of worship that ends in the collapse of the enemy's stronghold. Joshua sets the procession in motion on the bare word of God, and faith begins its silent march.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Six Days of Marching
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For six days Israel marches once around Jericho in silence, the armed men before the trumpet-blowing priests, the ark in the midst, the rear guard behind. Joshua commands the people not to shout until the day he tells them.
verseByVerse.theology: The six days of silent marching are a sustained test of patient faith. Obedience without immediate result requires trust in God's timing. The disciplined silence of the people, holding their shout until commanded, models submission to God's appointed moment rather than human impatience.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg noted the discipline of waiting — six days of marching with no visible result demands faith that God's word will not return void. Ferguson observed that much of the Christian life is faithful, unglamorous repetition, trusting that God acts in his own time.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them... Joshua commanded the people, You shall not shout... until the day I tell you to shout. So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary: The procession sets out exactly as commanded. The trumpets sound 'before the LORD' — the ark, God's throne, is in the midst of the march, so the whole circuit is conducted in the presence of God. And Joshua imposes a striking discipline: 'You shall not shout... until the day I tell you.' The people march in total silence, save for the blaring of the rams'-horn trumpets. Only the sound of God's announcement (the trumpets) breaks the silence; the voice of the people is held back until the appointed moment. This restraint is itself an act of faith and submission. There is no premature triumphalism, no shouting before the time. And then, anticlimactically, 'they came into the camp and spent the night.' Day one ends with no wall fallen, no battle fought — just one silent circuit and a return to camp. Begg noted the discipline of such waiting: a full day of marching with no visible result, and the command to do it again tomorrow. Faith must trust that God's word will not return void even when nothing seems to happen. Wenham observes that the daily return to camp heightens the suspense and tests the people's perseverance. The watching Canaanites must have grown bold, even mocking — what kind of army marches in silence and goes home? But Israel's confidence rested not on appearances but on the bare word of the LORD: the wall will fall on the day he says.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD... And the second day they marched around the city once and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Joshua rose early in the morning' — again the mark of eager obedience — and the second day's march unfolds exactly like the first: once around the city, then back to camp. 'So they did for six days.' The narrator compresses the repetition into a single summarizing phrase, but we must not pass over it too quickly. Six days of identical, unglamorous obedience. Six days of marching in silence around a wall that did not fall. Six days of enduring whatever taunts the Canaanites hurled from the ramparts. Six days of trusting that the seventh would bring what the first six had not. Ferguson observed that much of the Christian life is precisely this — faithful, unglamorous repetition, trusting that God acts in his own time and not on our schedule. The daily discipline of obedience, the patient continuance in well-doing when no result is visible, is the very substance of faith. Calvin notes that the prolonged marching was designed to exercise and strengthen Israel's faith, weaning them from the demand for immediate results and teaching them to wait on the LORD's appointed hour. There is profound encouragement here for the believer who labors and prays and obeys and sees nothing change: the six days are not wasted. The God who appointed the seventh day for the wall to fall is faithful, and the patient faith of the six days will be vindicated. Keep marching; the wall will fall on God's day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Seventh Day and the Fall of the Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the seventh day they march around seven times. At Joshua's command, the people shout, the trumpets blare, and the wall falls down flat. The city is devoted to destruction; only Rahab and her household are spared. The silver, gold, bronze, and iron are devoted to the LORD's treasury.
verseByVerse.theology: The wall falls by faith (Heb. 11:30), at God's appointed time, by his power alone. The herem (devotion to destruction) is an eruption of God's judgment on a civilization whose iniquity was full — a sober preview of final judgment. Yet Rahab is saved by the scarlet cord: mercy in the midst of judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin stressed that the wall fell by God's power, not the shout itself — the shout was the act of faith, not the cause. Sproul observed that the herem foreshadows the final judgment, when the city of man falls before the City of God. Rahab's rescue is grace breaking into judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times. And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.
verseByVerse.commentary: The seventh day dawns, and the pattern intensifies — seven circuits instead of one. The number of completion is multiplied to its fullness: the seventh circuit on the seventh day. The whole structure has built to this moment of divinely appointed climax. And at the seventh time, after the trumpets blast, Joshua gives the command that has been held back all week: 'Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.' Note the ground of the shout: not 'shout, and the city will be given,' but 'shout, for the LORD has given you the city.' The shout is not a magical incantation that topples the wall; it is the response of faith to an accomplished gift. The victory is already granted in heaven; the shout is the people's amen, their confession that God has done it. Calvin stressed precisely this — the wall fell by God's power, not by the volume of the shout; the shout was the act of faith, not the cause of the miracle. Sproul observed that the seventh-day, seventh-circuit timing teaches that God acts on his own schedule, at the fullness of time, not a moment before. There is a beautiful trajectory here toward the last day: as the wall of Jericho fell at the seventh trumpet on the seventh day, so the kingdoms of this world will fall 'at the last trumpet' (1 Cor. 15:52), when the seventh angel sounds and 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord' (Rev. 11:15). Faith shouts in confidence, for the LORD has given the city.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent. But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction... But all silver and gold... are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before the shout brings down the wall, Joshua announces the terms of the conquest, and they are sobering. The city is 'devoted to the LORD for destruction' — the Hebrew herem, the ban. Jericho, as the firstfruits of the land, is given wholly to God; nothing is to be taken as spoil, for the whole city is an offering of judgment to the LORD. This is no ordinary war of plunder; it is an act of divine justice. Sproul observed that the herem foreshadows the final judgment, when the impenitent city of man falls before the City of God; the iniquity of the Canaanites, in God's patient reckoning, had finally become full (Gen. 15:16). But in the very midst of the pronouncement of judgment, mercy shines: 'Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers.' The Canaanite harlot and her household are spared, the lone exception to the ban, saved because of her faith. Judgment and mercy meet, as they always meet, at the place of the blood — at the scarlet cord. The silver and gold are 'holy to the LORD,' set apart for his treasury; the firstfruits belong to God. Calvin notes that the devotion of the firstfruits to God consecrated the whole conquest as his work. The warning against taking the devoted things (v. 18) will prove tragically prophetic in the very next chapter, when Achan's greed brings the ban's curse upon Israel itself.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city. Then they devoted all in the city to destruction...
verseByVerse.commentary: 'And the wall fell down flat.' After six days of silent marching and seven circuits on the seventh, after a week of faith with no visible result, the moment comes — and the great fortress wall of Jericho collapses utterly. The phrase 'fell down flat' suggests the wall dropped straight down where it stood, so that 'the people went up into the city, every man straight before him' — they climbed in over the rubble at every point, the city wide open before them. There was no breach to storm, no gate to batter; the whole defense simply fell. Hebrews 11:30 enshrines this as a monument of faith: 'By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been encircled for seven days.' Faith marched in obedience; God brought down the wall. Calvin marvels that the fall came not by human contrivance but by the naked power of God, in answer to faith. The captured city is then devoted to destruction according to the herem — a scene that troubles the modern reader and ought to sober us all. We must not soften it dishonestly: it is a real and terrible judgment. Yet we must read it rightly, as the eruption of God's holy justice upon a culture that burned its children to idols, a localized preview of the final judgment when the King returns with a sword from his mouth. The same God who shouted down the wall will one day bring down every stronghold of human defiance. Jericho is a warning written in rubble: the city that bars its gates against the living God cannot stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — Rahab Saved and the City Cursed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua sends the two spies to bring Rahab and her family out of the city, and they dwell in Israel to this day. Jericho is burned, and Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds it. The LORD is with Joshua, and his fame spreads through all the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Rahab and her household are rescued out of the doomed city — the firstfruits of the Gentiles, grafted into the people of God and into the Messiah's line (Matt. 1:5). The curse on Jericho and the spread of Joshua's fame both testify that the LORD is with him. Mercy and judgment are displayed side by side.
