verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson noted that Rahab dwelling 'in Israel to this day' is the gospel in miniature — a Gentile sinner brought into the covenant community. Begg observed that the same God who judged Jericho saved Rahab; the cross is where that judgment and that mercy meet forever.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her... So Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary: As the city burns, the two spies are sent to keep the oath sworn under the scarlet cord: 'Go into the prostitute's house and bring out the woman and all who belong to her.' And so it is done — Rahab, her father, mother, brothers, and all her household are led out of the doomed city to safety. The promise made on the rooftop is kept to the letter; the scarlet cord proved true. The narrator adds the wondering note: 'she has lived in Israel to this day.' The Canaanite harlot, plucked out of the firstfruits city of judgment, is grafted into the covenant people of God — and, as Matthew's Gospel reveals, into the very line of the Messiah (Matt. 1:5). Ferguson observed that 'she dwelt in Israel to this day' is the gospel in miniature: a Gentile sinner, marked for destruction, brought into the people of God by grace through faith. Here is the breathtaking scope of God's mercy — that in the midst of the most severe judgment in the book, the lone survivor is a foreigner and a prostitute, saved entirely by grace. Begg noted that the same God who judged Jericho saved Rahab; the cross is the place where that judgment and that mercy meet forever, where the wrath that fell on the city falls instead on the substitute, and the sinner walks free. Rahab is living proof that no one is beyond the reach of grace, and that the gospel was always destined for the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates. So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua pronounces a solemn curse on anyone who would rebuild Jericho — a prophecy fulfilled centuries later in the days of Ahab, when Hiel of Bethel rebuilt the city at the cost of his firstborn and youngest son (1 Kings 16:34). The curse marks Jericho as a permanent monument to God's judgment; the firstfruits city of the ban is to remain a ruin, a perpetual warning. The chapter closes with the great refrain that has governed the whole book: 'So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.' The promise of 1:5 — 'I will be with you' — and of 3:7 — 'I will exalt you' — is fulfilled. Joshua's fame spreads not because of his generalship but because the LORD was with him; the glory belongs to God, and the renown of his servant is the byproduct of the divine presence. Wenham notes that this concluding refrain frames the Jericho narrative as the demonstration of God's faithfulness to his promises to Joshua. The fall of Jericho has proved that the LORD fights for his people, that the foolishness of God is wiser than men, that no wall can stand before him, and that even in the fiercest judgment his mercy gathers the believing. Joshua's fame, spreading through all the land, is finally the fame of his God — and it points forward to the greater Joshua, whose name is above every name, whose fame will fill the whole earth, and with whom the Father is forever well pleased.

6.theology:
Salvation by Grace, Not by Works. The walls fall not by siege engines or human strategy but by trumpets, a shout, and the bare power of God, 'so that no human being might boast' (1 Cor. 1:27–29). Hebrews 11:30 enshrines it as the triumph of faith. The conquest of the great fortress is a dramatization of the gospel: God gives the victory, and faith simply obeys and takes it.

Judgment and Mercy at the Place of the Blood. The herem upon Jericho is a real and terrible judgment, an eruption of God's justice on a civilization whose iniquity was full — a preview of final judgment. Yet in the midst of it, Rahab is saved by the scarlet cord. Judgment and mercy meet, as they always meet, at the place of the blood, foreshadowing the cross where wrath and grace embrace.

God's Appointed Time and the Last Trumpet. The seven days, seven trumpets, and seventh-day climax declare that God acts at his appointed fullness of time, not a moment before. As Jericho fell at the seventh trumpet, the kingdoms of this world will fall at the last trumpet when Christ returns (1 Cor. 15:52; Rev. 11:15). The fall of Jericho is a preview of the final victory of the kingdom of God.
6.examples:
Then: An army was commanded to defeat an impregnable fortress by marching in silence and shouting — no swords, no siege. For six days nothing happened; the Canaanites jeered from the walls. But on the seventh day, at the seventh circuit, faith shouted and God brought down the wall, that no flesh might boast. In the rubble, judgment fell on the city and mercy gathered a harlot into the people of God.

Now: We face strongholds that no human strategy can topple — entrenched sin, hardened hearts, the defiant kingdoms of this age. The lesson of Jericho is that the battle is the LORD's; we obey his seemingly foolish commands (preach the cross, pray, wait, march in faith) and trust him to bring down the wall in his time. And we remember that the same God who judges the impenitent city saves every Rahab who flees to the scarlet cord — for the cross is where his judgment and his mercy meet forever.

7.title: Achan's Sin and the Defeat at Ai
7.text: <sup>1</sup>But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel, and said to them, "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai.<sup>3</sup>And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few."<sup>4</sup>So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai,<sup>5</sup>and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.<sup>6</sup>Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads.<sup>7</sup>And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!<sup>8</sup>O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies!<sup>9</sup>For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"<sup>10</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?<sup>11</sup>Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings.<sup>12</sup>Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.<sup>13</sup>Get up! Consecrate the people and say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD, God of Israel, "There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you."<sup>14</sup>In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. And the tribe that the LORD takes by lot shall come near by clans. And the clan that the LORD takes shall come near by households. And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man.<sup>15</sup>And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD, and because he has done an outrageous thing in Israel.'"<sup>16</sup>So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken.<sup>17</sup>And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken. And he brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was taken.<sup>18</sup>And he brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.<sup>19</sup>Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me."<sup>20</sup>And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did:<sup>21</sup>when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."<sup>22</sup>So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath.<sup>23</sup>And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones.<sup>26</sup>And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
7.overview:
From the heights of Jericho to the dust of defeat at Ai — chapter 7 is one of the great hinges of the book, and one of its most sobering lessons. The victory at Jericho seemed to promise unbroken triumph, but the very next engagement ends in humiliating defeat. Thirty-six men of Israel die before the small town of Ai, and the hearts of the people 'melted and became as water' (v. 5). What went wrong? The answer is given in the first verse, before the battle is even fought: 'the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things.' One man, Achan, had secretly taken from the spoil of Jericho what God had devoted to himself — and the sin of one brought defeat upon all.

Here is the doctrine of corporate solidarity, of federal headship, written into Israel's history. 'The people of Israel broke faith,' says verse 1 — though it was one man's act. The sin of one member infects the whole body. This offends our individualistic instincts, but it is woven through all of Scripture, and it reaches its climax in the two great federal heads: in Adam all die, and in Christ all are made alive (1 Cor. 15:22; Rom. 5). Achan's hidden sin teaches that we are not the isolated individuals we imagine; we are bound together, and sin is never merely private.

The chapter also gives us Joshua's anguished prayer (vv. 6–9), the painful process of detection by lot (vv. 14–18), and Achan's confession (vv. 19–21) — 'I saw... I coveted... I took... I hid.' It is the anatomy of every sin, the very pattern of Eden: I saw, I desired, I took. And it ends in the valley of Achor, the valley of 'trouble,' where judgment falls on Achan and his household. Yet even here, grace has the last prophetic word: Hosea would one day promise that God will make 'the Valley of Achor a door of hope' (Hos. 2:15). The place of judgment becomes, in God's redemptive purpose, a gateway to mercy.

Above all, this chapter teaches the holiness of God. The God who fights for his people is a holy God who will not tolerate sin in the camp. He cannot be presumed upon; victory is not automatic. Sin, even hidden sin, even one man's sin, breaks fellowship and forfeits blessing. Calvin observed that God here teaches Israel — and us — that obedience and holiness are not optional extras to faith but its necessary fruit, and that the God who is gracious is also not to be trifled with.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Achan secretly takes from the devoted things of Jericho, and the LORD's anger burns against Israel. Confident after Jericho, Israel sends only a small force against Ai, and they are routed; thirty-six men die and the people's hearts melt.
verseByVerse.theology: The hidden sin of one man brings corporate guilt and defeat on the whole nation — the doctrine of federal solidarity. Presumption (sending a small force without seeking God) compounds the problem. God's blessing is not automatic; sin in the camp forfeits his fighting presence.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul stressed that this teaches the seriousness of sin and the reality of corporate guilt. MacArthur noted Israel's self-confidence after Jericho — they relied on the previous victory rather than the present God. Defeat is the fruit of both hidden sin and presumption.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan... of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens with a thunderous 'But' — the great adversative that turns the tide of the narrative. Jericho has fallen in triumph, but. The triumph is poisoned at the root by a hidden sin. And note the staggering grammar of corporate guilt: 'the people of Israel broke faith' — though the very same verse names a single culprit, 'Achan took some of the devoted things.' One man sinned, yet the whole nation is reckoned guilty, and 'the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.' This is the doctrine of federal solidarity, deeply offensive to our individualism and yet woven through all of Scripture. We are not the isolated atoms we imagine; we are members of a body, and the sin of one infects the whole. Sproul stressed that this teaches both the seriousness of sin and the reality of corporate guilt — sin is never merely private. The principle reaches its climax in the two federal heads of humanity: 'in Adam all die' and 'in Christ all are made alive' (1 Cor. 15:22). As one man's sin condemned the race, one Man's righteousness saves it. Achan's secret theft, then, is a dark window into our solidarity in sin under Adam — and a pointer to our greater solidarity in righteousness under Christ. The anger of the LORD burns, and the army marches to Ai unaware that the battle is already lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai... and said to them, Go up and spy out the land. And the men went up and spied out Ai. And they returned to Joshua and said to him, Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few.
verseByVerse.commentary: Flushed with the triumph at Jericho, Israel grows presumptuous. The scouts return with a confident report: Ai is a small town, 'they are few,' so there is no need to send the whole army — two or three thousand men will do. Notice what is missing from this council of war: there is no mention of inquiring of the LORD. At Jericho, every step was directed by God's explicit command; here, the strategy is devised by human assessment of the odds. The contrast is deliberate and instructive. MacArthur noted Israel's self-confidence after Jericho — they relied on the memory of the previous victory rather than on the present guidance of the living God. Past blessing became the ground of present presumption. There is a perennial danger here for the people of God: that yesterday's victories breed a self-sufficiency that no longer feels the need to seek the LORD today. The scouts' reasoning is entirely sensible by worldly standards — why exhaust the whole army against a tiny target? — but it leaves God out of the equation. Calvin observes that this prayerless confidence was itself a kind of sin, a forgetting that the conquest depended wholly on God's presence and not on the size of the enemy. The small force will march out, and they will discover that without the LORD, even the smallest enemy is too great.

verseByVerse.quote: So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai, and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men... and the hearts of the people melted and became as water.
verseByVerse.commentary: The result is humiliating disaster. The three thousand confident warriors flee before the men of Ai; thirty-six Israelites are cut down. The number is small by the standards of ancient warfare, but the spiritual shock is immense: Israel, who had watched the walls of Jericho fall flat without a fight, now runs from a backwater town. And the phrase that follows is the very phrase that had described the Canaanites: 'the hearts of the people melted and became as water.' The same terror that God had sent upon Jericho's kings (5:1) now grips Israel itself. The fighting presence of God has been withdrawn, and without it, Israel is no stronger than any other nation. This is the sober lesson: the God who fights for his people will not fight for a people harboring unconfessed sin in the camp. Victory is not automatic; it is the fruit of God's presence, and that presence is forfeited by sin. Wenham notes the deliberate reversal — the conquerors become the conquered, the fearsome become the fearful. Calvin observes that God permitted this defeat to expose the hidden sin and to teach Israel that their strength was never their own. The melting hearts of Israel are a mercy in disguise; the defeat drives Joshua to his knees, and the disaster will uncover the sin that, left hidden, would have festered and destroyed. Sometimes God's severest providences are his kindest, exposing what must be dealt with before it spreads.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua and the elders tear their clothes, fall before the ark, and put dust on their heads. Joshua pours out a raw lament, questioning why God brought them across the Jordan only to be destroyed, and pleading for God's great name.
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua's prayer models honest lament — bringing confusion and grief directly to God. Yet his deepest concern, voiced in v. 9, is for God's name and glory among the nations. True intercession appeals not to our worthiness but to God's reputation and covenant honor.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson noted that Joshua, like Moses, intercedes on the ground of God's glory, not Israel's merit. Begg observed that lament is a legitimate and even faithful form of prayer — God invites us to bring our bewilderment to him, not to suppress it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads. And Joshua said, Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us?
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua's response to the defeat is to fall on his face before the ark of the LORD, tearing his clothes and casting dust on his head — the postures of deepest mourning and repentance. He lies there 'until the evening,' a whole day prostrate before God. And out of his anguish comes a raw, almost reproachful lament: 'Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all... to destroy us?' His words echo the very complaints of the wilderness generation he had once opposed (cf. Num. 14:3) — 'would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!' (v. 7). This is not the polished prayer of a man with all the answers; it is the honest bewilderment of a leader whose world has just collapsed. And yet there is something deeply faithful in it. Begg observed that lament is a legitimate and even faithful form of prayer; God invites his people to bring their confusion and grief to him rather than to suppress it. Joshua does not abandon God in his distress; he runs to God, falling before the ark. The Psalms are full of such honest cries. Calvin notes that while Joshua's words betray a measure of weakness and even unbelief, his very prostration before the ark shows that his faith, though shaken, had not failed. The man of faith may stagger; he does not let go. And God will answer — not with rebuke for the lament, but with the diagnosis of the real problem.

verseByVerse.quote: O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies! For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua's lament rises, at its climax, to its truest and noblest note: 'And what will you do for your great name?' Here is the heart of biblical intercession. Joshua's ultimate concern is not Israel's survival for its own sake but the honor of God's name among the nations. If Israel is destroyed, he reasons, the Canaanites will conclude that the LORD was unable to bring his people in, and God's reputation will be dragged through the dust. This is exactly how Moses had interceded at Sinai and Kadesh — appealing not to Israel's worthiness (they had none) but to God's glory before the watching world (Exod. 32:12; Num. 14:13–16). Ferguson noted that Joshua, like Moses, intercedes on the ground of God's glory, not Israel's merit. This is the key to all true prayer: we have no claim on God in ourselves, but we may plead his own name, his own covenant, his own honor. 'For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt' (Ps. 25:11). The believer's confidence in prayer rests not on his own goodness but on God's commitment to his own glory — a commitment supremely displayed in the gospel, where God acts 'to show his righteousness... so that he might be just and the justifier' (Rom. 3:26). Joshua has found the one unanswerable argument; he appeals to God's great name. And God, who is jealous for his glory, will answer — but first he will deal with the sin that dishonored it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD tells Joshua to get up: the problem is not God's faithlessness but Israel's sin. Israel has taken devoted things and lied. God will not be with them until the devoted thing is destroyed. The nation must consecrate itself and the guilty party will be identified by lot.
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be present with a people harboring sin: 'I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things' (v. 12). Holiness is the condition of fellowship and victory. Sin must be identified, confessed, and removed — there is no shortcut around dealing with it.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul observed that God's first word is 'Get up' — there is a time to pray and a time to act on what is wrong. Calvin noted that God's refusal to be with a sinning Israel underscores that his presence is a gift conditioned on covenant fidelity, not a possession to be presumed.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, Get up! Why have you fallen on your face? Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things... Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies... I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's first word to the prostrate Joshua is bracing: 'Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?' There is a time to lie before God in prayer and a time to rise and act on what is wrong. Sproul observed that God redirects Joshua from mourning to obedience — the problem is not unanswered prayer but unaddressed sin. And then comes the diagnosis, blunt and devastating: 'Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant.' The defeat at Ai was not God's faithlessness but Israel's sin. The chain of verbs traces the offense: they have taken, stolen, lied, and hidden. And the verdict follows: 'the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies' — and most chilling of all, 'I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.' The fighting presence of God, the very heart of the conquest, is withdrawn while sin festers in the camp. Calvin noted that God's refusal to be with a sinning Israel underscores that his presence is a gift conditioned on covenant fidelity, not a possession to be presumed. Here is a truth the church must never forget: holiness is the condition of God's manifest presence. Sin grieves the Spirit and forfeits blessing. There is no shortcut around it — no amount of prayer, no remembrance of past victories, can substitute for dealing decisively with the sin in the camp. 'If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened' (Ps. 66:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Get up! Consecrate the people and say, Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD... There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things... And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has...
verseByVerse.commentary: God prescribes the remedy: consecration and detection. The people must consecrate themselves, and then God will identify the guilty party through a process of narrowing lots — tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, man by man. The sin cannot remain hidden; it must be brought into the light and dealt with. There is a sobering finality in the prescribed judgment: the guilty one 'shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD.' The devoted thing that was meant for God, having been stolen, now brings the curse of the ban upon the one who took it. The thief becomes himself herem, devoted to destruction. Calvin notes that the elaborate process of detection by lot served both to expose the sin justly and to impress upon all Israel the gravity of covenant transgression. There is also mercy hidden in the method: the lot moves slowly, tribe to clan to household, giving the guilty man ample opportunity to step forward and confess before he is finally exposed. God's justice is never hasty; it leaves room for repentance. The lesson for the church is clear: hidden sin must be brought to light and dealt with for the health of the whole body. 'Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy' (Prov. 28:13). The night before the detection, all Israel lies under the shadow of the coming exposure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By lot, the guilt is traced to the tribe of Judah, the clan of Zerah, the household of Zabdi, and finally to Achan. Joshua urges him to give glory to God and confess. Achan confesses: 'I saw... I coveted... I took... I hid them in the earth.'
verseByVerse.theology: Achan's confession follows the exact pattern of the fall: he saw, he coveted, he took, he hid (cf. Gen. 3:6). It is the anatomy of all sin. 'Give glory to the LORD' (v. 19) reveals that honest confession honors God's justice and truth. Sin always promises gain and delivers ruin.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller noted that Achan's sequence — saw, coveted, took, hid — is the universal grammar of temptation, the same as Eve's in Eden. Begg observed that confession 'gives glory to God' by acknowledging that he is right and we are wrong; it is the doorway back to mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken. And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken... and Achan the son of Carmi... of the tribe of Judah, was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary: The detection unfolds exactly as God ordained — and there is something terrible and inexorable about it. 'Joshua rose early' once more, and the lots begin to narrow the field: the tribe of Judah is taken, then the clan of Zerah, then the household of Zabdi, and finally the individual, 'Achan the son of Carmi.' The net tightens link by link, and one imagines the mounting dread in Achan's heart as each lot falls closer to him, each round a fresh summons to confess before the final exposure. Yet he remains silent through it all, hardening himself, hoping perhaps to escape detection to the very end. The irony is bitter: Achan belongs to Judah, the royal tribe, the tribe of the coming King, the lion of Judah from whom Messiah would come. Sin invades even the most honored line. Wenham notes the deliberate, suspenseful narrowing, which underscores both the certainty of divine justice and the foolishness of trying to hide from the God who sees all. 'Be sure your sin will find you out' (Num. 32:23). Calvin observes that the gradual process left Achan every opportunity to repent, so that his continued silence only deepened his guilt. There is no hiding from God; the lot that seems like chance is the instrument of his all-seeing providence. The man who buried his stolen treasure in the earth is dug out by the finger of God, and stands at last exposed before all Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said to Achan, My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done... And Achan answered, ...when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold... then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent...
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua's address is tender even in the moment of judgment: 'My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel.' Confession, he says, is a way of giving glory to God — of acknowledging that God is right and the sinner is wrong, that God's verdict is just and true. Begg observed that confession 'gives glory to God' by vindicating his justice and his omniscience; it is the doorway back to mercy. And then Achan confesses, and his words are the very anatomy of sin: 'I saw... I coveted... I took... I hid.' This is the exact grammar of the fall in Eden — Eve 'saw that the tree was good... took of its fruit and ate' (Gen. 3:6) — and the grammar of David's sin with Bathsheba, and of every temptation since. Keller noted that this sequence is the universal pattern of sin: the eye sees, the heart covets, the hand takes, and then comes the futile attempt to hide. James traces the same descent: 'desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death' (James 1:15). Note the objects of Achan's lust — a beautiful Babylonian cloak, silver, gold. The things were devoted to God; Achan made them his idols. Calvin notes that the confession, though it could not avert the temporal penalty, was nonetheless a genuine giving of glory to God's justice. The buried treasure is exhumed; the sin that promised gain has delivered ruin, for himself and for thirty-six men already dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–26 — Judgment in the Valley of Achor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The stolen goods are found buried in Achan's tent and spread before the LORD. Achan, his family, his possessions, and the devoted things are taken to the Valley of Achor, stoned and burned. A heap of stones is raised, and the LORD turns from his burning anger. The place is named the Valley of Achor — trouble.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is severe because the holiness of God and the integrity of the covenant community are at stake. Yet the Valley of Achor ('trouble') becomes, in Hosea 2:15, 'a door of hope' — the place of judgment transformed by grace. Sin's wages is death; but God's redemptive purpose turns even judgment toward hope.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul observed that the severity warns us never to trifle with God's holiness. Ferguson noted Hosea's astonishing promise: the Valley of Achor becomes a door of hope — pointing to the cross, where the place of judgment becomes the gateway to mercy for all who believe.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath. And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel, and they laid them down before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The messengers run to Achan's tent and find the stolen goods exactly where he said — the cloak, the silver beneath it, the bar of gold, all buried in the earth. The hidden things are dug up and 'laid down before the LORD.' There is a quiet but profound theology in that phrase. What Achan had stolen from God and hidden in the dark is now brought back and spread out before God in the light. Sin loves the darkness; grace and justice bring all things into the open. 'Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known' (Luke 12:2). The treasure that Achan thought he had secured for himself is publicly displayed as the evidence of his guilt before all Israel. Calvin notes that the goods are brought 'before the LORD' because the offense was ultimately against God, whose devoted things had been profaned. There is something almost pitiable in the smallness of it all — a cloak, some silver, a wedge of gold — for which Achan forfeited his life, his family, and thirty-six other lives. Sin always overpromises and underdelivers; it offers a beautiful cloak and pays out in death. The buried treasure, exhumed and exposed, becomes a sermon to all Israel on the folly of coveting what God has forbidden and the impossibility of hiding anything from the eyes of him to whom we must give account.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan... and the cloak and the bar of gold... and they brought them up to the Valley of Achor... And all Israel stoned him with stones... And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
verseByVerse.commentary: The judgment is carried out: Achan, his household, his livestock, and the devoted things are taken to a valley, stoned, and burned, and a great heap of stones is raised over the place — a grim memorial of judgment, the dark counterpart to the memorial stones of Gilgal. The valley is named Achor, 'trouble,' echoing Joshua's words: 'Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today' (v. 25). The severity troubles us, and it should. The inclusion of Achan's family in the judgment reflects, in part, the doctrine of corporate solidarity (though they may also have been complicit in concealing the goods). Sproul observed that the severity warns us never to trifle with the holiness of God; sin is no light thing in his sight. 'Then the LORD turned from his burning anger' — fellowship is restored, the camp is cleansed, and the conquest can resume. But the most astonishing word about the Valley of Achor comes centuries later from the prophet Hosea: God promises to make 'the Valley of Achor a door of hope' (Hos. 2:15). Ferguson marveled at this — the place of judgment transformed into a gateway of hope. Here is the gospel in shadow. At the cross, the place of judgment, where the wrath of God against sin was poured out in full, becomes the very door of hope and mercy for all who believe. The valley of trouble becomes the door of hope, because there Another bore the trouble that we deserved. Achan's heap of stones points beyond itself to the hill where judgment and mercy met forever.

7.theology:
The Holiness of God and the Seriousness of Sin. The God who fights for his people is a holy God who will not dwell with sin in the camp. One man's hidden sin forfeited the fighting presence of God and cost thirty-six lives. 'I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things' (v. 12). Holiness is the condition of God's manifest presence; sin is never trivial, never merely private.

Federal Solidarity and the Two Adams. 'The people of Israel broke faith' though one man sinned (v. 1). We are bound together; the sin of one infects the body. This offends our individualism but runs through all Scripture, climaxing in the two federal heads: in Adam all die, in Christ all are made alive (1 Cor. 15:22; Rom. 5). Achan's solidarity in sin points to our greater solidarity in Christ's righteousness.

The Valley of Achor as a Door of Hope. The place of judgment becomes, in Hosea 2:15, 'a door of hope.' This is the gospel trajectory: at the cross, the place where God's wrath against sin was fully poured out becomes the gateway of mercy. The valley of trouble becomes the door of hope because Another bore our trouble.
7.examples:
Then: After the glory of Jericho, Israel was routed at tiny Ai because one man had secretly coveted and stolen what belonged to God. The hidden sin of one brought defeat, death, and the withdrawal of God's presence on the whole nation, until the sin was exposed, confessed, and judged in the Valley of Achor.

Now: We are tempted to think our sin is private, hidden, our own business — but Achan teaches that sin is never merely individual; it grieves the Spirit, breaks fellowship, and harms the whole body of Christ. The same grammar of temptation — I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid — operates in us still. Yet the gospel turns the Valley of Achor into a door of hope: at the cross, the place of judgment became the gateway of mercy, so that the believer who confesses and forsakes sin finds, not the stones of Achor, but the open door of grace.

8.title: Ai Defeated and Covenant Renewal at Mount Ebal
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land.<sup>2</sup>And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night.<sup>4</sup>And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready.<sup>5</sup>And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them.<sup>6</sup>And they will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city. For they will say, 'They are fleeing from us, just as before.' So we will flee before them.<sup>7</sup>Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will give it into your hand.<sup>8</sup>And as soon as you have taken the city, you shall set the city on fire. You shall do according to the word of the LORD. See, I have commanded you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.<sup>10</sup>Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai.<sup>11</sup>And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai.<sup>12</sup>He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city.<sup>13</sup>So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.<sup>14</sup>And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness.<sup>16</sup>So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them, and as they pursued Joshua they were drawn away from the city.<sup>17</sup>Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand." And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.<sup>19</sup>And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire.<sup>20</sup>So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers.<sup>21</sup>And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city, and that the smoke of the city went up, then they turned back and struck down the men of Ai.<sup>22</sup>And the others came out from the city against them, so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. And Israel struck them down, until there was left none that survived or escaped.<sup>23</sup>But the king of Ai they took alive, and brought him near to Joshua.<sup>24</sup>When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open wilderness where they pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down with the edge of the sword.<sup>25</sup>And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai.<sup>26</sup>But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction.<sup>27</sup>Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua.<sup>28</sup>So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day.<sup>29</sup>And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.<sup>30</sup>At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,<sup>31</sup>just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool." And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings.<sup>32</sup>And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.<sup>33</sup>And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law.<sup>35</sup>There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is a chapter of restoration. The sin of Achan has been purged, the camp cleansed, and now God comes again to a chastened Joshua with the very words of his first commissioning: 'Do not fear and do not be dismayed' (v. 1). The God who disciplines is the God who restores. The defeat at Ai is reversed, and the victory that pride and sin had forfeited is now granted to a humbled and obedient people. There is gospel here for every believer who has fallen: failure is not final with God. He who chastens also lifts up; the same God who said 'I will be with you no more' (7:12) now says again 'I have given into your hand' (8:1).

The battle for Ai is won by an ambush — and notice the difference from Jericho. At Jericho, Israel did nothing but march and shout; God did it all. At Ai, God commands strategy, ambush, and the full use of military means. Both victories are God's, but God works through different means in different seasons — sometimes by sheer miracle, sometimes through the diligent use of ordinary instruments. The Reformed instinct holds these together: God is sovereign over the outcome, and he ordains the means, including human effort and wisdom, to accomplish his ends. Joshua stretches out his javelin (v. 18, 26) as Moses stretched out his staff, and Ai falls.

But the climax of the chapter is not the battle; it is the covenant renewal at Mount Ebal (vv. 30–35). Just as Moses had commanded (Deut. 27), Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones, offers sacrifices, writes the law on stones, and reads aloud the blessings and the curses before all Israel — men, women, children, and the sojourners among them. Right after a great failure and its restoration, Israel pauses to renew its covenant with God. This is profoundly significant. The first major act in the land after dealing with sin is not further conquest but corporate worship and re-commitment to the Word of God.

The altar on Ebal — the mountain of cursing — is itself a gospel picture. The sacrifices are offered on the mountain associated with the curse, for it is precisely on the place of the curse that atonement must be made. Christ would one day become a curse for us, hanging on the tree on the mountain of judgment, that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations (Gal. 3:13–14). And the law written on stones, read in the hearing of all, anticipates the day when God would write his law not on stone but on the hearts of his people (Jer. 31:33).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With Achan's sin purged, God speaks again to Joshua with the words of his first call: 'Do not fear.' He grants Ai into Israel's hand and now permits them to take its spoil and livestock as plunder, and reveals the strategy of ambush.
verseByVerse.theology: God restores the fallen and recommissions them with the same gracious words as before. Failure is not final; the God who disciplines also lifts up. The permission to take spoil (in contrast to Jericho's total ban) shows God's freedom in disposing of his gifts.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg noted that 'do not fear' is the word of a restoring God to a chastened people — grace after discipline. Ferguson observed that God meets the recovering church not with reproach but with renewed commission, as Christ restored Peter after his denial.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sin purged, God speaks again — and the first words are pure grace: 'Do not fear and do not be dismayed.' These are the very words of Joshua's original commission (1:9), now spoken afresh to a man and a nation crushed by failure. The God who had said 'I will be with you no more' (7:12) now restores the relationship and renews the promise. Failure is not final with God. Begg noted that 'do not fear' is the word of a restoring God to a chastened people — grace after discipline, not reproach after failure. There is deep gospel comfort here for every believer who has fallen. The same God who disciplines is the God who lifts up and recommissions. We see the pattern fulfilled in the risen Christ's tender restoration of Peter, who had denied him three times: not 'how could you?' but 'do you love me?... feed my sheep' (John 21). And once more the promise rings: 'I have given into your hand the king of Ai' — the accomplished-gift grammar of grace returns. This time, the whole army is to go up ('all the fighting men'), correcting the presumptuous half-measure of the previous attempt. Calvin notes that God's renewed assurance was necessary to restore the shattered confidence of a people who had tasted defeat. The discipline has done its work; now grace abounds, and the conquest resumes under the smile of a God who delights to restore.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it.
verseByVerse.commentary: God grants two things here: a sobering continuity and a gracious difference. The continuity: 'do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho' — the judgment of the ban falls again on a Canaanite city. The difference: 'only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves.' Whereas Jericho was wholly devoted to God as the firstfruits of the land, with nothing to be taken, Ai's spoil is now permitted to Israel. This reveals God's freedom in disposing of his gifts. The very thing Achan was destroyed for taking from Jericho, Israel is now freely given at Ai. The difference was never the value of the goods but the command of God; Achan's sin was not greed for wealth as such but defiance of God's explicit word. Wenham notes the deliberate contrast, which highlights that the issue at Jericho was obedience, not asceticism — God may withhold or give as he pleases, and the creature's duty is simply to obey. There is also strategy now: 'Lay an ambush against the city, behind it.' Unlike Jericho, where Israel only marched and shouted, Ai will fall through ordinary military means under God's direction. Calvin observes that God varies his methods to teach that all victory is from him whether by miracle or by means. The God who toppled walls by a shout now grants victory through a well-laid ambush — and both are equally his doing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–23 — The Ambush and the Fall of Ai
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua sets thirty thousand men in ambush behind the city, then advances with the main force as a decoy. When the men of Ai pursue, the ambush takes the empty city and sets it ablaze. Caught between two forces, Ai is utterly destroyed and its king captured.
verseByVerse.theology: God ordains and works through human means — strategy, courage, and effort — as truly as through miracle. Joshua's outstretched javelin (vv. 18, 26), like Moses' staff, marks the victory as God's gift. The destruction is the execution of God's judgment, with Joshua acting under explicit divine command.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur noted that God's use of ordinary tactics at Ai teaches that faith is not passivity; we plan, work, and fight, trusting God for the outcome. Sproul observed that the outstretched javelin, like Moses' rod at Rephidim, signified that the victory was the LORD's.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night. And he commanded them, Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it... when they come out against us... we will flee before them... Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city...
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua, now leading the whole army as God commanded, devises the ambush in detail. A picked force is set in concealment behind the city by night; the main body will advance as a decoy and, when the men of Ai sally out (emboldened by their earlier victory), Israel will feign flight, drawing the defenders away from the city. Then the ambush will rise, seize the undefended town, and set it on fire, and the fleeing force will turn and crush the enemy between two forces. The plan is shrewd, careful, and entirely conventional — and it is wholly within the will of God, for God himself had said, 'Lay an ambush' (v. 2). MacArthur noted that God's use of ordinary tactics at Ai teaches that faith is not passivity; the believer plans, works, and fights, trusting God for the outcome. There is no contradiction between trusting God and using means; the same God who ordains the end ordains the means. Calvin observes that Joshua's diligent generalship is no failure of faith but its proper expression — faith does not despise wisdom and effort but employs them in obedient dependence on God. The previous defeat had come not from too little strategy but from prayerless presumption; now, under God's command and with the whole army, careful planning serves the divine purpose. The lesson stands for the church: we pray as though everything depends on God and work as though everything depends on us, knowing that in truth everything depends on God who works through our labors.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people... And the king of Ai saw this, and... hurried and went out early to the appointed place... He did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city. And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled...
verseByVerse.commentary: The plan unfolds with precision. Joshua rises early — the recurring mark of his eager obedience — and advances with the main force. The king of Ai, seeing the Israelite army approach and remembering his earlier triumph, hurries out to give battle, 'not knowing that there was an ambush against him behind the city.' Overconfidence undoes him, just as it had nearly undone Israel. Joshua and his men 'pretended to be beaten and fled,' luring the entire fighting force of Ai out in hot pursuit, away from the now-defenseless city. Not a man was left in Ai; all went out after Israel, leaving the city wide open. Wenham notes the dramatic irony — the very tactic of feigned flight exploits the enemy's pride, the same pride that had blinded Israel before Ai's first walls. The narrator lingers on the detail that the gates were left open and the city unguarded; the trap is perfectly sprung. There is a sobering lesson in the king of Ai's fate: he repeats Israel's earlier error of presumption, charging out in confidence based on a past victory, and walks straight into destruction. Pride goes before a fall. Calvin observes that God so governs the hearts of the wicked that their very confidence becomes the snare that destroys them. The men of Ai, sure of another easy victory, run headlong away from their own city and into the jaws of the ambush. The decoy has worked; the city is undefended; the moment of God's appointed victory has come.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Joshua, Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand. And Joshua stretched out the javelin... And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place... and they captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire... So all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai.
verseByVerse.commentary: At God's command, Joshua stretches out the javelin in his hand toward Ai — and holds it outstretched until the city is utterly destroyed (v. 26). The gesture deliberately recalls Moses stretching out his staff over the Red Sea and his hands at Rephidim (Exod. 14:16; 17:11). Sproul observed that the outstretched javelin, like Moses' rod, signified that the victory was the LORD's, not the army's — the human instrument lifted up in dependence, the divine power accomplishing the work. The moment the javelin is raised, the ambush springs: the hidden force rushes the empty city, captures it, and sets it ablaze. The smoke rising from Ai is the signal that seals the doom of the pursuing army, who now find themselves caught between the turning decoy and the men pouring out of the burning city. Twelve thousand fall that day; the city is annihilated according to the ban. Once again we must read this sober scene rightly — as the execution of God's judgment on a Canaanite city, carried out under explicit divine command, a localized eruption of the justice that will one day fill the earth. Wenham notes the careful theological framing: the javelin held aloft throughout the battle keeps the focus on God as the true author of the victory. The victory that pride had forfeited at Ai's first assault is now granted to a humbled, obedient, God-directed people — and the smoke of the city rises as a monument to the truth that the LORD fights for his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–29 — The King of Ai and the Heap of Stones
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel destroys all the inhabitants of Ai. Joshua holds out the javelin until the destruction is complete and burns the city to a ruin. The king of Ai is hanged on a tree until evening, then buried under a great heap of stones at the city gate.
verseByVerse.theology: The complete execution of the ban underscores the gravity of God's judgment. The king hanged on a tree and taken down by evening fulfills the law (Deut. 21:22–23), which Paul applies to Christ becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:13). Even here, the shadow of the cross falls.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin noted the heap of stones as a perpetual memorial of God's judgment. Ferguson observed that the law of taking down the hanged man by evening, lest the land be defiled, finds its deepest meaning at Calvary, where the cursed One was buried before nightfall.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai... all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down... For Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary: The destruction is total, and the narrator emphasizes that 'Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin' until the work was complete. The image is striking — the outstretched javelin held aloft throughout the entire battle, like Moses' hands held up at Rephidim until Amalek was defeated (Exod. 17:11–12). The sustained gesture signifies sustained dependence on God; the victory is not won in a single stroke but through perseverance in the posture of faith and obedience. Calvin notes that the unwavering javelin teaches the necessity of steadfastness; we are not to begin a work of obedience and then grow weary, but to persevere to the end. There is a sober comprehensiveness to the judgment — 'all the inhabitants' — that reminds us this is the execution of the herem, the divine ban, upon a city whose iniquity had become full. We must neither soften this dishonestly nor read it as license for human aggression; it is a particular, time-bound act of divine justice, carried out under explicit command, a foreshadowing of the final judgment. Wenham observes the deliberate parallel to Moses, binding Joshua's leadership to the great deliverer who went before him and underscoring the continuity of God's saving and judging work. The victory once forfeited by sin is now fully granted to obedience; the outstretched hand, held firm to the end, has accomplished the purpose of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua... And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary: This time Israel takes the spoil 'according to the word of the LORD' — the same act that destroyed Achan is now obedience, because God has commanded it. The difference is always the word of God. The king of Ai is hanged on a tree until evening and then, at sunset, taken down and buried under a heap of stones. This precise detail — taken down before nightfall — fulfills the law of Deuteronomy 21:22–23: 'his body shall not remain all night on the tree... for a hanged man is cursed by God.' And here the shadow of the cross falls unmistakably across the page. Paul lifts that very law and applies it to Christ: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree' (Gal. 3:13). Ferguson observed that this law finds its deepest meaning at Calvary, where the cursed One was hanged on a tree and buried before nightfall, that the land — and the world — might not be defiled by the unborne curse. The king of Ai, hanged and buried under stones, is a dark type pointing forward to the King of kings who would take the curse upon himself, be lifted up on a tree, and be laid in a tomb before sunset, that his people might be redeemed from the curse forever. Calvin notes the heap of stones as a perpetual memorial of God's judgment. Even in this scene of judgment, grace whispers: the curse borne, the body taken down, the way of blessing opened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–35 — Covenant Renewal at Mount Ebal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, offers burnt and peace offerings, and writes a copy of the law on stones. All Israel — with elders, officers, judges, and sojourners — stands divided between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal as Joshua reads aloud all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse.
verseByVerse.theology: Immediately after failure and restoration, the first great act in the land is corporate worship and covenant renewal. The altar on Ebal, the mountain of cursing, is where atonement is made — a gospel picture of Christ becoming a curse on the mount of judgment. The law read to all, including women, children, and sojourners, shows the Word belongs to the whole covenant community.
verseByVerse.examples: Stott noted the centrality of the Word — the conquest pauses for the public reading of Scripture. Keller observed that the altar on the mount of cursing prefigures the cross, where the curse was borne so the blessing might flow. Begg stressed the inclusion of 'little ones' — covenant children belong to the assembly of God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded... an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool. And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings. And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses...
verseByVerse.commentary: Remarkably, the first great construction in the promised land is not a fortress or a palace but an altar. And it is built on Mount Ebal — the mountain of cursing (Deut. 27:13). Why offer sacrifices on the mountain of the curse? Because it is precisely on the place of the curse that atonement must be made. Keller observed that the altar on the mount of cursing prefigures the cross, where the curse was borne so that the blessing might flow. The burnt offerings (signifying total consecration and atonement) and peace offerings (signifying restored fellowship and communion) are offered on the mount of judgment — a gospel picture of Christ, who became a curse on the hill of judgment that we might have peace with God. The altar is of uncut stones, untouched by iron tools (Exod. 20:25), for human workmanship adds nothing to God's appointed way of atonement; the way to God is by his provision, not our improvement. And Joshua writes 'a copy of the law of Moses' on stones — the Word at the center of the covenant life of the nation. Stott noted the centrality of the Word: the conquest itself pauses for the writing and reading of Scripture. There is a profound order here: after failure (Achan), after restoration (Ai), the people do not rush on to more conquest but stop to worship, to atone, and to re-anchor themselves in the Word of God. The renewed life begins at the altar and the Book.

verseByVerse.quote: And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests... Half of them stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal... And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse... There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners...
verseByVerse.commentary: The whole nation is arranged in a great covenant assembly, exactly as Moses had commanded (Deut. 27): half the tribes before Mount Gerizim (the mount of blessing), half before Mount Ebal (the mount of cursing), with the ark and the priests in the valley between. And Joshua reads aloud 'all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse.' The covenant sets before Israel the two ways: obedience leading to blessing, disobedience leading to curse — the same fork that runs through all of Scripture and stands before every soul. Note the radical inclusivity of the assembly: 'the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners' are all present to hear the Word. The covenant is not for the elite or for adult males only; it embraces the whole community — women, children, and even the foreigners who had attached themselves to Israel. Begg stressed the inclusion of the 'little ones' — covenant children belong to the assembly of God's people and are to hear his Word from the earliest age. The presence of the sojourner is a quiet anticipation of the gospel's reach to the nations; Rahab's people have a place in the assembly. Keller observed that the two mountains, blessing and curse, find their resolution only at the cross, where Christ took the curse of Ebal that the blessing of Gerizim might flow freely to all who believe. The renewed nation stands beneath the Word, and the Word divides the way of life from the way of death. And the great hope is that one day God would write this law not on stones but on hearts (Jer. 31:33), in a covenant sealed by better blood than bulls and goats.

8.theology:
The God Who Restores the Fallen. After the disaster of Achan's sin, God comes to Joshua with the very words of his first commission: 'Do not fear.' Failure is not final with God; the same Lord who disciplines also restores and recommissions, as Christ restored Peter after his denial. The victory once forfeited by sin is granted afresh to a humbled and obedient people.

God Works Through Means as Truly as Through Miracle. Jericho fell by a shout; Ai falls by an ambush. Both victories are wholly God's, but God ordains and works through human strategy, courage, and effort. Faith is not passivity; we plan and labor and fight, trusting God for the outcome. The outstretched javelin marks the victory as the LORD's, even amid the most ordinary means.

The Altar on the Mount of Cursing and the Centrality of the Word. The first great act in the land after dealing with sin is worship and covenant renewal. The altar on Ebal, the mount of cursing, is where atonement is made — prefiguring Christ, who became a curse on the hill of judgment that the blessing might flow (Gal. 3:13). And the law read to all — women, children, sojourners — anchors the renewed people in the Word, pointing to the day God writes his law on the heart.
8.examples:
Then: A chastened nation, freshly restored after the sin of Achan, returned to Ai and won by obedient strategy the victory pride had forfeited. Then, instead of pressing on, they paused on the mountains of blessing and cursing to build an altar, offer sacrifice, and hear the whole law read aloud — the whole community, women and children and sojourners, recommitting to the Word of God.

Now: When we fall, the gospel does not leave us in the dust of defeat; the God who disciplines comes again with 'do not fear,' restoring and recommissioning his people. And we learn that trusting God never means doing nothing — we plan, work, and fight in dependence on him. Above all, like Israel at Ebal, the path of renewal after failure runs through the altar and the Book: to the cross, where Christ bore our curse, and to the Word, which God now writes upon our hearts.

9.title: The Gibeonite Deception
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this,<sup>2</sup>they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.<sup>3</sup>But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,<sup>4</sup>they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended,<sup>5</sup>with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly.<sup>6</sup>And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."<sup>7</sup>But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?"<sup>8</sup>They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you? And where do you come from?"<sup>9</sup>They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt,<sup>10</sup>and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth.<sup>11</sup>So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Come now, make a covenant with us."'<sup>12</sup>Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly.<sup>13</sup>These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. And these garments and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey."<sup>14</sup>So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.<sup>16</sup>At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them.<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim.<sup>18</sup>But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.<sup>19</sup>But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them.<sup>20</sup>This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them."<sup>21</sup>And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.<sup>22</sup>Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us?<sup>23</sup>Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God."<sup>24</sup>They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you—so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing.<sup>25</sup>And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."<sup>26</sup>So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them.<sup>27</sup>But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
9.overview:
After the dramatic victories of Jericho and Ai, chapter 9 turns to a subtler danger — not the open assault of enemies but the cunning deception of those who would survive by guile. The Gibeonites, a people of Canaan dwelling nearby, hear of Israel's conquests and devise a ruse. They come dressed in worn-out clothes and carrying moldy bread, pretending to be travelers from a distant country, and they beg Israel to make a covenant of peace with them. The strategy works. Israel inspects the evidence, finds it convincing, and makes a treaty — and the fatal verse stands at the center of the chapter: 'they did not ask counsel from the LORD' (v. 14).

Here is one of the great cautionary lessons of the book. Israel had just learned at Ai the cost of presumption, yet they fall again into the same error in a different form. They trust their own assessment of the evidence — the moldy bread looked old, the clothes looked worn, the story sounded plausible — and they fail to do the one thing that would have saved them: inquire of the LORD. Sproul observed that the leaders relied on their senses and their reason but neglected prayer, and so were deceived by appearances. How often the people of God are taken in not by obvious evil but by plausible deception, because we lean on our own understanding rather than seeking the wisdom of God.

And yet — and this is the wonder of the chapter — God overrules even Israel's prayerless folly. Though the covenant was made under false pretenses, it was sworn in the name of the LORD, and so it is binding. Israel must keep its oath, even at cost to themselves. The Gibeonites are spared, made servants of the sanctuary — 'cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God' (v. 23). What human error and deception accomplished, God weaves into his redemptive purpose: a Canaanite people are brought, however irregularly, into the service of the living God.

There is grace here that anticipates the gospel. The Gibeonites, like Rahab, are Canaanites who survive the conquest by casting themselves on Israel and their God. Their deception was sinful, but their underlying motive — 'we have heard a report of him... your servants' (v. 24) — was a kind of fearful faith, a recognition that safety lay only with the people of God. They become servants of the house of God, drawing the water and cutting the wood for the worship of the LORD. Centuries later, the temple servants (Nethinim) and the Gibeonites still served. God's mercy is wider than our errors, and he gathers even the deceivers, even the foreigners, into the service of his house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Kings Unite Against Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of the Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite, and other nations west of the Jordan gather together to fight against Joshua and Israel as a united coalition.
verseByVerse.theology: The kings respond to God's mighty acts not with repentance like Rahab but with hardened, organized resistance. The same revelation that softens some hardens others. Human alliances against God's purposes are doomed, however numerous.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes the contrast between the united kings' defiance and the Gibeonites' shrewd self-preservation. Calvin observed that the gathering of the kings against Israel was, in truth, a gathering against God — and Psalm 2 declares such conspiracies vain.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland... heard of this, they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same news that converted Rahab and terrified the kings now hardens them into organized resistance. Hearing of the fall of Jericho and Ai, the kings of the land 'gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.' Here is a sobering truth: the same revelation of God's power produces opposite effects in different hearts. Rahab heard and believed; the Gibeonites heard and schemed for survival; these kings heard and united in defiance. The gospel is 'a fragrance from death to death' to some and 'from life to life' to others (2 Cor. 2:16); the difference lies not in the message but in the heart God is at work upon. Calvin observed that the gathering of the kings against Israel was, in truth, a gathering against God himself — and Psalm 2 declares all such conspiracies vain: 'Why do the nations rage... The One enthroned in heaven laughs.' The kings imagine that unity and numbers can prevail against the people whose God dried up the Jordan and toppled Jericho's walls; their alliance is a monument to the folly of resisting the Almighty. Wenham notes the deliberate contrast the narrator sets up: the kings choose open war and will be destroyed, while the Gibeonites in the next verses choose cunning surrender and will survive. Two responses to the irresistible advance of God's people — defiance unto death, or submission unto life. The chapter is a study in how men respond to the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Gibeonites, hearing of Israel's victories, act with cunning. They disguise themselves as travelers from a far country with worn-out clothes, patched sandals, and moldy bread, and come to Joshua at Gilgal seeking a covenant of peace.
verseByVerse.theology: The Gibeonites' deception is sinful, yet beneath it lies a fearful recognition that safety is found only with God's people. Unlike the defiant kings, they seek refuge — a flawed but real instinct toward the God of Israel. The elaborate disguise tests whether Israel will rely on sight or on God's counsel.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg noted that the enemy often comes not in open assault but in plausible disguise. Ferguson observed that the Gibeonites, like Rahab, sought to align with God's people out of fear of his power — a self-preserving faith, however imperfect.
