verseByVerse.quote: But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai, they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended... And they went to Joshua... and said, We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Gibeonites take a third path, distinct from both Rahab's open faith and the kings' open war: they choose cunning survival through deception. Knowing that Israel was forbidden to make treaties with the peoples of Canaan (Deut. 7:1–2; 20:15–18) but permitted to make peace with distant cities, they disguise themselves as travelers from a far country — worn-out sacks, mended wineskins, patched sandals, moldy bread. The disguise is elaborate and convincing. And they make their request: 'make a covenant with us.' Begg noted that the enemy often comes not in open assault but in plausible disguise; the most dangerous deceptions are the ones that look entirely reasonable. Yet we should not miss what drives the Gibeonites. Beneath the deception lies a genuine, if fearful, recognition that safety is found only with the people of Israel's God. Ferguson observed that the Gibeonites, like Rahab, sought to align themselves with God's people out of fear of his power — a self-preserving faith, however imperfect and however wrongly pursued. Their method was sinful; their underlying instinct — to flee to the God of Israel rather than fight him — was, in its way, wiser than the kings' defiance. Calvin notes that the Gibeonites' ingenuity, though deceitful, sprang from a true terror of the LORD. The ruse is set; the test now falls on Israel — will they discern the truth, or trust their eyes?

verseByVerse.quote: But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?... They said to Joshua, We are your servants... we have come because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt... This our bread was still warm when we took it... and now, behold, it is dry and crumbly.
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel's first instinct is, commendably, suspicion: 'Perhaps you live among us; how can we make a covenant with you?' They sense the danger. But the Gibeonites have an answer for every objection, and their key argument is shrewdly framed: 'we have come because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt.' Notice they speak only of the older, distant deeds — Egypt, the Transjordan kings — and carefully omit the recent victories at Jericho and Ai, which would have betrayed their nearness. The deception is layered with cunning. And then the physical evidence is produced: the dry, crumbly bread that was 'warm' when they set out, the cracked wineskins, the worn garments. The senses are persuaded. There is poignant irony in the Gibeonites' words 'because of the name of the LORD your God' — for in this, at least, they spoke truth. They had indeed heard the report of the LORD and were terrified into seeking refuge. Wenham notes the skill of the speech, which mingles genuine confession of God's fame with calculated falsehood about their origin. Calvin observes that the very plausibility of the evidence was the snare; Israel's eyes told them one thing, but their eyes were not the proper guide. The test is whether Israel will discern by sight and reason alone, or pause to seek the counsel of the LORD who alone sees the heart. The whole chapter now hangs on a single decision.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel samples the Gibeonites' provisions but does not ask counsel from the LORD. Joshua makes peace and a covenant with them, sworn by the leaders of the congregation.
verseByVerse.theology: The pivotal verse of the chapter: 'they did not ask counsel from the LORD' (v. 14). The failure is not malice but prayerlessness — relying on sight and reason rather than seeking God's wisdom. The Urim and Thummim were available; God's counsel was accessible. Self-reliance, even sincere, leads God's people astray.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul stressed that the leaders trusted their senses and reason but neglected prayer. Keller noted that the great peril here is not gross sin but prayerless decision-making — leaning on our own understanding (Prov. 3:5–6) even in matters that seem obvious.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the hinge of the whole chapter, and one of the most quietly devastating verses in Joshua: 'they did not ask counsel from the LORD.' The men of Israel examined the evidence — they 'took some of their provisions,' sampling the moldy bread, inspecting the worn gear — and on the basis of their own investigation, they were satisfied. They trusted their senses and their reason. And the one thing they neglected was the one thing that would have saved them: to inquire of the LORD. The means were readily available; the high priest bore the Urim and Thummim precisely so that Israel could seek God's guidance in just such decisions (Num. 27:21). God's counsel was accessible; they simply did not seek it. Sproul stressed that the leaders trusted their senses and their reason but neglected prayer, and so were deceived by mere appearances. Keller noted that the great peril here is not gross or scandalous sin but prayerless decision-making — the subtle self-reliance that leans on its own understanding rather than acknowledging God in all its ways (Prov. 3:5–6). How searching this is for the church. We are rarely tempted to consciously rebel against God; far more often we simply proceed without him, making our decisions on the basis of evidence and reason that seem entirely sound, never pausing to seek his face. The bread looked old; the case seemed clear; why pray? And precisely there, in the gap left by prayerlessness, the deception found its way in. Calvin observes that this neglect was the root of all the trouble that followed, a warning that even the wise are deceived when they fail to consult the only One who sees the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant is made, and crucially, it is sealed with an oath: 'the leaders of the congregation swore to them.' This oath, sworn in the name of the LORD, will prove to be the binding hinge of everything that follows. Joshua and the leaders, persuaded by the false evidence, grant the Gibeonites peace and pledge to let them live. The decision is made hastily, on faulty information, without divine counsel — and yet, because it was sworn before God, it cannot simply be undone. Here we begin to see the gravity of an oath in the sight of God. To swear in his name is to invoke him as witness and guarantor; to break such an oath is to profane his name and treat him with contempt. Wenham notes that the solemn oath transforms a mistaken treaty into a binding obligation that Israel will be held to, even at cost to themselves. There is a sobering lesson here about the weight of our words and commitments before God. The world breaks its promises whenever they become inconvenient; the people of God are called to keep their word even when it hurts — 'who swears to his own hurt and does not change' (Ps. 15:4). Calvin observes that though the covenant was obtained by fraud, the sanctity of the oath sworn in God's name rendered it inviolable. The error was real; the consequences will be costly; but the honor of God's name now requires that Israel keep faith even with those who deceived them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later Israel learns the Gibeonites are near neighbors. The congregation grumbles against the leaders, but the leaders refuse to break the oath sworn by the LORD. They resolve to let the Gibeonites live but make them servants — cutters of wood and drawers of water.
verseByVerse.theology: Though deceived, Israel honors the oath sworn in God's name, for to break it would profane him and bring wrath. The integrity of God's people in keeping their word, even to their own hurt, reflects God's own covenant faithfulness. God's name is more sacred than our convenience.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observed that the leaders' refusal to break the oath, even when it cost them, models the integrity God requires. Begg noted that keeping a costly promise honors the God in whose name it was sworn — a witness the watching world rarely sees.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them... But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.
verseByVerse.commentary: The truth comes out within three days: the supposed distant travelers are in fact near neighbors, Canaanites living right among the cities Israel is to conquer. The deception is exposed. And here the integrity of God's people is put to the test. Israel could easily rationalize breaking the treaty — it was obtained by fraud, after all; surely a covenant won by lies is no covenant at all. But the leaders refuse to attack, 'because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel.' The oath was sworn in God's name, and that name is more sacred than Israel's convenience or even than the command to destroy the Canaanites. To break the oath would be to profane the name of the LORD before the watching nations. Ferguson observed that the leaders' refusal to break the oath, even when it cost them and even when they had been deceived, models the integrity God requires of his people. The congregation, meanwhile, 'murmured against the leaders' — the old wilderness sin of grumbling returns. They are angry at being bound to a treaty they never wanted. Wenham notes the tension between the people's frustration and the leaders' commitment to the sanctity of the oath. Begg noted that keeping a costly promise honors the God in whose name it was sworn — a rare and powerful witness in a world that breaks its word the moment it becomes inconvenient. The leaders choose the harder, holier path: they will keep faith, because God keeps faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But all the leaders said to all the congregation, We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them. And the leaders said to them, Let them live. So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation...
verseByVerse.commentary: The leaders' reasoning is theologically profound: 'we may not touch them... lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore.' They understand that to break an oath sworn in the LORD's name would invoke God's wrath upon themselves — a truth borne out centuries later when Saul violated this very covenant by killing Gibeonites, and a three-year famine fell upon Israel as a result (2 Sam. 21:1–2). The name of God is not to be trifled with; an oath sworn in his name binds even when extracted by deceit. So the leaders find a middle way that honors both the oath (the Gibeonites live) and the consequences of the deception (the Gibeonites serve): they become 'cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation.' The Gibeonites are spared but reduced to servitude. Yet even this servitude, as the next verses reveal, is no mere drudgery — it becomes service to the house of God. Calvin observes that the leaders rightly judged the sanctity of the oath to outweigh every other consideration, teaching that the people of God must be people of their word. There is a quiet beauty in the outcome: a Canaanite people, who should have perished under the ban, are instead grafted into the service of Israel and ultimately into the service of the LORD's sanctuary. What deception sought as mere survival, God turns into a place near his house. The integrity of Israel's leaders, refusing to break faith even with deceivers, becomes the channel through which mercy reaches even the Gibeonites.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Gibeonites Made Servants of the House of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua confronts the Gibeonites for their deception and pronounces that they will be perpetual servants — cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. They submit, confessing they acted out of fear because they had heard of the LORD's command. Joshua delivers them from the people's hand.
verseByVerse.theology: God overrules a prayerless, deceived decision for his own redemptive purpose. The Gibeonites, like Rahab, are Canaanites brought into the service of the living God — a foretaste of the gathering of the nations. Their service 'for the house of God' (v. 23) elevates servitude into a place near the worship of the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul observed that God's sovereignty is so vast that he weaves even our errors into his good purposes. Keller noted that the Gibeonites, by grace, end up serving at God's altar — judgment was due, but mercy made them servants of the sanctuary, a picture of grace to the undeserving.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, Why did you deceive us...? Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God. They answered Joshua, Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land... So we feared greatly for our lives... and did this thing.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua confronts the Gibeonites with their deception — 'Why did you deceive us?' — and pronounces their sentence: perpetual servitude as 'cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God.' Note that crucial phrase — 'the house of my God.' Their servitude is not mere menial labor for Israel; it is service connected to the worship and sanctuary of the LORD. And the Gibeonites' answer is striking: 'it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded... to give you all the land... So we feared greatly for our lives, and did this thing.' Their motive, beneath the deception, was fear of the LORD and his sworn purpose — the same terror that gripped all Canaan, but turned, in their case, toward seeking refuge rather than waging war. Like Rahab, they had heard the report of God's mighty acts and concluded that resistance was futile; unlike the kings, they sought to live by submitting. Keller noted that the Gibeonites, by grace, end up serving at God's altar — judgment was due to them as Canaanites, but mercy made them servants of the sanctuary, a picture of grace reaching the undeserving. Calvin observes that the Gibeonites' confession, though it came after the deception, was an honest acknowledgment that they had cast themselves on Israel's God out of dread of his power. The sentence is real, but it is a sentence to a place near the house of God — a far better fate than the destruction that fell on the defiant kings. Their fear, however imperfectly expressed, drove them to the only safe place: the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them. But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with a quiet but profound resolution: Joshua 'delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them.' The Gibeonites, who deserved destruction under the ban and who survived by deceit, are now protected by Joshua himself from the wrath of the congregation. And their appointed service is now defined with even greater precision: 'cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD.' They serve not only the people but 'the altar of the LORD' — they are brought into the very orbit of the worship of God, supplying the wood for the sacrifices and the water for the rites. What began as a deceptive bid for mere survival ends as service at the altar of the living God. Sproul observed that God's sovereignty is so vast that he weaves even our errors — Israel's prayerless folly, the Gibeonites' deception — into his good and redemptive purposes. The mistake was real and costly, yet God brought from it the gathering of a Canaanite people into the service of his sanctuary, a foretaste of the day when the nations would stream to the house of the LORD. Wenham notes that the Gibeonites' descendants (the Nethinim, temple servants) endured for centuries, a living memorial of mercy. Here is the gospel logic: the deceiver and the foreigner, who deserved judgment, are spared by grace and given a place near the altar — a picture of every sinner brought, undeserving, into the service and worship of God. God's mercy is wider than our errors, and his purpose stands even through our folly.

9.theology:
The Peril of Prayerless Decision. The central failure is captured in one verse: 'they did not ask counsel from the LORD' (v. 14). The danger was not gross sin but self-reliance — trusting sight and reason rather than seeking God's wisdom, when his counsel was readily available. The church's great peril is rarely conscious rebellion; far more often it is proceeding without God, leaning on our own understanding (Prov. 3:5–6).

The Sanctity of the Oath and God's Covenant Faithfulness. Though the treaty was won by deceit, Israel kept it because it was sworn in the LORD's name. To break it would profane his name and bring his wrath (cf. 2 Sam. 21). The people of God keep their word even to their own hurt (Ps. 15:4), reflecting the God who keeps every promise. His name is more sacred than our convenience.

God's Sovereignty Overruling Human Folly. God weaves even Israel's prayerless error and the Gibeonites' deception into his redemptive purpose. The Gibeonites, like Rahab, are Canaanites spared by grace and brought into the service of God's altar — a foretaste of the gathering of the nations. God's mercy is wider than our errors, and his purpose stands through our folly.
9.examples:
Then: Israel was deceived by moldy bread and worn sandals into a covenant they would never have made, because they trusted the evidence of their eyes and 'did not ask counsel from the LORD.' Yet because they had sworn in God's name, they kept faith even with the deceivers — and God overruled the whole sorry affair to bring a Canaanite people into the service of his altar.

Now: We are rarely tempted to open rebellion; we are constantly tempted to prayerless self-reliance — making decisions on plausible evidence without seeking God's face. Gibeon warns us to acknowledge God in all our ways. And when we have given our word in his name, we keep it even at cost, for his name is sacred. Above all, we take comfort that God's sovereign mercy is wider than our blunders: he gathers even the undeserving — even the deceivers and the foreigners — into the service and worship of his house.

10.title: The Sun Stands Still
10.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai and had devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them,<sup>2</sup>he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors.<sup>3</sup>So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying,<sup>4</sup>"Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel."<sup>5</sup>Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.<sup>6</sup>And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah.<sup>11</sup>And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.<sup>12</sup>At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon."<sup>13</sup>And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day.<sup>14</sup>There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel.<sup>15</sup>So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.<sup>16</sup>These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.<sup>17</sup>And it was told to Joshua, "The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah."<sup>18</sup>And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them,<sup>19</sup>but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand."<sup>20</sup>When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out, and when the remnant that remained of them had entered into the fortified cities,<sup>21</sup>then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.<sup>22</sup>Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave."<sup>23</sup>And they did so, and brought those five kings out to him from the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.<sup>24</sup>And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight."<sup>26</sup>And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening.<sup>27</sup>But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.<sup>28</sup>As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>29</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah.<sup>30</sup>And the LORD gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. And he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it; he left none remaining in it. And he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>31</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish and laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>32</sup>And the LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, as he had done to Libnah.<sup>33</sup>Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish. And Joshua struck him and his people, until he left none remaining.<sup>34</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon. And they laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>35</sup>And they captured it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. And he devoted every person in it to destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish.<sup>36</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron. And they fought against it<sup>37</sup>and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns, and every person in it. He left none remaining, as he had done to Eglon, and devoted it to destruction and every person in it.<sup>38</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir and fought against it<sup>39</sup>and he captured it with its king and all its towns. And they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. Just as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and to its king.<sup>40</sup>So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded.<sup>41</sup>And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon.<sup>42</sup>And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.<sup>43</sup>Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
10.overview:
The treaty with Gibeon, made in folly, becomes the occasion of one of the greatest displays of God's power in all of Scripture. Five Amorite kings, enraged that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, unite to attack the city. The Gibeonites send an urgent plea to Joshua, and Israel — honoring the covenant they had sworn — marches all night to relieve their new vassals. What human error bound them to, God uses to bring about a thunderous victory. The chapter is a sustained demonstration that 'the LORD fought for Israel' (v. 14, 42).

God himself takes the field. He throws the enemy into panic (v. 10), and then, as the kings flee, 'the LORD threw down large stones from heaven' — a supernatural hailstorm that killed more of the enemy than Israel's swords (v. 11). And then comes the great miracle: at Joshua's audacious command, 'Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon' (v. 12), the sun and moon halt in the sky, and the day is prolonged so that Israel can complete the victory. 'There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man' (v. 14). The God who made the heavens bends the heavens to serve the prayer of his servant and the cause of his people.

This miracle has been much debated, but the inspired text presents it plainly as an act of God in answer to Joshua's faith. Calvin marveled that the Creator who set the sun in its course could halt it at his pleasure, and that he condescended to do so at the prayer of a man — a testimony to the power of bold, believing prayer offered in the will of God. Sproul stressed that the God who governs the cosmos is the same God who fights for his people; the heavens themselves are his servants in the salvation of his own.

The chapter then sweeps through the rapid conquest of the southern cities — Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, Debir. City after city falls, 'because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel' (v. 42). The refrain hammers home the book's central truth. And in the striking scene of the five kings hiding in a cave (vv. 16–27), where Joshua's commanders place their feet on the necks of the conquered kings, we glimpse a picture of the ultimate triumph: every enemy made a footstool, every power subdued beneath the feet of the people of God, in fulfillment of the promise that Christ will reign 'until he has put all his enemies under his feet' (1 Cor. 15:25).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem, fearing Israel because Gibeon (a great city) had made peace, gathers four other Amorite kings to attack Gibeon and punish its defection.
verseByVerse.theology: The world rages against those who align with God's people. Gibeon's peace with Israel makes it a target — discipleship invites opposition. The kings' fear, like the kings of Psalm 2, drives them to futile conspiracy against the LORD's purposes.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes the irony that Israel's deceptive ally now becomes the cause of a great victory. Begg observed that those who throw in their lot with God's people will share both their battles and their deliverances.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai... and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them, he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city... Then Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron... saying, Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The defection of Gibeon — a great city, larger than Ai — sends shockwaves through the Canaanite kings. Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem (whose name means 'lord of righteousness,' a dark counterpart to Melchizedek, 'king of righteousness') 'feared greatly' and rallied a coalition of five Amorite kings, not first against Israel but against Gibeon, to punish its defection and make an example of it. The world rages against those who align themselves with the people of God. Gibeon's peace with Israel, however irregularly obtained, marked it for the fury of its former allies; to side with God's people is to inherit their enemies. Begg observed that those who throw in their lot with God's people will share both their battles and their deliverances — and Gibeon, having sought refuge with Israel, will now experience Israel's God fighting on its behalf. The kings' alliance echoes Psalm 2: the rulers of the earth take counsel together against the LORD and his anointed, only to find their conspiracy vain. Wenham notes the irony that Israel's deceptive ally now becomes the occasion of a great victory — God weaves even the consequences of Israel's prayerless treaty into a triumph for his name. The kings imagine they are merely punishing a traitor city; in truth they are marching against the people of the living God, and their assault on Gibeon will become the stage for one of the mightiest displays of God's power in all of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.
verseByVerse.commentary: Five kings, with all their combined armies, encamp against the single city of Gibeon. The numbers are overwhelming; the cities named — Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon — represent the major powers of the southern hill country. By every human calculation, Gibeon is doomed. A lone city, recently made a servant-vassal of Israel, now faces the assembled might of five kingdoms. Yet the very massing of these forces against Gibeon will prove to be their undoing, for it draws them all together into one place where God can deal with them in a single, decisive blow. Calvin observed that God often allows the wicked to gather their full strength precisely so that their destruction may be the more complete and his glory the more manifest. There is a pattern here that runs through Scripture: the enemies of God's people unite in seemingly invincible array, only to be shattered at a stroke. Pharaoh's whole army at the Red Sea, the kings here at Gibeon, the gathered nations at Armageddon — the massing of human power against God serves only to magnify the totality of his victory. Wenham notes the deliberate listing of all five kings by name and city, underscoring the scale of the threat and, by contrast, the magnitude of the deliverance to come. Gibeon, the deceiver-city now under Israel's protection, stands on the brink of destruction — and is about to discover that the God of Israel keeps covenant even with those who came to him by crooked paths, and that he fights for all who shelter among his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Israel Marches and God Fights
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gibeon pleads for help. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal. God assures him not to fear, for the enemy is given into his hand. The LORD throws the Amorites into panic, and as they flee, he hurls great hailstones from heaven, killing more than Israel's swords.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel keeps its costly covenant with Gibeon, marching all night to honor a treaty made in error — covenant faithfulness even when inconvenient. God himself fights: panic and hailstones from heaven are his weapons. 'The LORD threw down large stones' — the Creator's cosmos serves the salvation of his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson noted that Israel's all-night march to keep faith with Gibeon mirrors God's relentless faithfulness to his own covenant. Sproul observed that the hailstones reveal God as the true warrior; Israel's part was obedience, God's part was victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua... Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us... So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him... And the LORD said to Joshua, Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Gibeon's desperate plea comes: 'Come up to us quickly and save us and help us.' And Joshua responds — not by reconsidering whether the treaty was binding, not by abandoning the deceivers to their fate, but by marching at once to honor the covenant Israel had sworn. He leads the whole army up from Gilgal, evidently through the night (v. 9), an arduous uphill march to relieve the besieged city. Ferguson noted that Israel's all-night march to keep faith with Gibeon mirrors God's own relentless faithfulness to his covenant — Israel keeps its word even when the word was given in error and the ally is unworthy. Here is covenant faithfulness at cost, the very thing the world finds incomprehensible: to spend yourself for those who deceived you, because you swore in the name of the LORD. And as Joshua marches, God speaks the great word of every battle: 'Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands.' Once more the accomplished-gift grammar of grace: the victory is already deeded before the battle is joined. The same assurance given before Jericho and Ai is given again. Calvin observes that God's word of encouragement strengthens Joshua for the daunting task of facing five united armies. 'Not a man of them shall stand before you' — the outcome is certain because God has decreed it. Israel's part is to march in faith and obedience; God's part is to give the victory. The all-night march is the obedience of faith; the assurance from heaven is the ground of all courage.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal. And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel... And as they fled before Israel... the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them... and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua's all-night march achieves total surprise — 'he came upon them suddenly.' But the narrator is careful to attribute the victory to its true author: 'the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel.' The same God who melted the hearts of Jericho's kings now scatters the Amorite coalition in terror. And then comes the supernatural artillery of heaven: as the enemy flees down the descent of Beth-horon, 'the LORD threw down large stones from heaven' — a devastating hailstorm — and the text makes the astonishing point that 'there were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.' God's weapons slew more than Israel's. The victory was overwhelmingly his. Sproul observed that the hailstones reveal God as the true warrior in this battle; Israel's part was the obedience of marching and fighting, but God's part was the decisive slaughter from heaven. The Creator who fashioned the clouds and the hail (Job 38:22–23) deploys them in the salvation of his people. There is a sobering note here too: the same hail that destroyed the Amorites foreshadows the day of judgment, when 'great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each' will fall upon the impenitent (Rev. 16:21). Calvin marvels that God armed the very heavens against the enemies of his church, proving that all creation is his servant. Israel marched and struck, but it was the LORD who fought, and the LORD who won. The cosmos itself is enlisted in the cause of God's people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua, in the sight of Israel, commands the sun to stand still at Gibeon and the moon in the Valley of Aijalon. The sun stops in the midst of heaven and does not set for about a whole day, so Israel can complete the victory. There has been no day like it, for the LORD heeded the voice of a man.
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest cosmic miracle of the book: God halts the heavens in answer to a man's bold, believing prayer. 'The LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel' (v. 14). The Creator bends creation to serve the prayer of his servant — a testimony to the power of prayer offered in God's will and the supremacy of God over the cosmos.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin marveled that the God who set the sun in its course halted it at a man's word. Sproul stressed that the same God who governs the cosmos fights for his people. Begg noted the audacity of Joshua's faith — he prayed a 'cosmic' prayer because he knew a cosmic God.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies...
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the breathtaking heart of the chapter. In the heat of battle, with the day racing toward sunset and the enemy not yet fully destroyed, Joshua does something staggering: 'in the sight of Israel' he addresses the sun and moon themselves — 'Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon.' This is prayer of cosmic audacity. And the text reports the wonder plainly: 'the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies.' The day was prolonged so that Israel could complete the victory God had given. Much ink has been spilled over the mechanics of this miracle, but the inspired text presents it as a genuine act of God in answer to Joshua's faith. Begg noted the sheer audacity of Joshua's faith — he prayed a cosmic prayer because he knew a cosmic God; his confidence in God's power was so total that nothing seemed beyond the reach of believing prayer. Calvin marveled that the God who set the sun in its course could halt it at a man's word, and did so for the sake of his people. The poetic citation of the Book of Jashar (v. 13) preserves the memory of this wonder in Israel's worship and song. There is profound encouragement here for the praying believer: the God we serve is the Lord of heaven and earth, and no request offered in faith and in accordance with his will is too great for him. Joshua prayed and the sun stood still — not because of Joshua's power, but because the God who fights for his people commands the very heavens.

verseByVerse.quote: There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel. So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator pauses to underscore the uniqueness of the day: 'There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel.' Two wonders are joined here. The first is the cosmic miracle itself — a day like no other in all history. The second, and perhaps the more astonishing, is the condescension of God: 'the LORD heeded the voice of a man.' The infinite Creator, who needs nothing and is accountable to none, bent his ear to the prayer of his servant and altered the heavens in response. This is the dignity God grants to the prayers of his people. James reminds us that 'Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently' and heaven obeyed (James 5:17); the God who heeded Joshua heeds his children still. And the climactic phrase seals the theme of the whole book: 'for the LORD fought for Israel.' The miracle was not for Joshua's glory but as the instrument of God's own warfare on behalf of his people. Sproul stressed that the same God who governs the cosmos fights for his people — the Lord of the sun and moon is the Lord of his church's battles. Calvin notes that the phrase 'no day like it before or since' marks this as a singular monument to God's power and to the efficacy of believing prayer. Joshua then returns to Gilgal, the victory complete. The God who made the heavens has proven that he will move heaven and earth to save his people and answer their prayers — a foretaste of the day when the sun will be darkened and the heavens shaken at the return of the greater Joshua.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–27 — The Five Kings in the Cave
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The five kings flee and hide in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua has them sealed in while Israel pursues the routed armies, then brings them out. He has his commanders place their feet on the kings' necks, encourages the army, executes the kings, and hangs their bodies until evening, then seals them in the cave.
verseByVerse.theology: The feet on the necks of the conquered kings is a vivid picture of total victory and the subjugation of every enemy — fulfilled when Christ puts all enemies under his feet (1 Cor. 15:25; Ps. 110:1). 'Do not be afraid... thus the LORD will do to all your enemies' (v. 25) turns a battle into a sermon of assurance.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul saw in the feet on the necks a foreshadowing of Christ's triumph over every power. Ferguson noted that Joshua turns the moment into encouragement for the army — every victory of God is meant to strengthen faith for the battles still ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah. And it was told to Joshua... Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them, but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies... And when Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out...
verseByVerse.commentary: The five kings, the heads of the coalition, flee the battlefield and hide in a cave at Makkedah — a vivid image of the powers of this world cowering before the advance of God's people. Joshua, with cool generalship, orders the cave sealed with large stones and guarded, but commands the army not to stop there: 'Pursue your enemies... do not stay there yourselves.' The priority is the complete destruction of the enemy forces; the kings can wait. There is wisdom here — Joshua does not let the capture of the leaders distract from the larger victory God has given. The kings, sealed in their cave behind rolled stones, are a picture of doomed authority — the rulers who raged against God's people now trapped in the dark, awaiting judgment. Calvin observes that the sealing of the cave reflects Joshua's confidence that the kings, like the whole coalition, were already given into his hand; there was no urgency, for their doom was certain. Wenham notes the deliberate detail of the 'large stones' rolled against the cave's mouth — the same kind of stones God had rained from heaven, now sealing the fate of the kings. The army completes the rout, striking the enemy 'with a great blow until they were wiped out.' The victory is total. And the kings, trapped in the cave, will soon be brought out to demonstrate publicly the complete subjugation of every enemy of God's people. The hiding place of the wicked becomes the place of their judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said, Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave... Joshua said to the chiefs of the men of war..., Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings... Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight. And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees.
verseByVerse.commentary: The kings are brought out, and Joshua summons his commanders: 'put your feet on the necks of these kings.' In the ancient world, this was the ultimate image of total conquest — the victor's foot upon the neck of the vanquished, the enemy reduced to a footstool. And Joshua turns this dramatic moment into a sermon of assurance: 'Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies.' He repeats the very words of his own commissioning (1:9), passing the courage God gave him on to his men, and grounding it in the visible proof before their eyes — the conquered kings beneath their feet. Ferguson noted that Joshua turns the moment into encouragement for the army; every victory of God is meant to strengthen faith for the battles still ahead. But the deepest meaning reaches far beyond this battle. The feet on the necks of the kings is a foreshadowing of the ultimate triumph of Christ, who will reign 'until he has put all his enemies under his feet' (1 Cor. 15:25), the Lord who sits at God's right hand until his enemies are made his footstool (Ps. 110:1). Sproul saw in this scene a foreshadowing of Christ's complete victory over every hostile power — sin, death, Satan, and the kingdoms of this world, all brought beneath his feet. The kings are then executed and hanged on trees until evening (again fulfilling Deut. 21:23, and again sealed with stones in the cave). For the church militant, the lesson is one of unshakable confidence: the enemies that now seem so mighty are already destined to be a footstool beneath the feet of Christ and his people. 'Thus the LORD will do to all your enemies.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–43 — The Conquest of the Southern Cities
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua sweeps through the southern cities — Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, Debir — striking each with the edge of the sword and devoting them to destruction. He conquers the whole region in one campaign, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: The rapid, comprehensive conquest is summarized with the refrain 'because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel' (v. 42). The completeness of the victory testifies to the faithfulness of God to his promise. The judgment on the cities executes the divine ban on a culture ripe for judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes the formulaic repetition emphasizing total, God-given victory. MacArthur observed that the relentless refrain keeps the glory where it belongs — not on Joshua's strategy but on God who fought.

verseByVerse.quote: As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day... he left none remaining. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah... to Lachish... to Eglon... to Hebron... to Debir... he devoted to destruction every person in it...
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrative now sweeps through a rapid catalog of conquered cities — Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, Debir — each falling in turn to Joshua's southern campaign. The repetition is deliberate and formulaic, almost liturgical: city after city captured, none remaining, devoted to destruction. Wenham notes that the formulaic repetition emphasizes the total, God-given nature of the victory; the relentless rhythm conveys the unstoppable advance of the people of God under his hand. We must read these verses, as the whole conquest, with sober honesty. This is the execution of the divine ban (herem) upon a Canaanite civilization whose iniquity had become full (Gen. 15:16) — a localized, time-bound eruption of God's judgment into history, carried out under explicit divine command. It is neither a charter for human aggression nor a pattern for the church, which wages war 'not against flesh and blood' (Eph. 6:12). It is, rather, a preview of the final judgment, when the King of kings will subdue every stronghold of rebellion. The comprehensiveness of the conquest also testifies to God's faithfulness: every promise he made to give Israel the land is being fulfilled before our eyes. Calvin observes that the swift fall of so many fortified cities, which should have required years of siege, proves that the victory was God's gift, not the fruit of Israel's strength. The campaign that began with the relief of Gibeon becomes the conquest of the whole south — accomplished, the next verse will insist, by the LORD himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua struck the whole land... He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded. And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary: The southern campaign is summarized, and the summary lands on the great refrain that governs the entire book: 'because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.' This is the theological heartbeat of Joshua. The conquest of the whole southern region 'at one time' — a feat of staggering military improbability — is explained not by Joshua's generalship, not by Israel's valor, but by the simple, towering fact that God fought for his people. MacArthur observed that the relentless refrain keeps the glory exactly where it belongs: not on Joshua's strategy but on the God who fought. The victory was 'just as the LORD God of Israel commanded' — obedience to God's word and the fighting presence of God's power, together, secured the land. There is a beautiful completeness here: what God promised in chapter 1 ('I have given you the land') is being fully accomplished, region by region. Calvin notes that the phrase 'at one time' magnifies the wonder — what would naturally have taken years was done in a single campaign because God was the warrior. And Joshua returns again to Gilgal, the base camp, the place of the memorial stones, having added the whole south to Israel's possession. The chapter that began with a treaty made in folly ends with a conquest accomplished by God — a vivid demonstration that the Lord overrules our errors, keeps our costly covenants, answers our boldest prayers, subdues every enemy beneath our feet, and fights, always fights, for his people. 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (Rom. 8:31).

10.theology:
The LORD Fights for His People. This chapter is the book's thesis dramatized. God throws the enemy into panic, rains hailstones from heaven that kill more than Israel's swords, halts the sun and moon, and subdues five kings — and the refrain twice declares 'the LORD fought for Israel' (vv. 14, 42). The victory is overwhelmingly God's; Israel's part is faith and obedience, God's part is the conquest.

The Power of Believing Prayer. 'The LORD heeded the voice of a man' (v. 14). The Creator bent the heavens in answer to Joshua's audacious prayer. The God who governs the cosmos condescends to heed the prayers of his servants — a testimony that no request offered in faith and in accordance with his will is too great for the Lord of heaven and earth.

Every Enemy a Footstool. The feet placed on the necks of the conquered kings foreshadow the ultimate triumph of Christ, who reigns until all his enemies are made his footstool (Ps. 110:1; 1 Cor. 15:25). 'Thus the LORD will do to all your enemies' (v. 25). The powers that rage against God's people are already destined for defeat beneath the feet of Christ.
10.examples:
Then: Honoring a costly covenant, Israel marched all night to save the city that had deceived them — and God took the field, hurling hailstones from heaven and halting the sun in the sky so his people could finish the victory. Five kings who had raged against God's people ended with the feet of Israel's commanders on their necks, a living sermon: 'thus the LORD will do to all your enemies.'

Now: We face coalitions of opposition that seem invincible, and we are tempted to fear. But the lesson of Gibeon's long day is that the LORD fights for his people, bends the very heavens to their aid, and heeds their believing prayers. Like Joshua, we may pray boldly to a cosmic God. And we live in the certainty that every enemy of Christ — sin, death, hell, and every hostile power — is already destined to be a footstool beneath his feet, and ours in him.

11.title: The Northern Campaign Completed
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph,<sup>2</sup>and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor on the west,<sup>3</sup>to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah.<sup>4</sup>And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.<sup>5</sup>And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them by the waters of Merom and fell upon them.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. And they struck them until he left none remaining.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.<sup>10</sup>And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms.<sup>11</sup>And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction; there was none left that breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire.<sup>12</sup>And all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured, and struck them with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded.<sup>13</sup>But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned.<sup>14</sup>And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave any who breathed.<sup>15</sup>Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>16</sup>So Joshua took all that land, the hill country and all the Negeb and all the land of Goshen and the lowland and the Arabah and the hill country of Israel and its lowland<sup>17</sup>from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death.<sup>18</sup>Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.<sup>19</sup>There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle.<sup>20</sup>For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>21</sup>And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities.<sup>22</sup>There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.<sup>23</sup>So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
11.overview:
With the south subdued, the conquest turns north. Jabin king of Hazor gathers an even greater coalition than Adoni-zedek had — a vast host 'in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots' (v. 4). Here is the most formidable military force Israel has yet faced, with the technological advantage of chariots, the tanks of the ancient world. Against such odds, Israel's faith might well have failed. But the word comes again: 'Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel' (v. 6). The God who fights for his people is not impressed by horses and chariots; 'some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God' (Ps. 20:7).

Joshua is commanded to do something striking with the captured chariots and horses: hamstring the horses and burn the chariots (v. 6, 9). Israel is not to adopt the enemy's instruments of trust. The victory is to be remembered as God's, won without reliance on the military technology in which the nations trusted. Sproul observed that God deliberately stripped away every ground of human confidence so that the glory would be his alone — Israel must not learn to trust in chariots, lest they forget the LORD.

The campaign is comprehensive. Hazor, 'the head of all those kingdoms' (v. 10), is captured and burned. City after city falls. And the chapter sounds, again and again, the great refrain of obedience: 'Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded' (v. 15). This is the high-water mark of Joshua's obedience — total, exact, comprehensive faithfulness to the word of God. The conquest succeeds because faith obeys.

The chapter closes with one of the most precious words in the book: 'And the land had rest from war' (v. 23). After the long years of slavery, wilderness, and conquest, the people of God enter rest. This rest is a type, a shadow, of the greater rest that remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). Canaan's rest from war points to the soul's rest in Christ, who says, 'Come to me... and I will give you rest' (Matt. 11:28), and ultimately to the eternal Sabbath rest of the new creation, where the wars are over forever and the people of God dwell in unbroken peace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jabin king of Hazor gathers a vast northern coalition with horses and chariots like the sand of the sea. God tells Joshua not to fear, for he will give them over. Israel falls on them suddenly at the waters of Merom and defeats them, hamstringing the horses and burning the chariots as commanded.
verseByVerse.theology: God is not intimidated by superior numbers or military technology. 'Do not be afraid' grounds Israel's courage in God's promise, not their odds. The hamstringing of horses and burning of chariots strips away every ground of human trust so glory goes to God alone (Ps. 20:7).
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul noted that God removed every human prop so the victory would be unmistakably his. Begg observed that faith does not measure the enemy's strength but the greatness of God who has already promised the victory.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to... the kings who were in the northern hill country... and they came out, with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots. And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The northern coalition assembled by Jabin of Hazor dwarfs anything Israel has yet faced. The narrator piles up the description to overwhelming effect: 'a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.' This is the most formidable military force in the book — vast in numbers and, crucially, equipped with chariots and cavalry, the advanced military technology of the age, the armored divisions before which infantry typically scattered. By every human measure, Israel is hopelessly outmatched; they have no chariots, no cavalry, only foot soldiers facing the massed armor of the north. The phrase 'like the sand on the seashore' deliberately echoes God's promise to multiply Abraham's offspring (Gen. 22:17) — but here it describes the enemy, as if to say that the foe seems as innumerable as God's own promises. Begg observed that faith does not measure the enemy's strength but the greatness of the God who has already promised the victory; the question is never how large the army but how great the God. Calvin notes that God permitted the enemy to gather their full and terrifying strength precisely so that the victory might display his power beyond all doubt. The waters of Merom become the stage for a confrontation between human might at its most impressive and the God who needs no army. Israel's only hope lies in the word that is about to come from heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire. So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them... and they struck them... And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary: Against the terrifying horde, God speaks the word that has anchored every battle: 'Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel.' The accomplished-gift grammar of grace returns once more; the victory is deeded before it is fought, complete with a timetable — 'tomorrow at this time.' And then God commands something theologically pointed: 'You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire.' Israel is not to capture and keep the enemy's military technology; the horses are to be crippled and the chariots burned. Why? So that Israel will never learn to trust in chariots and horses, never adopt the instruments in which the nations placed their confidence. Sproul noted that God deliberately removed every human prop so that the victory would be unmistakably his; Israel must remain a people whose only trust is in the LORD. The lesson is enshrined in the Psalms: 'Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God' (Ps. 20:7). There is a perennial application: the people of God are forever tempted to trust the world's instruments of power and security, but we are called to trust the LORD alone. Joshua obeys to the letter — 'just as the LORD said to him' — and the great northern coalition, for all its chariots and numbers, is annihilated. The God who fights for his people is not impressed by armor; he gives the victory and forbids his people the very weapons that might tempt them to forget him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua captures Hazor, the head of all those kingdoms, kills its king, and burns the city. He devotes all the cities and their kings to destruction according to the command given through Moses. The refrain sounds: Joshua left nothing undone of all that the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.theology: The high-water mark of Joshua's obedience: 'he left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses' (v. 15). Total, exact, comprehensive obedience to God's word is the secret of the conquest's success. Faith that obeys fully receives the promise fully.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur stressed that Joshua's complete obedience — leaving nothing undone — is the model for the believer's response to God's Word. Calvin noted that the chain of command (LORD to Moses to Joshua) underscores that the conquest was governed throughout by the word of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms. And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction... And Joshua burned Hazor with fire... And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary: Hazor, described as 'formerly the head of all those kingdoms,' is the chief city of the north, the seat of Jabin's power and the linchpin of the coalition. Joshua captures it, executes its king, devotes its inhabitants to destruction, and burns the city to the ground — the only northern city explicitly said to be burned, marking it out as the center of resistance. The fall of the head city symbolizes the collapse of the whole northern power. The spoil and livestock, however, Israel takes as plunder, just as at Ai, according to God's permission — the difference, always, being the explicit command of God. We must continue to read these scenes with sober reverence: this is the execution of the divine ban upon a Canaanite civilization ripe for judgment, a particular and time-bound act of God's justice, not a template for human warfare. Wenham notes that the burning of Hazor, the head of the kingdoms, decisively ends organized resistance in the north. Calvin observes that the comprehensive destruction was carried out in obedience to God's command through Moses, so that the conquest remained throughout an act of obedience to the divine word rather than mere territorial ambition. The fall of mighty Hazor, with all its chariots burned and its king slain, demonstrates once more that no power, however great, can stand before the people whose God fights for them. The head of the kingdoms lies in ashes; the conquest of the north is nearly complete.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is the theological summit of Joshua's leadership, the high-water mark of his obedience: 'He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.' Notice the unbroken chain of command and revelation: the LORD commanded Moses, Moses commanded Joshua, and Joshua did it all. The word of God flows from heaven through Moses to Joshua to fulfillment, and at no point is it diluted, delayed, or partially obeyed. Joshua's obedience is total, exact, and comprehensive — he leaves nothing undone. MacArthur stressed that Joshua's complete obedience is the model for the believer's response to God's Word: not selective obedience, not partial compliance, not obedience in the areas we find convenient, but doing all that God has commanded, leaving nothing undone. This is the secret of the conquest's success — faith that obeys fully receives the promise fully. Calvin noted that the chain of command underscores that the conquest was governed throughout by the word of God, not by Joshua's own designs; the leader's glory was simply that he did exactly what God said. There is a searching standard here for every Christian. We are prone to a partial obedience that obeys God where it suits us and quietly leaves undone the commands we find hard. But the obedience God blesses is the obedience that leaves nothing undone. 'If you love me, you will keep my commandments' (John 14:15) — not some of them, but all. Joshua's epitaph might well be this verse: he did all that the LORD commanded. May it be said of us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — The Whole Land Taken; The Land Has Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua takes the whole land — the hill country, the Negeb, the lowland, and the slopes. He makes war a long time with all the kings; not one city made peace except Gibeon, for the LORD hardened their hearts. He cuts off the Anakim. And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereign hardening of the kings' hearts (v. 20) parallels Pharaoh — God ordains even the enemy's resistance for his purpose of judgment. The cutting off of the Anakim (the giants who terrified the first generation) shows that what once seemed insurmountable falls before God. 'The land had rest' is a type of the rest that remains in Christ (Heb. 4).
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul noted the sovereignty of God in hardening hearts, as with Pharaoh — judgment is God's prerogative. Ferguson observed that the rest of the land foreshadows the soul's rest in Christ and the eternal Sabbath of the new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua took all that land... There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle. For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction... just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary: The summary of the conquest sweeps across the whole land — hill country, Negeb, lowland, slopes — all taken by Joshua over a long campaign. And the narrator notes a striking exception and a profound theological cause. The exception: not one city made peace except Gibeon. The cause: 'it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle.' Here is the sovereignty of God in judgment, stated as plainly as anywhere in Scripture. The Canaanite kings' relentless, suicidal resistance was, beneath the surface of their own choices, the outworking of God's sovereign hardening — exactly as with Pharaoh, whose heart God hardened so that judgment might fall (Exod. 9:16; Rom. 9:17–18). Sproul noted the sovereignty of God in hardening hearts, as with Pharaoh; judgment is God's prerogative, and he ordains even the resistance of the wicked for his righteous purposes. This is a hard doctrine, and Scripture does not soften it. God, in justice, gave these nations over to the hardness they had chosen, so that the iniquity which had become full (Gen. 15:16) might meet its appointed judgment. We must hold this with reverence and trembling, remembering that God 'has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills' (Rom. 9:18), and that the same sovereign grace that hardened these kings had softened Rahab and the Gibeonites. The God who fights for his people is the God who governs the hearts of their enemies; nothing in the conquest, or in history, escapes his sovereign hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir... Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities. There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator records a detail freighted with meaning: 'Joshua cut off the Anakim from the hill country.' The Anakim were the giants — the very giants whose presence had terrified the first generation of spies forty years earlier. 'There we saw the Nephilim... and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers' (Num. 13:33). It was the dread of these giants, more than anything, that had caused the wilderness generation to shrink back in unbelief and forfeit the land. And now, in a single understated verse, those same giants are 'cut off' by Joshua. What had seemed utterly insurmountable to unbelief falls before the obedience of faith. The giants that terrified one generation are destroyed by the next, because the difference was never the size of the giants but the size of their faith in God. Ferguson and others have drawn out the lesson: the obstacles that loom impossibly large to unbelief are brought low when faith takes God at his word. The 'giants' in our own lives — the besetting sins, the fears, the impossibilities that paralyze us — are not too great for the God who fights for his people. Calvin notes that the destruction of the Anakim was the final answer to the cowardice of the spies, a vindication of faith over the fear that had cost a generation the land. The note that some Anakim remained in the Philistine cities (Gaza, Gath, Ashdod) quietly foreshadows a future giant of Gath named Goliath — and another shepherd-deliverer who would fell him in the name of the LORD of hosts.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter — and the conquest narrative — reaches its goal in one of the most beautiful phrases in the book: 'And the land had rest from war.' After the centuries of slavery in Egypt, the forty years of wilderness wandering, and the long years of conquest, the people of God enter rest. The wars are over; the inheritance is secured; the land is given 'according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses' — every promise fulfilled. And Joshua distributes it 'for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments,' anticipating the long division of the land in the chapters to come. But it is the word 'rest' that sings. Ferguson observed that the rest of the land foreshadows the soul's rest in Christ and the eternal Sabbath of the new creation. The writer of Hebrews makes the connection explicit and unforgettable: Canaan's rest was real, but it was not the final rest; 'if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on. So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God' (Heb. 4:8–9). The rest of the land points beyond itself to the rest Christ gives the weary soul — 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matt. 11:28) — and ultimately to the eternal rest of the new heaven and new earth, where the wars are over forever and the people of God dwell in unbroken peace in the presence of their King. The land had rest from war; and that rest is a foretaste of the everlasting rest that remains for all who belong to the greater Joshua.

11.theology:
The LORD Versus Chariots and Giants. God is not intimidated by superior numbers, advanced technology (chariots), or terrifying foes (the Anakim/giants). He commands the chariots burned and the horses hamstrung so Israel will trust him alone (Ps. 20:7), and he topples the very giants who terrified an earlier generation. What is impossible to unbelief falls before the obedience of faith.

Total Obedience to the Word. The high-water mark of the conquest is Joshua's complete obedience: 'he left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses' (v. 15). The unbroken chain — LORD to Moses to Joshua to fulfillment — shows that faith that obeys fully receives the promise fully. Partial obedience is not the obedience God blesses.

The Rest That Remains. 'The land had rest from war' (v. 23) is a type of the rest Christ gives the weary soul and the eternal Sabbath of the new creation. Hebrews 4 makes the connection: Joshua's rest was real but not final; a greater rest remains for the people of God in Christ, who alone gives rest to all who come to him.
11.examples:
Then: Israel faced a horde like the sand of the sea, armored with chariots and cavalry, and the giants who had once terrified their fathers. But God said 'do not be afraid,' commanded them to burn the very chariots they might have trusted, and gave the whole land into their hands — until at last 'the land had rest from war.'

Now: We are tempted to trust the world's chariots — its power, security, and strategies — rather than the LORD. And we face giants that paralyze us with fear. But the God who fights for his people topples giants and burns chariots, that we might trust him alone. And weary as we are from the long warfare of the Christian life, we look to the rest that remains: the rest Christ gives the heavy-laden now, and the eternal Sabbath of the new creation, where the wars are over forever.

12.title: The Roll Call of Defeated Kings
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward:<sup>2</sup>Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley as far as the river Jabbok, the boundary of the Ammonites, that is, half of Gilead,<sup>3</sup>and the Arabah to the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, southward to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah;<sup>4</sup>and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei<sup>5</sup>and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the boundary of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead to the boundary of Sihon king of Heshbon.<sup>6</sup>Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them.
