And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments,<sup>8</sup>in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites):<sup>9</sup>the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one;<sup>10</sup>the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;<sup>11</sup>the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;<sup>12</sup>the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;<sup>13</sup>the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;<sup>14</sup>the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;<sup>15</sup>the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;<sup>16</sup>the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;<sup>17</sup>the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;<sup>18</sup>the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;<sup>19</sup>the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;<sup>20</sup>the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;<sup>21</sup>the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;<sup>22</sup>the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;<sup>23</sup>the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one;<sup>24</sup>the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is, at first glance, a mere list — a roll call of thirty-one defeated kings, two east of the Jordan (conquered under Moses) and twenty-nine west of the Jordan (conquered under Joshua). But it is far more than a catalog. It is a monument of praise, a victory memorial inscribed in the names of vanquished kings. Each name represents a fortified city, a throne, a power that had stood against the people of God — and each is now listed among the defeated. The chapter is the answer, in stone-cold record, to the promise of chapter 1: 'No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life' (1:5).

The list is bracketed by a profound theological structure. It begins by recalling the victories under Moses east of the Jordan — Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan (vv. 1–6) — and then catalogs the twenty-nine kings defeated under Joshua west of the Jordan (vv. 7–24). The two leaders, Moses and Joshua, the law and grace, are joined in the one work of God. What was begun under Moses is completed under Joshua; the conquest is one continuous act of divine faithfulness spanning both mediators, just as the work of redemption spans the old covenant and the new, finding its completion in Christ.

The repeated phrase 'one' after each king — 'the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, one' (vv. 9ff) — has a drumbeat quality, like the tolling of a bell. Each 'one' is a testimony to the thoroughness of God's victory and the certainty of his promise. Calvin observed that the careful enumeration was meant to fix in Israel's memory the full extent of God's faithfulness, that they might never doubt his power or forget his mercy. Not one king was too strong; not one city could stand. Thirty-one times, the powers of Canaan fell.

For the church, this roll call points forward to the final muster of defeated powers beneath the feet of Christ. As thirty-one kings fell before Joshua, so every principality and power, every rule and authority, every enemy of the cross, will be subdued beneath the feet of the greater Joshua, who must reign 'until he has put all his enemies under his feet' (1 Cor. 15:25). The list of defeated kings is a preview of the final triumph, when the kingdoms of this world become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (Rev. 11:15). Every name on the list is a trophy of grace and a guarantee of the victory to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Kings Defeated Under Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter first recalls the kings defeated east of the Jordan under Moses: Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, whose lands Moses gave to the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.theology: The conquest is one continuous work of God spanning two mediators, Moses and Joshua. What was begun under the law (Moses) is completed under Joshua (Jesus) — a picture of redemption fulfilled in Christ. The eastern victories are remembered as part of the one inheritance.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that beginning with Moses' victories ties the whole conquest into one divine work. Ferguson observed that Moses began what only Joshua could complete — the law could not bring the people in, but Joshua (Jesus) does.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise... Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer... and the Arabah...
verseByVerse.commentary: The roll call begins not with Joshua's conquests but with the victories God gave under Moses, east of the Jordan — beginning with Sihon king of the Amorites. The narrator deliberately reaches back before the crossing of the Jordan to include the eastern conquests in the great tally of God's faithfulness. This framing is theologically significant: the conquest of the land is presented as one continuous work of God, begun under Moses and completed under Joshua. Wenham notes that beginning with Moses' victories ties the whole conquest into a single divine work spanning both mediators. The detail of Sihon's territory — from Aroer to the Arabah — anchors the record in real geography, real history. Sihon had refused Israel passage through his land and had come out to attack them; God gave him over, and his kingdom became the inheritance of the eastern tribes. Calvin observes that the inclusion of the Mosaic conquests reminds Israel that the whole work, from first to last, was the LORD's doing through his appointed servants. There is a beautiful redemptive-historical pattern here. What Moses began, Joshua completed; the work spanned two leaders but was one work of the one God. So too the work of redemption spans the old covenant and the new, the law and the gospel, finding its unity and completion in Christ. The first stones of the conquest were laid under Moses; the building was finished under Joshua — and the whole is the work of God.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei... Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second of the Mosaic conquests is Og king of Bashan, described as 'one of the remnant of the Rephaim' — that is, one of the giants, a man whose iron bedstead, Deuteronomy records, was over thirteen feet long (Deut. 3:11). Og was a fearsome figure, a giant king of a giant people, and his defeat under Moses was a monument to God's power over the mightiest of foes. The narrator twice calls Moses 'the servant of the LORD' — the highest title in Scripture — honoring the great mediator even as the focus shifts to Joshua's completion of the work. Moses gave the conquered eastern lands to Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh, the tribes who would later cross over armed to help their brothers (ch. 1, 4). Ferguson observed that Moses began what only Joshua could complete — a pattern rich with gospel meaning. The law, represented by Moses, could win victories and bring the people to the threshold, but the law could not bring them into the full inheritance; that required Joshua, whose name is Jesus. So Moses defeated Sihon and Og and settled the eastern tribes, but it was Joshua who led the people across the Jordan into the promised rest. Calvin notes that the careful record of Moses' victories preserves the memory of God's faithfulness through the whole journey. Two giants, Sihon and Og, fell under Moses; twenty-nine more kings would fall under Joshua. The work was one; the God was one; and the inheritance, begun under the law, was completed under grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–24 — The Twenty-Nine Kings Defeated Under Joshua
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter then lists the kings west of the Jordan defeated under Joshua — twenty-nine kings, each named with the refrain 'one,' from Jericho and Ai through the southern and northern cities. In all, thirty-one kings.
verseByVerse.theology: The roll call is a monument of praise to God's complete victory. The repeated 'one' tolls like a bell, testifying that not one king could stand before the people whose God fought for them. It fulfills the promise of 1:5 and foreshadows the final subjugation of every power beneath Christ's feet.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin noted the enumeration fixes God's faithfulness in Israel's memory. Sproul observed that the list is a preview of the last day, when every hostile power will be tallied among the defeated beneath the feet of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan... which Joshua gave to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments, in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb...
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator turns now to the conquests west of the Jordan, under Joshua. He surveys the full geographic sweep of the conquered territory — 'the hill country, the lowland, the Arabah, the slopes, the wilderness, and the Negeb' — every region of the land, from the mountains to the desert. The comprehensiveness is the point: the whole land, in all its varied terrain, has been given into Israel's hand. And the land is given 'to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments,' anticipating the great division of the inheritance that occupies the chapters to follow. This is the fulfillment, region by region, of the promise made to Abraham and renewed to Joshua. Calvin observes that the careful survey of all the conquered regions was meant to magnify the greatness of God's gift and the completeness of his faithfulness. There is a quiet doxology in this geography: every type of land, every region the eye could survey, now belongs to the people of God by the gift of God. Wenham notes that the listing of regions emphasizes the totality of the conquest west of the Jordan, setting the stage for the inheritance narratives. The God who promised has performed; the land in all its fullness is Israel's. And now the roll of the defeated kings begins — each one a testimony that no power in all that varied land could stand before the people whose God fought for them.

verseByVerse.quote: the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one; the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; the king of Eglon, one... the king of Makkedah, one...
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the roll call proper begins, and it has the cadence of a tolling bell: 'the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, one; the king of Jerusalem, one...' Each name is followed by that single, drumbeat word — 'one.' Each 'one' represents a king, a throne, a fortified city, a power that had stood against the advance of God's people — and each is now numbered among the defeated. The first names recall the great victories already narrated: Jericho, whose walls fell at a shout; Ai, where sin brought defeat and obedience brought triumph; the five kings of the southern coalition — Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon — who hid in the cave and ended with the feet of Israel's commanders on their necks. The repeated 'one' has a profound effect; it forces the reader to count, to dwell on each individual victory, to register the thoroughness of God's faithfulness. Calvin noted that the enumeration fixes God's faithfulness in Israel's memory, that they might never doubt his power. Not one of these kings was too strong; not one city could stand. The drumbeat 'one... one... one' is the sound of the promise of 1:5 being fulfilled before our eyes: 'No man shall be able to stand before you.' Each name is a trophy of grace, a monument to the truth that the LORD fights for his people. The list reads like a victory hymn, every 'one' a note of praise to the God who gave them all into Israel's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: ...the king of Tappuah, one... the king of Hazor, one... the king of Dor... the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
verseByVerse.commentary: The roll continues through the northern cities, including 'the king of Hazor, one' — the head of the great northern coalition whose chariots were burned and whose city was reduced to ashes. And the list reaches its grand total: 'in all, thirty-one kings.' Thirty-one times, the powers of Canaan rose against the people of God; thirty-one times, they fell. The number is precise, the record complete, the testimony unanswerable. Sproul observed that this list is a preview of the last day, when every hostile power will be tallied among the defeated beneath the feet of Christ. For the church, this roll call of vanquished kings points forward to the final muster of subdued powers. As thirty-one kings fell before Joshua, so every principality and power, every rule and authority, every enemy of the cross will be subdued beneath the feet of the greater Joshua, who 'must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet' (1 Cor. 15:25). On that day, the full list will be read — every power that ever raged against God's people, every spiritual force of wickedness, sin and death and hell itself — and after each, the word 'one,' tallied among the defeated, beneath the feet of Christ. The kingdoms of this world will become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever (Rev. 11:15). Thirty-one kings fell before Joshua; on the last day, every enemy will fall before Jesus. The roll call of Canaan's kings is a guarantee, written in history, of the final victory of the King of kings.

12.theology:
A Monument of God's Faithfulness. The roll call of thirty-one kings is a victory memorial, the precise record that not one power could stand before the people whose God fought for them. It fulfills the promise of 1:5 — 'No man shall be able to stand before you' — and fixes God's faithfulness in Israel's memory so they might never doubt his power.

One Continuous Work Through Two Mediators. The list joins the victories under Moses (east of Jordan) with those under Joshua (west of Jordan) into one divine work. What the law (Moses) began but could not complete, Joshua (Jesus) finished — a picture of redemption spanning old covenant and new, finding its unity and completion in Christ.

A Preview of Christ's Final Triumph. As thirty-one kings fell before Joshua, every hostile power — principality, authority, sin, death, and hell — will be subdued beneath the feet of the greater Joshua, who must reign until all his enemies are his footstool (1 Cor. 15:25; Rev. 11:15). The roll call is a guarantee, written in history, of the final victory of the King of kings.
12.examples:
Then: Israel looked back over the whole conquest and counted the cost of the enemy's defiance: thirty-one kings, thirty-one thrones, thirty-one cities that had stood against the people of God — and every one of them now numbered among the defeated. The list was a hymn of praise, each 'one' a testimony that the LORD fights for his people and no power can stand.

Now: We are surrounded by powers that seem invincible — the spiritual forces of evil, the entrenched kingdoms of this age, the enemies of sin and death. But the roll call of Canaan's kings assures us that every enemy of God is destined to be tallied among the defeated beneath the feet of Christ. The God who gave Joshua thirty-one kings will give his Son every enemy as a footstool. We fight not for victory but from victory, certain that the King of kings will subdue them all.

13.title: Land Still to Be Possessed
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess.<sup>2</sup>This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all those of the Geshurites<sup>3</sup>(from the Shihor, which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim,<sup>4</sup>in the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the boundary of the Amorites,<sup>5</sup>and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath,<sup>6</sup>all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, even all the Sidonians. I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh."<sup>8</sup>With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them:<sup>9</sup>from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon;<sup>10</sup>and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the boundary of the Ammonites;<sup>11</sup>and Gilead, and the region of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah;<sup>12</sup>all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); these Moses had struck and driven out.<sup>13</sup>Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day.<sup>14</sup>To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.<sup>15</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans.<sup>16</sup>So their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba;<sup>17</sup>with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon,<sup>18</sup>and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath,<sup>19</sup>and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley,<sup>20</sup>and Beth-peor, and the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth,<sup>21</sup>that is, all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated with the leaders of Midian, Evi and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land.<sup>22</sup>Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain.<sup>23</sup>And the border of the people of Reuben was the Jordan as a boundary. This was the inheritance of the people of Reuben, according to their clans with their cities and villages.<sup>24</sup>Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad, to the people of Gad, according to their clans.<sup>25</sup>Their territory was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer, which is east of Rabbah,<sup>26</sup>and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir,<sup>27</sup>and in the valley Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, having the Jordan as a boundary, to the lower end of the Sea of Chinnereth, eastward beyond the Jordan.<sup>28</sup>This is the inheritance of the people of Gad according to their clans, with their cities and villages.<sup>29</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was allotted to the half-tribe of the people of Manasseh according to their clans.<sup>30</sup>Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities,<sup>31</sup>and half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh for the half of the people of Machir according to their clans.<sup>32</sup>These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho.<sup>33</sup>But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.
13.overview:
With the conquest narrative complete, the book turns to the long division of the land — a section that modern readers are tempted to skim, but which is rich with theology and gospel. Chapter 13 opens with a poignant note: 'Now Joshua was old and advanced in years' (v. 1). The great warrior is aging, and the work is not finished. And God says the surprising thing: 'there remains yet very much land to possess.'

Here is one of the great tensions of the book, and indeed of the Christian life — the tension between the promised and the possessed, the 'already' and the 'not yet.' God had given Israel the whole land (1:3); the major powers had been broken; yet much remained to be taken. The inheritance was theirs by promise and by right, but it was not yet fully theirs in experience. So it is with the believer: in Christ we possess every spiritual blessing (Eph. 1:3), the victory is secured, and yet we are called to press on, to take possession of what is already ours, to 'work out' the salvation God works in us (Phil. 2:12–13). The land is given; the land must be taken.

The chapter then begins the allotment of the territory east of the Jordan, given by Moses to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. But the most precious verse in the chapter concerns the tribe of Levi, who received no territorial inheritance: 'the offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance' (v. 14), and again, 'the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance' (v. 33).

Here is the gospel jewel of the chapter. While the other tribes received land, the Levites received the LORD himself. They had no acreage, no borders, no fields — but they had God. And in the economy of grace, this was the richest inheritance of all. The Levites' portion is a picture of the deepest truth of salvation: the believer's true inheritance is not earthly possessions but God himself. 'The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup' (Ps. 16:5); 'whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you... God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever' (Ps. 73:25–26). To have God is to have everything; the Levites, landless, were the richest tribe of all.

sections.title: An Aging Leader and Unfinished Work
sections.commentary:
'Now Joshua was old and advanced in years.' The note is tender and sobering. The conqueror of Canaan, the man who crossed the Jordan and toppled Jericho, is now an old man, and God reminds him of his mortality even as he commissions the next phase of the work: 'there remains yet very much land to possess.' The reminder is gracious, not cruel — God is preparing Joshua to delegate, to ensure the work continues beyond his own life. The leader must learn that the kingdom of God does not depend on any one servant; the work is the LORD's, and he raises up others to carry it on.

God then catalogs the land that remains unconquered — the territory of the Philistines, the regions of the Geshurites, the land of the Sidonians, and more. The conquest had broken the back of organized Canaanite resistance, but pockets remained. And here the great tension surfaces: God says 'I myself will drive them out' (v. 6), yet Israel is commanded to 'allot the land' and possess it. Divine sovereignty and human responsibility stand side by side. God will drive out the nations; Israel must take possession.

This is the very paradox of the Christian life. The victory is won — Christ has triumphed over every power (Col. 2:15) — and yet we are called to press on, to take possession of the inheritance that is already ours. There is land yet to possess in every believer's life: territories of the heart not yet surrendered, sins not yet conquered, graces not yet attained. The promise that God himself will drive out the enemy does not excuse our passivity; it grounds our confidence as we labor. Calvin observed that God's promise to drive out the nations was meant to encourage Israel's efforts, not to replace them. The old warrior is told there is more to do — and so are we, until the inheritance is fully possessed and we enter the final rest.

sections.title: The Inheritance of the Eastern Tribes
sections.commentary:
The narrative turns to the territory east of the Jordan, already given by Moses to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh — the land of Sihon and Og, the kingdoms conquered before the crossing. The careful description of borders and cities anchors the inheritance in real geography. These tribes had chosen to settle in the east (Num. 32), and their portion is here formally recorded as part of the whole inheritance of Israel.

A sobering note intrudes in verse 13: 'the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day.' Here is the first hint of incomplete obedience, the seed of future trouble. The command was to dispossess the inhabitants fully; the failure to do so would, in later generations, become a snare — these remaining peoples would draw Israel into idolatry and compromise. What is left unconquered does not stay neutral; it becomes a thorn in the side and a snare to the soul (cf. Judg. 2:3).

There is a searching lesson here for the believer. The sins and compromises we fail to deal with decisively do not simply coexist peacefully with our faith; they become footholds for the enemy, snares that entangle us. The partial obedience that leaves Geshur and Maacath 'in the midst of Israel' is the pattern of every half-hearted sanctification that tolerates a cherished sin rather than driving it out. Ferguson noted that the unconquered pockets in the land mirror the unconquered pockets in the believer's heart — and that what we tolerate today will trouble us tomorrow. The inheritance is given fully; it must be possessed fully, lest the remnant we spare become the master we serve.

sections.title: The Levites' Portion: The LORD Himself
sections.commentary:
Twice in this chapter, framing the allotment of the eastern tribes, the narrator pauses on the tribe of Levi — and the words are among the most precious in all of Scripture. 'To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance' (v. 14); and again, 'But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them' (v. 33).

While every other tribe received fields, borders, and cities, Levi received no land at all. Humanly speaking, they were dispossessed, landless, with no territory to call their own. But in the economy of grace, theirs was the richest inheritance of all — for their inheritance was God himself. 'The LORD God of Israel is their inheritance.' They did not have land, but they had the Lord of the land; they did not have acreage, but they had the Almighty. And to have God is to have everything.

Here is the gospel jewel of the chapter, the truth that lifts the whole tedious-seeming division of land into glory. The believer's true inheritance is not earthly possession but God himself. The Psalmist had learned the Levite's secret: 'The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup' (Ps. 16:5); 'Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you... God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever' (Ps. 73:25–26). Keller often pressed this point: the deepest joy of salvation is not the gifts of God but the God of the gifts — not heaven's streets of gold but the face of Christ. The Levites, who seemed to have nothing, in truth possessed everything, because they possessed God. And this is the inheritance held out to every believer: 'all things are yours... and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's' (1 Cor. 3:21–23). The richest tribe in Israel was the one with no land, for they had the LORD — and so do all who are in Christ.

sections.title: The Detailed Allotments and the Faithfulness of God
sections.commentary:
The chapter records in careful detail the territories given to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh — city by city, border by border, region by region. To the modern reader these lists can seem tedious, a dry recitation of place-names long forgotten. But we must learn to read them with the eyes of faith, for they are, in fact, a monument to the faithfulness of God. Every name, every boundary, every allotted city is the fulfillment of a promise. God had sworn to give Israel the land, and here, in painstaking detail, the promise becomes property.

The very specificity is the point. God's promises are not vague generalities; they come to pass in concrete, particular, mappable reality. The land that was once only a word of promise to a wandering patriarch is now surveyed, divided, and possessed, tribe by tribe. Calvin observed that the careful recording of each tribe's inheritance was meant to assure Israel that God had fulfilled his word to the letter, leaving nothing of his promise unaccomplished.

There is great comfort here for the believer. The God who fulfilled his land-promise to Israel in such exact and particular detail is the God who will fulfill every promise made to us in Christ — not in vague outline but in glorious, concrete reality. The inheritance reserved for us is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven' (1 Pet. 1:4); and it is as certain, as particular, as surveyed and reserved, as the fields of Reuben and Gad. Not one word of all God's good promises will fail (cf. 21:45). The tedious-seeming lists of Joshua are, rightly read, a hymn to the meticulous faithfulness of a covenant-keeping God, who gives his people not approximations but the very substance of all he has sworn.

13.theology:
The Already and the Not Yet. God has given the whole land (1:3), yet 'there remains yet very much land to possess' (13:1). The inheritance is theirs by promise but not yet fully in experience. So the believer in Christ possesses every spiritual blessing (Eph. 1:3) and yet must press on to take possession, working out the salvation God works in (Phil. 2:12–13). The land is given; the land must be taken.

God Himself as the Believer's Inheritance. The Levites received no land, for 'the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance' (v. 33). The deepest truth of salvation is that our portion is not the gifts of God but God himself (Ps. 16:5; 73:25–26). To have God is to have everything; the landless tribe was the richest of all.

The Peril of Partial Obedience. The unconquered peoples left 'in the midst of Israel' (v. 13) foreshadow future snares. What we fail to drive out does not stay neutral but becomes a thorn and a trap. Half-hearted sanctification that tolerates a cherished sin will find that the spared remnant becomes a master.
13.examples:
Then: An aging Joshua was told that much land still remained to be possessed, even though God had already given it. Israel divided the inheritance tribe by tribe — and the tribe of Levi, given no land at all, received the richest portion of all: the LORD himself as their inheritance.

Now: The Christian lives in the tension of the already and the not yet — the victory is won in Christ, yet there is land in our hearts still to possess, sins still to drive out, graces still to take hold of. And we learn the Levite's secret: our true inheritance is not earthly possessions, not even heaven's gifts, but God himself. To have Christ is to have everything; like Levi, the believer who seems to have nothing in fact possesses all things, for the LORD is our portion forever.

14.title: Caleb's Inheritance
14.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit.<sup>2</sup>Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses for the nine and one-half tribes.<sup>3</sup>For Moses had given an inheritance to the two and one-half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them.<sup>4</sup>For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance.<sup>5</sup>The people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses; they allotted the land.<sup>6</sup>Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me.<sup>7</sup>I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart.<sup>8</sup>But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God.<sup>9</sup>And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'<sup>10</sup>And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old.<sup>11</sup>I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming.<sup>12</sup>So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."<sup>13</sup>Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance.<sup>14</sup>Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>15</sup>Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.
14.overview:
After the broad strokes of the eastern allotment, the narrative slows to focus, lovingly, on a single man — Caleb. And what a man he is. Eighty-five years old, he strides forward to claim his promised inheritance with the vigor of a warrior in his prime. Forty-five years earlier, Caleb had been one of the twelve spies sent to scout the land. Ten of them returned with a report of fear: 'the people are too strong; there are giants; we are like grasshoppers.' But two — Caleb and Joshua — brought back a report of faith: 'Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it' (Num. 13:30). For that faith, while a whole generation perished in the wilderness, God promised Caleb the very land his feet had trodden.

Now, after forty-five years of waiting — through the wilderness wandering, the crossing, and seven years of conquest — Caleb comes to collect on the promise. And his words ring with one of the great testimonies of persevering faith in all of Scripture: 'I wholly followed the LORD my God' (v. 8); 'I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me' (v. 11); 'Give me this hill country' (v. 12). Here is a faith that did not waver across forty-five years, that grew stronger with age, that asked not for the easy lowlands but for the hill country where the giants and the fortified cities still remained.

Caleb is the portrait of the believer who finishes well. He is not content to coast into old age on past victories; he wants the hardest territory, the place where the Anakim — the very giants that had terrified the ten spies — still dwelt. 'It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said' (v. 12). At eighty-five, his eye is not on retirement but on the giants yet to be conquered. The inheritance is worth fighting for, and Caleb means to fight.

The secret of Caleb's enduring strength is named four times in this chapter: he 'wholly followed the LORD' (vv. 8, 9, 14). Not partially, not when convenient, not until it grew hard — wholly. This is the faith that perseveres, that does not shrink back, that lays hold of the promise after decades of waiting. And Hebron, the city Caleb received, would become one of the most significant cities in Israel — the burial place of the patriarchs, the first capital of David. The man who wholly followed the LORD received an inheritance that endured. So shall all who follow Christ to the end receive the inheritance that does not fade.

sections.title: The Allotment Begins by Lot
sections.commentary:
The division of the land west of the Jordan begins, overseen by Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes. The inheritance is distributed 'by lot' (v. 2) — and this method is itself theologically significant. The casting of lots was understood in Israel not as chance but as the means by which God's sovereign will was made known: 'The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD' (Prov. 16:33). By dividing the land by lot, Israel acknowledged that the inheritance was God's gift, allotted according to his sovereign appointment, not human preference or power.

This guards against a profound danger: that the strong tribes would seize the best land and the weak be left with the scraps. Instead, God himself assigns each tribe its portion, so that every allotment is received as from his hand. The principle runs deep into the gospel. Our inheritance in Christ is not earned, not seized, not distributed according to our merit or strength, but given by the sovereign appointment of God, who 'apportions to each one individually as he wills' (1 Cor. 12:11). What we receive, we receive by grace and by God's sovereign choice.

The narrator also notes that the Levites received no land but cities to dwell in, and that the descendants of Joseph formed two tribes (Ephraim and Manasseh), preserving the number of twelve. Every detail reflects the careful, sovereign ordering of God over his people's inheritance. Calvin observed that the use of the lot taught Israel to receive their portion as God's gift, silencing all envy and contention. The land was not grasped but granted; not won by the strong but given by the Lord. And so it is with every blessing of salvation.

sections.title: Caleb's Testimony of Wholehearted Faith
sections.commentary:
Caleb steps forward, and his words are a window into forty-five years of persevering faith. He reminds Joshua of the day, long ago, when Moses sent the twelve spies from Kadesh-barnea. While ten brought back an evil report that melted the heart of the nation, Caleb says, 'I brought him word again as it was in my heart.' And then comes the refrain that defines his whole life: 'I wholly followed the LORD my God' (v. 8).

That word 'wholly' is the secret of Caleb. Not partially, not when it was convenient, not until the cost grew too high — but wholly, completely, without reservation. While the ten spies looked at the giants and trembled, Caleb looked at the giants and trusted God. While the nation wept and longed to return to Egypt, Caleb stood firm. And for that wholehearted faith, Moses had sworn an oath: 'the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God' (v. 9).

Here is the anatomy of a faith that endures. Caleb did not follow God halfheartedly, hedging his bets, keeping one eye on the giants and one on the exits. He followed wholly — and that wholeness sustained him through forty-five years of waiting for a promise. Ferguson observed that Caleb's wholehearted devotion is the mark of every believer who finishes well; the secret of perseverance is not a divided heart but a whole one, fixed on God. The world counsels moderation in religion, a balanced and managed devotion; but the faith that inherits the promise is the faith that follows the LORD wholly. 'Blessed are those who seek him with their whole heart' (Ps. 119:2). Caleb's testimony rebukes our halfheartedness and calls us to a faith that holds nothing back.

sections.title: Still Strong at Eighty-Five: Give Me This Mountain
sections.commentary:
Now comes one of the most stirring speeches in all the Old Testament. Caleb, eighty-five years old, stands before Joshua and declares: 'I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming' (v. 11). And then, the magnificent request: 'So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day... It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said' (v. 12).

Mark what Caleb asks for. Not the easy lowlands. Not a comfortable retirement plot. He asks for the hill country — the rugged highlands where the Anakim, the very giants that had terrified the ten spies forty-five years earlier, still dwelt in their fortified cities. At eighty-five, Caleb's eye is not on rest but on the giants yet to be conquered. 'Give me this mountain!' is the cry of a man who has not lost his fire, who refuses to coast into old age on past glories, who wants the hardest territory because that is where the LORD's power will be most displayed.

Here is the portrait of the believer who finishes well. Caleb attributes his enduring strength to God: it is the LORD who has 'kept me alive' (v. 10). And his confidence for the battle ahead rests not in his own vigor but in God's presence: 'It may be that the LORD will be with me.' Begg observed that Caleb models a faith that does not retire, that still hungers for the hardest assignments, that wants to die fighting giants rather than dozing in comfort. There is a holy ambition here that ought to mark the aging saint: not 'I have done enough,' but 'give me this mountain.' The Christian life is not meant to drift into spiritual retirement; like Caleb, we are to press on, to take new territory for Christ, to face our giants in the strength the LORD supplies, until our last breath. The inheritance is worth fighting for, and Caleb means to fight for it to the end.

sections.title: Hebron Given to Caleb
sections.commentary:
Joshua blesses Caleb and gives him Hebron as his inheritance — 'because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel' (v. 14). The refrain sounds for the third time in the chapter: he wholly followed the LORD. This is the inscription on Caleb's life, the reason for his reward. And the inheritance he receives is no ordinary plot of ground.

Hebron was one of the most significant places in all of Israel's history. It was where Abraham had pitched his tent and built an altar; it was the site of the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were buried — the burial place of the patriarchs. And it would become the first capital of King David, where he reigned for seven years before taking Jerusalem. The city of giants, which the ten spies had feared, becomes the inheritance of the man who wholly followed the LORD, and one of the holiest and most enduring cities in the nation.

The chapter closes with the note that 'the land had rest from war.' Caleb's faith, sustained across forty-five years and crowned at eighty-five, secures for him an inheritance that endures through the generations. There is a profound encouragement here for every believer who perseveres. The man who wholly followed the LORD received an inheritance that did not fade — an inheritance bound up with the patriarchs and the coming king, with the very line of the Messiah. So shall all who follow Christ to the end receive the inheritance that is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading' (1 Pet. 1:4). Calvin noted that Caleb's reward, given for his wholehearted devotion, demonstrates that God honors persevering faith and forgets none of the labor of love offered to him. Caleb fought his giants and won his mountain, and the city of his inheritance still stands as a monument to the God who rewards those who wholly follow him.

14.theology:
Wholehearted, Persevering Faith. Four times Caleb is said to have 'wholly followed the LORD' (vv. 8, 9, 14). The secret of a faith that endures across forty-five years and grows stronger with age is a whole heart, not a divided one. 'Blessed are those who seek him with their whole heart' (Ps. 119:2). God honors and rewards the faith that holds nothing back and does not shrink back.

The Believer Who Finishes Well. At eighty-five, Caleb cries 'give me this mountain' — not the easy lowlands but the hill country where the giants still dwell. The Christian life is not meant to drift into spiritual retirement; we press on to take new territory for Christ, facing our giants in the strength God supplies, until the end. His confidence rests not in his own vigor but in God's presence: 'It may be that the LORD will be with me.'

An Inheritance by Sovereign Grace. The land is divided by lot, acknowledging that the inheritance is God's sovereign gift, not human achievement (Prov. 16:33). Caleb's enduring inheritance at Hebron, bound up with the patriarchs and the coming king, points to the imperishable inheritance reserved in heaven for all who follow Christ to the end (1 Pet. 1:4).
14.examples:
Then: Forty-five years after standing alone with Joshua against ten faithless spies, Caleb came at eighty-five to claim his promise — not asking for comfort but crying 'give me this mountain,' the very hill country where the giants still dwelt. Because he had wholly followed the LORD, he received Hebron, the city of the patriarchs, an inheritance that endured.

Now: Caleb rebukes our halfhearted, hedge-betting religion and our temptation to spiritual retirement. The faith that inherits the promise is the faith that follows the LORD wholly and finishes well — that wants the hardest assignments, faces its giants in God's strength, and presses on to the end. The God who rewarded Caleb's persevering faith with an enduring inheritance will give all who wholly follow Christ the inheritance that never fades.

15.title: The Allotment of Judah
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south.<sup>2</sup>And their south boundary ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward.<sup>3</sup>It goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, turns about to Karka,<sup>4</sup>passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Brook of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary.<sup>5</sup>And the east boundary is the Salt Sea, to the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary on the north side runs from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan.<sup>6</sup>And the boundary goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes along north of Beth-arabah. And the boundary goes up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.<sup>7</sup>And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the valley. And the boundary passes along to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel.<sup>8</sup>Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem). And the boundary goes up to the top of the mountain that lies over against the Valley of Hinnom, on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary extends from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and from there to the cities of Mount Ephron. Then the boundary bends around to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim).<sup>10</sup>And the boundary circles west of Baalah to Mount Seir, passes along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), and goes down to Beth-shemesh and passes along by Timnah.<sup>11</sup>The boundary goes out to the shoulder of the hill north of Ekron, then the boundary bends around to Shikkeron and passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. Then the boundary comes to an end at the sea.<sup>12</sup>And the west boundary was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the boundary around the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>13</sup>According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron (Arba was the father of Anak).<sup>14</sup>And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.<sup>15</sup>And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher.<sup>16</sup>And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife."<sup>17</sup>And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife.<sup>18</sup>When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?"<sup>19</sup>She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.<sup>20</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>21</sup>The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,<sup>22</sup>Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah,<sup>23</sup>Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan,<sup>24</sup>Ziph, Telem, Bealoth,<sup>25</sup>Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor),<sup>26</sup>Amam, Shema, Moladah,<sup>27</sup>Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet,<sup>28</sup>Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah,<sup>29</sup>Baalah, Iim, Ezem,<sup>30</sup>Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah,<sup>31</sup>Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah,<sup>32</sup>Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine cities with their villages.<sup>33</sup>And in the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah,<sup>34</sup>Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam,<sup>35</sup>Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah,<sup>36</sup>Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, Gederothaim: fourteen cities with their villages.<sup>37</sup>Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad,<sup>38</sup>Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel,<sup>39</sup>Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon,<sup>40</sup>Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish,<sup>41</sup>Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages.<sup>42</sup>Libnah, Ether, Ashan,<sup>43</sup>Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib,<sup>44</sup>Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages.<sup>45</sup>Ekron, with its towns and its villages;<sup>46</sup>from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages.<sup>47</sup>Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea with its coastline.<sup>48</sup>And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,<sup>49</sup>Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir),<sup>50</sup>Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim,<sup>51</sup>Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages.<sup>52</sup>Arab, Dumah, Eshan,<sup>53</sup>Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah,<sup>54</sup>Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior: nine cities with their villages.<sup>55</sup>Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah,<sup>56</sup>Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah,<sup>57</sup>Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah: ten cities with their villages.<sup>58</sup>Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor,<sup>59</sup>Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages.<sup>60</sup>Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah: two cities with their villages.<sup>61</sup>In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah,<sup>62</sup>Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages.<sup>63</sup>But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
15.overview:
Judah receives the first and largest allotment west of the Jordan — fitting for the royal tribe, the tribe of the lion, from whom the kings of Israel and ultimately the King of kings would come. The detailed description of Judah's borders and cities fills the chapter, but woven into the geography are two arresting human stories and one sobering failure, each carrying gospel weight.

First, Caleb appears again — the man who wholly followed the LORD. Having received Hebron, he now drives out the three sons of Anak, the giants, fulfilling his bold request of the previous chapter (vv. 13–14). The faith that asked for the mountain now conquers the giants. Caleb's example continues to shine: the believer who trusts God not only claims the hard territory but takes it.

Second comes the charming account of Othniel and Achsah (vv. 15–19). Caleb offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captures Kiriath-sepher; Othniel rises to the challenge and wins both the city and the bride. Then Achsah, newly married, comes to her father with a bold request: 'Give me a blessing... give me also springs of water.' And Caleb gives her the upper and lower springs. It is a small domestic scene, but it pulses with a great spiritual principle: the children of those who wholly follow the LORD are encouraged to ask boldly for blessing, and a good father delights to give springs of living water to those who ask.

Third, the chapter ends on a note of failure: 'the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out' (v. 63). The very tribe that would one day give Israel its king could not take the city that would become the holy city, the city of David, the city of God. This unconquered Jebusite stronghold would wait until David's day to fall — a reminder that some victories are reserved for a greater son of Judah. The chapter thus holds together triumph and incompleteness, faith and failure, the giants conquered and the city unconquered, pointing always forward to the King who would finish what the tribe of Judah began.

sections.title: The Borders of Judah
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with the meticulous description of Judah's territory — its southern boundary along the wilderness of Zin and the Dead Sea, its eastern boundary the Salt Sea, its northern boundary running near Jerusalem, its western boundary the Great Sea (the Mediterranean). Judah received the largest and most prominent allotment, the heartland of the southern hill country, fitting for the royal tribe.

To the modern reader, these boundary descriptions seem dry, but they are freighted with meaning. Judah was the tribe of the lion (Gen. 49:9), the tribe to whom the scepter belonged, the tribe from which 'Shiloh' — the coming ruler — would come (Gen. 49:10). From Judah would come David, and from David's line, in the fullness of time, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Jesus Christ (Rev. 5:5). The careful staking out of Judah's borders is, in the deep design of God, the marking out of the territory of the royal line, the land that would cradle the kings and finally the King.

The precision of the boundaries also testifies, once more, to the faithfulness of God. The land promised to Abraham is now surveyed and assigned in concrete, particular detail. Calvin observed that the careful recording of Judah's borders served to assure the tribe of its rightful and divinely appointed inheritance. There is a quiet glory in this geography: these are the hills where David would keep sheep, where Bethlehem would cradle the Messiah, where the events of redemption would unfold. The borders of Judah are the borders of the land of the King — and they were measured out by the sovereign hand of God.

sections.title: Caleb Conquers the Giants
sections.commentary:
Within Judah's territory lay Hebron, given to Caleb. And now the narrator records the fulfillment of Caleb's bold request from the previous chapter: 'Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak' (v. 14). The man who at eighty-five had cried 'give me this mountain,' knowing the giants still dwelt there, now drives those very giants out.

This is the proof of Caleb's faith in action. It is one thing to ask boldly for the hard territory; it is another to actually take it. Caleb does both. The giants who had terrified the ten faithless spies forty-five years earlier — 'we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers' (Num. 13:33) — fall before the man who wholly followed the LORD. What unbelief had declared impossible, faith accomplishes. The difference, as always, was never the size of the giants but the object of one's trust.

There is a stirring lesson here for every believer. The giants in our lives — the besetting sins, the entrenched fears, the obstacles that seem insurmountable — are not too great for the God who fights for his people. Caleb did not merely survive into old age; he conquered giants in his old age. His faith was not nostalgic but active, not content to remember past victories but eager to win new ones. Ferguson noted that Caleb's conquest of the Anakim demonstrates that the promises of God are not merely to be admired but to be acted upon; faith that asks for the mountain must also climb it. The believer who trusts God claims the hard territory — and then, in God's strength, takes it. Caleb's giants fell; and so, in Christ, will ours.

sections.title: Othniel, Achsah, and the Springs of Blessing
sections.commentary:
Now comes one of the most charming and instructive vignettes in the book. Caleb, still the warrior-father, offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever will capture Kiriath-sepher (Debir). Othniel, Caleb's younger relative — who would later become Israel's first judge — rises to the challenge, takes the city, and wins the bride. Here is a young man cut from Caleb's cloth, a man of faith and valor, joined to a family that wholly followed the LORD.

But the heart of the scene is Achsah's bold request. Newly married and settled in the dry land of the Negeb, she comes to her father and says, 'Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water' (v. 19). She is not content with arid land; she wants the springs that make the land fruitful. And Caleb, the good father, gives her not one but two: 'he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.'

This small domestic exchange pulses with a great spiritual principle. The children of those who wholly follow the LORD are encouraged to ask boldly for blessing — and a good father delights to give. Achsah did not settle for the bare minimum; she asked for springs of living water, and she received abundantly. Begg observed that Achsah's boldness in asking is a model of faith's confidence before a generous God: 'You do not have, because you do not ask' (James 4:2); 'Ask, and it will be given to you' (Matt. 7:7). The springs of water point us to the living water Christ gives — 'a spring of water welling up to eternal life' (John 4:14). We serve a Father who is not stingy but lavish, who gives upper springs and lower springs, who delights to bless the bold requests of his children. Like Achsah, we are invited to come to our Father and ask for the springs.

sections.title: The Cities of Judah and the Unconquered Jebusites
sections.commentary:
The remainder of the chapter catalogs the many cities of Judah — in the Negeb, the lowland, the hill country, and the wilderness — a long list testifying to the rich and extensive inheritance of the royal tribe. Among them is Bethlehem, the little town where, centuries later, the Son of David would be born. The land of Judah was crowded with the future of redemption.

But the chapter ends on a sobering note of failure: 'But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day' (v. 63). The mighty tribe of Judah, conqueror of giants, could not take Jerusalem. The city that would become the holy city, the city of David, the place where the temple would stand and where the Messiah would be crucified and rise — that city remained in enemy hands.

This unconquered stronghold carries deep significance. Some victories were reserved for a greater son of Judah. It was David — the man after God's own heart, the king from Judah's line — who would finally take Jerusalem and make it the city of God (2 Sam. 5:6–9). Judah began the conquest of the land but could not finish the taking of the holy city; that awaited the king. And in this we see a pattern that runs to the very heart of the gospel: there are victories no one can win except the King himself. The greater Son of David, the Lion of Judah, would accomplish the conquest that no one else could — the conquest of sin, death, and hell, the taking of the true city of God. Calvin observed that the failure to take Jerusalem was a chastisement for incomplete obedience, yet also part of God's design to reserve that conquest for David. The chapter thus ends with triumph and incompleteness held together — the giants conquered, the holy city not yet taken — pointing always forward to the King who alone could finish the work.

15.theology:
The Territory of the King. Judah receives the first and largest allotment, the land of the royal tribe, the Lion from whom David and ultimately Christ would come (Gen. 49:9–10; Rev. 5:5). The borders of Judah are the borders of the land that would cradle the kings and the King; the geography is the stage of redemption, measured out by God's sovereign hand.

Bold Faith and a Generous Father. Achsah's bold request — 'give me also springs of water' — and Caleb's lavish reply (upper and lower springs) model the confidence God invites in his children. 'Ask, and it will be given' (Matt. 7:7). Our Father delights to give the springs of living water (John 4:14) to those who ask boldly, refusing to settle for arid land.

Victories Reserved for the King. Judah conquered giants but 'could not drive out' the Jebusites from Jerusalem (v. 63); that conquest awaited David. Some victories belong to the King alone — pointing to the greater Son of David, the Lion of Judah, who alone could conquer sin, death, and hell, and take the true city of God.
15.examples:
Then: Judah, the royal tribe, received the largest inheritance; Caleb drove out the giants he had asked to face; Achsah boldly asked her father for springs and received them in abundance. Yet even mighty Judah could not take Jerusalem — that victory was reserved for a coming king.

Now: Caleb teaches us to take the giants we trust God to defeat; Achsah teaches us to ask our Father boldly for the springs of living water, refusing to settle for less than his abundant blessing. And the unconquered Jebusite stronghold reminds us that the decisive victories — over sin, death, and hell — belong to the King alone. We do not save ourselves; we look to the Lion of Judah, the Son of David, who took the city no one else could take and won the war no one else could win.

16.title: The Allotment of Ephraim
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel.<sup>2</sup>Then going from Bethel to Luz, it passes along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites.<sup>3</sup>Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, then to Gezer, and it ends at the sea.<sup>4</sup>The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.<sup>5</sup>The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon,<sup>6</sup>and the boundary goes from there to the sea. On the north is Michmethath. Then on the east the boundary turns around toward Taanath-shiloh and passes along beyond it on the east to Janoah,<sup>7</sup>then it goes down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, and touches Jericho, ending at the Jordan.<sup>8</sup>From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea. Such is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Ephraim by their clans,<sup>9</sup>together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.<sup>10</sup>However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
16.overview:
The allotment now turns to the descendants of Joseph — Ephraim and Manasseh — who together formed a double portion in fulfillment of Jacob's blessing on Joseph's two sons (Gen. 48). Ephraim, though descended from the younger of Joseph's sons, received the prominence Jacob had prophesied when he crossed his hands to bless Ephraim above Manasseh (Gen. 48:14, 19). Chapter 16 describes Ephraim's territory in the central hill country, the heartland of the future northern kingdom.

Ephraim was a tribe of great significance. Joshua himself was an Ephraimite. Shiloh, where the tabernacle would rest, lay in Ephraim's territory. The tribe would grow so dominant that 'Ephraim' became a name for the entire northern kingdom in the prophets. The allotment to this leading tribe of Joseph is recorded with care, marking out the territory of a people destined for prominence — and, tragically, for later apostasy.

But the chapter ends, like the Judah allotment before it, on a note of incomplete obedience: 'they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer... but have been made to do forced labor' (v. 10). Rather than driving out the inhabitants as God commanded, Ephraim subjected them to forced labor — a compromise that traded obedience for economic advantage. The Canaanites who should have been removed were instead kept as a labor force, dwelling 'in the midst of Ephraim to this day.'

This compromise carries a sobering lesson. The failure to drive out the Canaanites — choosing convenience and profit over obedience — would prove to be a spiritual snare for generations. What Ephraim tolerated for economic gain became a corrupting presence in their midst. The pattern of half-hearted obedience, of tolerating what God commanded to be removed because it seems useful or profitable, is the seed of future ruin. The believer is warned: the sin we domesticate and put to 'forced labor' in our lives, thinking we have it under control, will in time master us.

sections.title: The Territory of the House of Joseph
sections.commentary:
The allotment to the descendants of Joseph is introduced, covering the territory that would be divided between Ephraim and Manasseh. The double portion given to Joseph's line fulfills the ancient blessing of Jacob, who adopted Joseph's two sons as his own and granted Joseph, through them, a double inheritance among the tribes (Gen. 48:5). Thus Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers, receives in his descendants the firstborn's double portion — a quiet testimony to the providence of God, who turned the evil intended against Joseph into great good (Gen. 50:20).

There is gospel resonance in this. Joseph, the rejected and betrayed brother who became the savior of his family, is a striking type of Christ — rejected by his own, yet exalted to save. And the double portion given to his sons reflects the abundant inheritance that flows from the exalted Savior to those who belong to him. The God who exalted the rejected Joseph and multiplied his inheritance is the God who exalted the rejected Christ and pours out an abundant inheritance upon his people.

The careful marking of the borders, from Jericho through Bethel and beyond, anchors the inheritance in real territory. Calvin observed that the fulfillment of Jacob's blessing on Joseph's sons, generations after it was spoken, testifies to the unfailing faithfulness of God to his word. What was promised on a deathbed in Egypt comes to pass in the division of Canaan. The God who keeps his word across generations is faithful still.

sections.title: The Borders of Ephraim
sections.commentary:
Ephraim's specific borders are described, encompassing the central hill country — a region of great strategic and spiritual importance. This was the heartland of Israel, the area where Shiloh would house the tabernacle, where Shechem witnessed the covenant renewals, where Joshua the Ephraimite would be buried. The tribe of Ephraim, though descended from Joseph's younger son, had been granted preeminence by Jacob's prophetic blessing, when the dying patriarch crossed his hands to put his right hand on Ephraim (Gen. 48:14–19).

This pattern — the younger preferred over the elder — runs throughout Genesis and into the gospel: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Ephraim over Manasseh. It is the recurring testimony that God's blessing flows not according to human convention or natural right, but according to his sovereign and gracious choice. 'The older shall serve the younger' (Rom. 9:12). God delights to overturn the expectations of men, to choose the unlikely, to elevate the lesser — that the glory might be his alone.

The note that some of Ephraim's cities lay within Manasseh's territory (v. 9) reflects the intertwining of the two Joseph tribes. The borders here are not perfectly tidy, a reminder that the inheritance of God's people is bound together, the tribes interwoven, no one tribe isolated from the others. Wenham notes the complexity of the Joseph allotments, reflecting their close kinship and shared inheritance. The territory of Ephraim, marked out in the heart of the land, was the stage for much of Israel's history — for good and, later, for grievous ill.

sections.title: The Compromise at Gezer
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends with a verse that sounds a warning note for the whole subsequent history of Israel: 'However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.' Here is compromise dressed up as practicality. God had commanded the Canaanites to be driven out; Ephraim, rather than obey, found a more profitable arrangement — they subjected the Canaanites to forced labor, turning disobedience into an economic asset.

This is one of the most instructive failures in the book. The temptation was not to open rebellion but to a 'reasonable' compromise: why destroy a useful labor force? Why not let the Canaanites stay and put them to work? It seemed sensible, even shrewd. But it was disobedience, and it traded the long-term spiritual health of the nation for short-term economic advantage. The Canaanites who should have been removed remained 'in the midst of Ephraim,' and in time their idolatry and their ways would corrupt the tribe and the nation.

Here is a sobering lesson for every believer. We are forever tempted to domesticate our sins rather than destroy them — to keep some cherished compromise 'under control,' to put our pet sin to 'forced labor,' imagining we have mastered it and made it useful. But sin tolerated is sin enthroned in waiting. What we fail to drive out will not stay subdued; the Canaanite we keep as a servant will become a master. Ferguson observed that Ephraim's compromise at Gezer is the pattern of every believer who tolerates a sin for the sake of convenience or gain — and finds, too late, that the tolerated thing has become a corrupting power. The command of God was clear and costly: drive them out. The compromise was easy and profitable: put them to work. And the compromise, repeated across the tribes, would one day undo the nation. Better to obey God fully, however costly, than to keep a profitable sin that will, in the end, destroy us.

16.theology:
God's Sovereign Choice. Ephraim, the younger of Joseph's sons, receives preeminence by Jacob's crossed-hands blessing (Gen. 48), continuing the Genesis pattern of the younger preferred over the elder. God's blessing flows not by human convention but by his sovereign, gracious choice (Rom. 9:12), that the glory might be his alone.

Joseph as a Type of Christ. The double portion given to Joseph's line reflects the abundant inheritance flowing from the rejected-then-exalted savior. Joseph, betrayed by his brothers yet exalted to save them, foreshadows Christ, rejected by his own yet exalted to pour out an abundant inheritance on his people.

The Danger of Profitable Compromise. Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites but 'made them do forced labor' (v. 10) — disobedience disguised as shrewd practicality. Sin domesticated and put to 'forced labor' is not mastered but enthroned in waiting. What we fail to drive out will become our master; profitable compromise is the seed of future ruin.
16.examples:
Then: Ephraim, the leading tribe of Joseph, received its inheritance in the heart of the land — but rather than drive out the Canaanites of Gezer as God commanded, they put them to forced labor, trading obedience for economic advantage. The compromise left a corrupting presence in their midst for generations.

Now: We are tempted to the same shrewd compromise — to domesticate our sins rather than destroy them, to keep some cherished disobedience 'under control' because it seems useful or profitable. But sin tolerated is sin enthroned in waiting; the Canaanite kept as a servant becomes a master. Better to obey God fully and costly than to keep a profitable sin that will, in the end, destroy us.

17.title: The Allotment of Manasseh and the Complaint of Joseph
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war.<sup>2</sup>And allotments were made to the rest of the people of Manasseh by their clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh the son of Joseph, by their clans.<sup>3</sup>Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>4</sup>They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father.<sup>5</sup>Thus there fell to Manasseh ten portions, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is on the other side of the Jordan,<sup>6</sup>because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead was allotted to the rest of the people of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>The territory of Manasseh reached from Asher to Michmethath, which is east of Shechem. Then the boundary goes along southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah.<sup>8</sup>The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the boundary of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary went down to the brook Kanah. These cities, to the south of the brook, among the cities of Manasseh, belong to Ephraim. Then the boundary of Manasseh goes on the north side of the brook and ends at the sea,<sup>10</sup>the land to the south being Ephraim's and that to the north being Manasseh's, with the sea forming its boundary. On the north Asher is reached, and on the east Issachar.<sup>11</sup>Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages; the third is Naphath.<sup>12</sup>Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land.<sup>13</sup>Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.<sup>14</sup>Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?"<sup>15</sup>And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you."<sup>16</sup>The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel."<sup>17</sup>Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only,<sup>18</sup>but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."
17.overview:
The allotment of the half-tribe of Manasseh west of the Jordan is recorded, including a notable feature: the daughters of Zelophehad receive an inheritance among their father's brothers (vv. 3–6), fulfilling the ruling God had given through Moses (Num. 27). In a patriarchal culture, this is a remarkable testimony to God's justice and care for the vulnerable — daughters with no brothers are not left without an inheritance but are granted a portion among the tribes. The God who divides the land is a God of justice, who provides for the marginalized.

But the heart of the chapter is the complaint of the house of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) and Joshua's bracing response.
